119878.e: Peat mosses keep growing at the top while they die off below. In the wet, acidic bog, the remains hardly decompose and become peat.
119878.m: Peat mosses build up raised bogs.

119879.q: Why are dried moss specimens in a herbarium easy to identify?
a: They swell up again in water and show their features
They keep their colour unchanged for ever when dry
They are identified only by their smell
119879.e: Mosses are poikilohydric and take up water again even after years. When softened, their leaves and cells show their shape under the microscope almost as if fresh.
119879.m: Dried mosses swell up again in water.

119880.q: Which moss makes its protonema shimmer golden green in cave entrances and rock crevices?
119880.e: The protonema of goblin gold (Schistostega pennata) has lens-shaped cells. They focus the weak light onto the chloroplasts and partly reflect it back.
119880.m: Goblin gold shimmers thanks to lens-shaped cells.

119881.q: Which soil animals are often studied as bioindicators of soil quality and pollution?
119881.e: Earthworms live in close contact with the soil and take it in with their food. Their number, species diversity and pollutant levels show the condition of the soil.
119881.m: Earthworms indicate the condition of a soil.

119980.q: In which lobe of the brain is the prefrontal cortex?
119980.e: The prefrontal cortex forms the very front part of the frontal lobe, directly behind the forehead.
119980.m: The prefrontal cortex is at the very front of the frontal lobe.

119981.q: Which abilities are mainly linked to the prefrontal cortex?
119981.e: The prefrontal cortex controls the so-called executive functions. These include planning actions, making decisions and holding back sudden impulses.
119981.m: The prefrontal cortex is the brain's planning and control centre.

119982.q: Which railway worker survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe in 1848 and afterwards changed a lot in personality?
119982.e: During a blast, an iron rod pierced Phineas Gage's skull. He survived, but was afterwards described as uncontrolled and erratic, which pointed to the role of the frontal lobe in social behaviour.
119982.m: The case of Phineas Gage showed that the frontal lobe helps shape personality.

119983.q: According to current knowledge, up to roughly what age does the prefrontal cortex mature?
119983.e: The prefrontal cortex is one of the brain regions that mature last. The rebuilding processes last into young adulthood, until about the mid-20s.
119983.m: The prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain areas to finish developing.

119984.q: Which memory system, which holds and works on information for a short time, depends strongly on the prefrontal cortex?
119984.e: In working memory, information is kept active for seconds, for example during mental arithmetic. Imaging studies show strong activity in the prefrontal cortex at such times.
119984.m: During mental arithmetic, working memory is busy in the frontal lobe.

119985.q: Why is leucotomy, in which nerve pathways to the frontal lobe were cut, now seen as a dark chapter of medicine?
a: It often changed personality and drive severely and permanently
It was too expensive for hospitals
119985.e: The operation made many patients calmer, but often also listless and without drive. Despite a Nobel Prize for Egas Moniz in 1949, it is no longer used today.
119985.m: Leucotomy is now seen as a warning example in medical history.

119986.q: Which messenger is especially important for the prefrontal cortex and is boosted by ADHD medicines such as methylphenidate?
119986.e: Methylphenidate blocks the reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline. This raises their concentration in the gap between the nerve cells, which can improve attention and impulse control.
119986.m: Methylphenidate increases the amount of dopamine between nerve cells.

119987.q: What is the part of the prefrontal cortex directly above the eye sockets that evaluates rewards called?
119987.e: Orbit is the technical term for the eye socket. The orbitofrontal cortex lies above it and is involved in decisions and in evaluating rewards.
119987.m: The orbitofrontal cortex lies above the eye sockets.

119988.q: Where does the hippocampus get its name from?
a: From the name of its discoverer
From the Latin word for memory
119988.e: Hippocampus is the Greek-Latin name for the seahorse. The curved part of the brain looks like this animal.
119988.m: The hippocampus looks like a seahorse.

119989.q: In which lobe of the brain is the hippocampus?
119989.e: The hippocampus lies on both sides in the inner part of the temporal lobe.
119989.m: The hippocampus sits deep in the temporal lobe.

119990.q: What did the famous patient “H. M.”, who had parts of both hippocampi removed in 1953, show?
a: The hippocampus is needed to form new memories
Without a hippocampus you can no longer see
119990.e: After the operation, H. M. could no longer remember new experiences permanently. Old memories and skills, however, were largely kept.
119990.m: The patient H. M. showed that the hippocampus stores new memories.

119991.q: Which technical term for part of the hippocampus recalls the ram's horns of an Egyptian god?
119991.e: The main part of the hippocampus is called cornu Ammonis, meaning Ammon's horn. Its curled shape recalls the ram's horn of the god Amun.
119991.m: Because of its shape, the hippocampus is also called Ammon's horn.

119992.q: Which cells in the hippocampus, whose discovery earned John O'Keefe the Nobel Prize in 2014, are active in particular places?
119992.e: Place cells fire when an animal is at a particular spot in space. They form a kind of inner map.
119992.m: Place cells in the hippocampus form an inner map.

119993.q: During which phase are memories transferred from the hippocampus to the cerebral cortex especially intensely?
119993.e: In deep sleep, content stored in the hippocampus during the day is replayed. This gradually consolidates it in the cerebral cortex.
119993.m: In deep sleep the brain consolidates what it has learnt.

119994.q: What is meant by adult neurogenesis, which is studied in the hippocampus?
a: The formation of new nerve cells in adulthood
The death of nerve cells in old age
The development of the brain in the embryo
The healing of bones after a fracture
119994.e: For a long time it was believed that no new nerve cells form in the adult brain. New formation has been found in the hippocampus, but how much happens in humans is disputed.
119994.m: New nerve cells can form in the hippocampus even in adulthood.

119995.q: Which sign is typical when the hippocampus is damaged early in Alzheimer's?
119995.e: In Alzheimer's, the hippocampus is one of the first brain regions affected. That is why gaps in short-term memory are noticed first.
119995.m: Alzheimer's damages the hippocampus early and with it remembering new things.

119996.q: What does the Greek name amygdala mean?
119996.e: Amygdala is the Greek word for almond. The structure is an almond-shaped group of nuclei in the temporal lobe.
119996.m: Because of its shape, the amygdala is named after the almond.

119997.q: Which feeling is the amygdala most closely linked with?
119997.e: The amygdala checks stimuli for danger in a flash and triggers fear and startle reactions. However, it is also involved in other feelings.
119997.m: The amygdala raises the alarm when there is danger.

119998.q: What did the patient “S. M.”, whose two amygdalae had been destroyed by a rare disease, show?
119998.e: S. M. had the rare Urbach-Wiethe syndrome. Even in dangerous situations she showed hardly any fear, which proves the role of the amygdala in fear.
119998.m: Without the amygdala, the feeling of fear is largely missing.

119999.q: Which functional system of the brain is the amygdala counted as part of?
119999.e: The limbic system processes feelings and is involved in memory. The amygdala and hippocampus, among others, are counted as part of it.
119999.m: The amygdala belongs to the limbic system of feelings.

120000.q: Which brain structure works closely with the amygdala in fear to store memories of dangerous experiences?
120000.e: The amygdala gives memories their emotional colour, the hippocampus stores the context. That is why frightening experiences are often remembered especially well.
120000.m: The amygdala and hippocampus store fear memories together.

120001.q: Why do you often get a fright even before you have consciously recognised a danger?
a: A fast nerve pathway reports stimuli directly to the amygdala
The cerebellum recognises dangers faster than the eyes
The muscles react entirely without the brain
The heart first sends a warning signal to the brain
120001.e: Some sensory stimuli reach the amygdala on a short, rough route, others more slowly through the cerebral cortex. That is why you flinch before you know exactly what is going on.
120001.m: The amygdala reacts to danger before we consciously recognise it.

120002.q: Which form of learning, in which a neutral stimulus is linked with an unpleasant event, depends especially on the amygdala?
120002.e: In fear conditioning, for example, a tone alone causes fear after being paired several times with a frightening stimulus. Without a working amygdala, this link can hardly be made.
120002.m: The amygdala learns which stimuli signal danger.

120003.q: Which stress hormone does the adrenal cortex release when the amygdala starts a hormone chain through the hypothalamus and pituitary during stress?
120003.e: The amygdala activates the hypothalamus, which stimulates the adrenal cortex through the pituitary. This then releases the stress hormone cortisol.
120003.m: Under stress, the amygdala starts a hormone chain that reaches the adrenal cortex.

120004.q: What is the main job of the thalamus?
a: To filter sensory information and pass it on to the cerebral cortex
To learn the fine-tuning of movements
120004.e: The thalamus is a relay station: almost all sensory signals pass through it to the cerebral cortex. That is why it is also called the “gateway to consciousness”.
120004.m: The thalamus is the gateway to consciousness.

120005.q: Which part of the brain does the thalamus belong to?
120005.e: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon. It lies deep inside between the cerebrum and the brainstem.
120005.m: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon.

120006.q: Which is the only sense that is not mainly passed to the cerebral cortex through the thalamus?
120006.e: Smell information goes from the olfactory bulb directly to the olfactory cortex without first being relayed in the thalamus. All other senses pass through the thalamus.
120006.m: Only smells take the direct route past the thalamus relay station.

120007.q: Through which brain structure do signals from the retina reach the visual cortex in the occipital lobe?
120007.e: The fibres of the optic nerve are relayed in a nucleus of the thalamus, the lateral geniculate body. From there the visual pathways run to the visual cortex.
120007.m: Visual information is also relayed in the thalamus.

120008.q: In a rare prion disease, mainly the thalamus is destroyed. Which ability do people affected increasingly lose?
120008.e: In fatal familial insomnia, misfolded prions mainly destroy nuclei of the thalamus. The people affected increasingly lose the ability to sleep.
120008.m: Without an intact thalamus, sleep can break down.

120009.q: What does the Greek word “thalamos” mean?
120009.e: In Ancient Greek, thalamos meant an inner room or a bedroom. The name suits its hidden position deep in the brain.
120009.m: The thalamus is named after an inner chamber.

120010.q: What can occur on the opposite side of the body after a stroke in the thalamus?
a: Severe pain that is hard to treat
A loss of the sense of smell
120010.e: In thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome), people suffer severe pain on the opposite side of the body after a thalamic stroke, because the thalamus processes sensory signals wrongly.
120010.m: Damage to the thalamus can cause agonising pain.

120011.q: Which method can reduce severe shaking of the hands by having an electrode in the thalamus influence nerve cells electrically?
120011.e: In deep brain stimulation, a thin electrode is placed in a nucleus of the thalamus. Weak electrical pulses can clearly reduce severe shaking, for example in essential tremor.
120011.m: Electrodes in the thalamus can reduce severe shaking.

120012.q: What are the basal ganglia mainly responsible for?
120012.e: The basal ganglia are groups of nuclei deep in the cerebrum. In loops with the cerebral cortex, they promote intended movements and hold back unwanted ones.
120012.m: The basal ganglia choose which movement is carried out.

120013.q: Where in the brain are the basal ganglia?
a: On the surface of the cerebellum
120013.e: The basal ganglia are clusters of nerve cells deep in the cerebrum, below the cortex. They are closely linked through loops with the cerebral cortex and the thalamus.
120013.m: The basal ganglia lie deep in the cerebrum.

120014.q: For which disease of the basal ganglia is deep brain stimulation with implanted electrodes often used?
120014.e: In deep brain stimulation, an electrode is placed permanently in a nucleus of the basal ganglia. In many people with Parkinson's, this eases stiffness and tremor.
120014.m: Deep brain stimulation helps many people with Parkinson's.

120015.q: In which inherited disease with involuntary, sweeping movements do mainly nerve cells in the striatum die?
120015.e: Huntington's disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant way. The loss of nerve cells in the striatum leads to excessive, dance-like movements.
120015.m: Huntington's disease damages the striatum and causes involuntary movements.

120016.q: Which system in the brain, which also includes parts of the basal ganglia, plays a central role in addiction?
120016.e: Part of the basal ganglia belongs to the reward system. Addictive substances activate this system especially strongly, which is why people want them again and again.
120016.m: Addiction is closely linked to the reward system in the brain.

120017.q: Which part of the basal ganglia is called “pale globe” in translation?
120017.e: Globus means globe, pallidus means pale. The globus pallidus looks lighter than its surroundings because of many myelinated fibres.
120017.m: The globus pallidus is the pale globe of the basal ganglia.

120018.q: Which form of learning is especially linked with the basal ganglia?
120018.e: When actions are repeated often, the basal ganglia increasingly take over their control. That is how routines such as brushing your teeth become automatic habits.
120018.m: Habits are anchored in the basal ganglia.

120019.q: Which disorder with motor and vocal tics is linked with a malfunction of the basal ganglia?
120019.e: In Tourette syndrome, involuntary movements and sounds occur. It is thought that disturbed inhibition in the loops of the basal ganglia contributes to this.
120019.m: In Tourette syndrome, the movement selection of the basal ganglia is disturbed.

120020.q: Which messenger is missing in Parkinson's because the cells that make it for the basal ganglia die?
120020.e: In Parkinson's, nerve cells in the substantia nigra that supply dopamine to the basal ganglia die. Without dopamine, movements become slow and stiff.
120020.m: In Parkinson's, the basal ganglia lack dopamine.

120021.q: What job does the corpus callosum have in the brain?
a: It connects the two halves of the brain
It protects the brain from knocks
120021.e: The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of nerve fibres. Through it, the left and right halves of the brain exchange information.
120021.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

120022.q: Which syndrome, in which one hand seems to act on its own, can occur after damage to the corpus callosum?
120022.e: In alien hand syndrome, one hand carries out movements that the person does not intend. It can occur after the corpus callosum is cut or after other brain damage.
120022.m: After damage to the corpus callosum, a hand can seem controlled by someone else.

120023.q: Roughly how many nerve fibres make up the corpus callosum?
120023.e: The corpus callosum contains about 200 to 250 million nerve fibres. This makes it by far the largest fibre connection between the hemispheres.
120023.m: Hundreds of millions of fibres connect the two halves of the brain.

120024.q: For which condition is the corpus callosum sometimes cut by surgery?
120024.e: In a callosotomy, the corpus callosum is cut so that epileptic seizures can no longer spread from one half of the brain to the other. The operation is only considered in severe cases that cannot be treated otherwise.
120024.m: Cutting the corpus callosum can stop seizures from spreading.

120025.q: In which half of the brain are the most important language centres in most people?
120025.e: In most people, especially right-handers, language is processed mainly in the left half of the brain. Experiments with split-brain patients also showed this.
120025.m: Language is usually in the left half of the brain.

120026.q: A split-brain patient sees an object only in the left visual field. What typically happens?
a: He cannot name it, but can find it by touch with his left hand
He can name it, but cannot find it by touch
He does not see the object at all
120026.e: The left visual field is processed in the right hemisphere, while language is usually on the left. Without the corpus callosum, the information does not reach the language centre, but the right half of the brain can control the left hand.
120026.m: Without the corpus callosum, the speaking half of the brain does not know what the other half sees.

120027.q: What was special about the brain of Kim Peek, the real person behind the film “Rain Man”?
a: He had only one brain hemisphere
120027.e: Kim Peek was born with agenesis of the corpus callosum, meaning without a corpus callosum. He had an extraordinary memory for thousands of books.
120027.m: Kim Peek lived without a corpus callosum and had an enormous memory.

120028.q: What is the corpus callosum mainly made of?
120028.e: The corpus callosum is made of nerve fibres wrapped in a fatty myelin layer. This makes the tissue look white.
120028.m: The corpus callosum is a large bundle of white matter.

120029.q: Who is Broca's area named after?
120029.e: In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca described a patient who had lost the ability to speak and had damage in the left frontal lobe. The region has carried his name ever since.
120029.m: In 1861 Paul Broca found a speech centre in the frontal lobe.

120030.q: In which brain hemisphere is Broca's area located in most right-handed people?
120030.e: In over 90 per cent of right-handed people, language is mainly based in the left hemisphere. Broca's area lies there in the lower frontal lobe.
120030.m: In most people, language sits on the left.

120031.q: What could Broca's famous patient still do fairly well despite losing his speech?
120031.e: The patient could hardly speak any more but understood much of what was said to him. From this Broca concluded that speaking is controlled by its own area of the brain.
120031.m: When Broca's area is damaged, understanding is often preserved.

120032.q: How does a person with Broca's aphasia typically speak?
120032.e: In Broca's aphasia, producing speech is a struggle and there is little grammar. Understanding language, on the other hand, is usually fairly well preserved.
120032.m: In Broca's aphasia, speaking is laborious and choppy.

120033.q: Which language centre is mainly responsible for understanding language?
120033.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls speaking. Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is especially important for understanding language.

120034.q: Because of its main disorder, what is Broca's aphasia also called?
120034.e: Broca's aphasia mainly affects the production of speech. That is why it is also called motor or expressive aphasia.
120034.m: Broca's aphasia mainly disturbs speaking itself.

120035.q: What is the most common cause of a sudden loss of language (aphasia) in adults?
120035.e: In a stroke, part of the brain no longer receives blood. If it hits the language centres in the left hemisphere, aphasia can suddenly occur.
120035.m: A stroke can suddenly take away a person's language.

120036.q: What is the leaving out of function words and endings, typical of Broca's aphasia, called?
120036.e: In agrammatism, sentences consist mainly of content words, such as “Me hospital go”. Small words and grammatical endings are missing.
120036.m: Agrammatism is language without the building blocks of grammar.

120037.q: Which doctor described the language centre in the temporal lobe named after him in 1874?
120037.e: In 1874 the German neurologist Carl Wernicke described patients who spoke fluently but hardly understood language. He linked this to a region in the temporal lobe.
120037.m: Carl Wernicke discovered the centre for understanding language.

a: In the rear part of the upper temporal gyrus
In the occipital lobe near the visual cortex
120038.e: Wernicke's area usually lies in the left hemisphere in the rear section of the superior temporal gyrus, close to the auditory cortex.
120038.m: Wernicke's area lies near the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

a: A language disorder after brain damage
120039.e: In aphasia, understanding, speaking, reading or writing are disturbed because language centres in the brain are damaged. The voice and hearing are usually fine.
120039.m: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain damage.

120040.q: How does a person with Wernicke's aphasia typically speak?
120040.e: In Wernicke's aphasia, speech flows but contains wrong or invented words. Those affected often do not notice their mistakes because their understanding is impaired.
120040.m: In Wernicke's aphasia, people say a lot but little of it makes sense.

120041.q: What is a common cause of Wernicke's aphasia?
120041.e: Usually a stroke damages the language centre in the temporal lobe. With a broken jaw or diseased vocal cords, only the mechanics of speaking are disturbed, not the understanding of language.
120041.m: Wernicke's aphasia is often caused by a stroke.

120042.q: Which second language centre is mainly responsible for speaking?
120042.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls the production of speech. Wernicke's area, by contrast, is important for understanding language.
120042.m: Broca stands for speaking, Wernicke for understanding.

120043.q: In which brain hemisphere are the language centres located in most people?
120043.e: In most right-handed people and also in many left-handed people, Broca's and Wernicke's areas lie in the left hemisphere.
120043.m: The language centres are usually in the left hemisphere.

120044.q: What does a person with Wernicke's aphasia find especially difficult?
120044.e: Wernicke's area is responsible for understanding language. If it is damaged, those affected understand poorly what they hear, even though their hearing is good.
120044.m: In Wernicke's aphasia, mainly understanding is impaired.

120045.q: Who is Alzheimer's disease named after?
120045.e: In 1906 the German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer described the typical changes in the brain of a patient with severe forgetfulness.
120045.m: Alzheimer's disease bears the name of Alois Alzheimer.

120046.q: Which deposits outside the nerve cells are typical of Alzheimer's disease?
120046.e: Fragments of the protein beta-amyloid clump together between nerve cells to form plaques. Together with tau fibrils, they are considered a hallmark of the disease.
120046.m: In Alzheimer's, beta-amyloid clumps between the nerve cells.

120047.q: Which protein forms the typical fibre bundles inside nerve cells in Alzheimer's?
120047.e: Tau protein normally stabilises the cell skeleton. In Alzheimer's it is altered and clumps into neurofibrillary tangles that damage nerve cells.
120047.m: Clumped tau protein destroys nerve cells from the inside in Alzheimer's.

120048.q: According to the WHO, roughly what share of all cases of dementia is Alzheimer's disease?
120048.e: The World Health Organization estimates that Alzheimer's makes up 60 to 70 per cent of all dementia cases. This makes it the most common form of dementia.
120048.m: Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia.

120049.q: Which ability is usually affected first in Alzheimer's disease?
120049.e: The disease usually begins in brain regions around the hippocampus. That is why those affected first find it hard to remember recent events, while old memories last longer.
120049.m: Alzheimer's usually starts with forgetting new things.

120050.q: Which risk factor increases the likelihood of Alzheimer's disease the most?
120050.e: The risk rises considerably with every decade of life. Genes, high blood pressure and lack of exercise also play a role.
120050.m: Age is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer's.

120051.q: Which group of drugs is used to treat the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease?
120051.e: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil slow the breakdown of the messenger substance acetylcholine. They can ease the symptoms for a while but do not cure the disease.
120051.m: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors ease Alzheimer's but do not cure it.

120052.q: Which brain structure, important for storing new memories, is damaged early in Alzheimer's?
120052.e: The hippocampus transfers new experiences into long-term memory. Because it is affected early, those affected forget new things first.
120052.m: In Alzheimer's, the hippocampus suffers early.

120053.q: Which English doctor described the “shaking palsy” in an essay in 1817?
120053.e: James Parkinson published “An Essay on the Shaking Palsy” in 1817. The disease was later named after him.
120053.m: James Parkinson described the shaking palsy in 1817.

120054.q: What are drugs called that directly imitate the effect of dopamine at its receptors in Parkinson's?
120054.e: An agonist activates a receptor just like the natural messenger substance. Dopamine agonists thus partly replace the missing dopamine.
120054.m: Dopamine agonists act on the receptors like dopamine.

120055.q: What is the main Parkinson's symptom of slowed movements called?
120055.e: Brady means slow, kinesia means movement. Those affected start movements with a delay, walk with small steps and have a quiet voice and small handwriting.
120055.m: Bradykinesia is the typical slowing of movement in Parkinson's.

120056.q: When does the typical tremor in Parkinson's disease mainly occur?
120056.e: The Parkinson's tremor is a resting tremor that often fades during purposeful movements. Because of the finger movement it is also called a pill-rolling tremor.
120056.m: Parkinson's tremor shows mainly when the hand is resting.

120057.q: Which actor founded one of the largest foundations for Parkinson's research after his diagnosis?
120057.e: Michael J. Fox was diagnosed in 1991 at a young age. In 2000 he founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation, which funds research into Parkinson's.
120057.m: Michael J. Fox campaigns for Parkinson's research.

120058.q: Which messenger substance is lacking in the brain in Parkinson's disease?
120058.e: In Parkinson's, nerve cells in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine die. The shortage disrupts the control of movement.
120058.m: In Parkinson's, the brain lacks dopamine.

120059.q: Which sensory disorder often appears years before the movement problems in Parkinson's?
120059.e: Many of those affected notice years before diagnosis that their sense of smell is getting worse. The smell disorder is considered an important early sign.
120059.m: A weaker sense of smell can be an early sign of Parkinson's.

120060.q: Which of these signs is one of the main symptoms of Parkinson's disease?
120060.e: Typical signs are slowed movements, a tremor at rest and muscle stiffness (rigidity). If the arm is moved passively, it often gives way in jerks, like a cogwheel.
120060.m: Muscle stiffness is a main sign of Parkinson's.

120061.q: Why is World Parkinson's Day held on 11 April?
a: Dopamine was discovered on that day
It is the day the WHO was founded
James Parkinson died on that day
120061.e: James Parkinson was born on 11 April 1755. In 1817 he was the first to describe the shaking palsy.
120061.m: World Parkinson's Day falls on James Parkinson's birthday.

120062.q: What is the Glasgow Coma Scale, used by emergency services for head injuries, for?
120062.e: The scale checks whether someone opens their eyes, speaks and moves. This allows the level of consciousness to be judged quickly and comparably.
120062.m: The Glasgow Coma Scale measures how awake a person is.

120063.q: Which sign after a fall on the head needs a doctor's examination immediately?
a: A small bump with no other symptoms
A slight scratch on the forehead
A brief headache that quickly goes away
120063.e: If someone becomes more and more drowsy after a head injury or vomits, there may be bleeding or swelling in the brain. Then you must call the emergency number at once.
120063.m: Drowsiness and vomiting after a head injury are warning signs.

120064.q: Which three areas does the Glasgow Coma Scale assess?
a: Eye opening, verbal and motor response
120064.e: It scores eye opening (1 to 4), the verbal response (1 to 5) and the best motor response (1 to 6).
120064.m: The Glasgow scale checks eyes, speech and movement.

120065.q: What is the mildest form of traumatic brain injury called?
120065.e: A concussion (commotio cerebri) is a short-term disturbance of function without detectable tissue damage. Typical symptoms are headache, nausea and gaps in memory.
120065.m: A concussion is the mildest traumatic brain injury.

120066.q: Why should someone be watched after a head injury, even if they feel well again after a short loss of consciousness?
a: Bleeding inside the skull may only show itself later
The brain no longer needs oxygen afterwards
Otherwise they might catch a cold
120066.e: With some bleeds inside the skull, those affected at first seem awake again. Only when more blood collects does their condition suddenly become worse and life-threatening.
120066.m: After a head injury, danger can still come later.

120067.q: What is bleeding beneath the tough outer membrane of the brain (dura) called?
120067.e: “Sub” means under, and a “haematoma” is a bruise or collection of blood. A subdural haematoma therefore lies under the dura, an epidural haematoma above it, right against the bone.
120067.m: A subdural haematoma is bleeding under the dura.

120068.q: What life-threatening consequence can a sharp rise in pressure inside the skull have?
a: Drying out of the cerebrospinal fluid
120068.e: Because the skull cannot give way, swelling pushes parts of the brain towards the opening at the base of the skull. If the brainstem is trapped, breathing and circulation fail.
120068.m: High pressure in the skull can trap the brainstem.

120069.q: Why is swelling of the brain particularly dangerous in adults?
a: The swelling moves into the spine
The brain then stops making nerve cells
120069.e: Because the bony skull is rigid, swelling makes the pressure inside rise sharply. This can crush brain tissue and damage vital centres.
120069.m: There is hardly any room for extra volume inside the rigid skull.

120070.q: Which progressive brain disease is seen in athletes who take many blows to the head, such as boxers?
120070.e: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy develops after repeated, often mild head injuries. In boxers it used to be called “dementia pugilistica”.
120070.m: Repeated blows to the head can damage the brain permanently.

120071.q: What was the main aim of the European Human Brain Project?
a: To research and simulate the brain with computers
To replace brain surgery with robots
120071.e: The Human Brain Project wanted to bring together knowledge about the brain and recreate it with supercomputers. This was also meant to lead to new approaches for medicine and computer science.
120071.m: The Human Brain Project wanted to understand the brain in the computer.

120072.q: Which Swiss university did the Human Brain Project start from?
120072.e: The project was coordinated from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL) and later brought together over a hundred partner institutions in Europe.
120072.m: The Human Brain Project had its origin at EPFL.

120073.q: Who mainly funded the Human Brain Project?
120073.e: The project was paid for mainly by the EU through its research programmes. The participating countries also contributed.
120073.m: The Human Brain Project was an EU research project.

120074.q: Why is a complete simulation of the human brain so difficult?
a: It has around 86 billion nerve cells with countless connections
It has only a few but huge cells
It works entirely without electrical signals
120074.e: Each nerve cell is connected to thousands of others. This enormous number of connections exceeds even the power of today's supercomputers.
120074.m: The brain is extremely complex because of its many connections.

120075.q: What total budget was originally planned for the Human Brain Project?
120075.e: The project was planned with about one billion euros over ten years, funded by the EU and the participating countries.
120075.m: The Human Brain Project was planned with around one billion euros.

120076.q: Which important result did the Human Brain Project deliver, among others?
120076.e: Researchers created digital maps of the brain showing where each brain region lies. These atlases remain available for research.
120076.m: The Human Brain Project created digital maps of the brain.

120077.q: Which earlier project at EPFL simulated parts of the rat cerebral cortex from 2005?
120077.e: The Blue Brain Project first reconstructed and simulated a cortical column of the rat on a supercomputer. It was the basis for the later Human Brain Project.
120077.m: The Blue Brain Project paved the way for the Human Brain Project.

120078.q: What happened in the Human Brain Project in 2014?
a: Hundreds of researchers criticised it in an open letter
120078.e: In an open letter to the European Commission, many neuroscientists criticised the leadership and aims of the project. Afterwards the management was reorganised.
120078.m: The Human Brain Project had to be restructured after strong criticism.

120079.q: What do neuromorphic computers, like those developed in the Human Brain Project, imitate?
120079.e: Neuromorphic chips process signals in a similar way to nerve cells, with short pulses. They use much less energy than normal computers.

120080.q: What condition must the restoring force meet for a harmonic oscillation to occur?
a: It is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it
It is always the same size
It grows with the square of the displacement
It acts in the direction of the displacement
120080.e: If F = -k·x, a harmonic oscillation occurs. A linear force law, as with an ideal spring, is the requirement for this.
120080.m: A harmonic oscillation needs a linear force law.

120081.q: What kind of function describes the displacement of a harmonic oscillation over time?
120081.e: The displacement follows x(t) = A·sin(ωt + φ). That is why harmonic oscillations are also called sinusoidal oscillations.

120082.q: By how much is the velocity of a harmonic oscillation out of phase with the displacement?
120082.e: The derivative of sin(ωt) is ω·cos(ωt), and the cosine is shifted by 90° from the sine. So the velocity is greatest when the displacement is zero.
120082.m: Velocity and displacement are a quarter period apart.

120083.q: Where is the magnitude of the acceleration greatest in a harmonic oscillation?
120083.e: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement, a = -ω²·x. At the turning points the displacement is greatest, so the acceleration is too.
120083.m: The acceleration is strongest at the turning points.

120084.q: A body oscillates according to x(t) = 0.05 m · sin(10 s⁻¹ · t). What is its maximum acceleration?
120084.m: The maximum acceleration is the amplitude times the angular frequency squared.

120085.q: How does the total energy of a harmonic oscillation change when the amplitude is tripled?
120085.e: The total energy is E = ½·k·A². It grows with the square of the amplitude, so by a factor of 3² = 9.
120085.m: The energy of an oscillation grows with the square of the amplitude.

120086.q: How can a harmonic oscillation be pictured as coming from another motion?
a: As the projection of uniform circular motion
As the projection of free fall
As the shadow of a straight-line motion
As the combination of two throws
120086.e: If you watch the shadow of a point moving uniformly in a circle on a wall, it moves back and forth exactly sinusoidally. The angular velocity of the circle equals the angular frequency.
120086.m: The shadow of circular motion oscillates harmonically.

120087.q: Which differential equation describes an undamped harmonic oscillation?
120087.e: From F = m·a and F = -k·x, it follows that ẍ = -(k/m)·x. With ω² = k/m you get ẍ = -ω²·x, whose solutions are sine and cosine functions.
120087.m: In harmonic oscillations the acceleration is proportional to the negative displacement.

120088.q: Which formula gives the period of a mass on a spring?
120088.e: For a mass on a spring with mass m and spring constant D, T = 2π·√(m/D). A larger mass lengthens the period, a stiffer spring shortens it.
120088.m: With a mass on a spring, more mass makes the oscillation slower.

120089.q: A body of 0.2 kg oscillates on a spring with D = 80 N/m. What is the period?
120089.m: The period of a mass on a spring follows from the mass and the spring constant.

120090.q: How does the period of a mass on a spring change when the mass is multiplied by nine?
120090.e: The period is proportional to √m. With nine times the mass, it becomes longer by a factor of √9 = 3.
120090.m: The period grows with the square root of the mass.

120091.q: What happens to the period of a mass on a spring if you take it from the Earth to the Moon?
120091.e: The gravitational acceleration does not appear in the formula T = 2π·√(m/D). Mass and spring constant are the same on the Moon as on Earth.
120091.m: A mass on a spring oscillates at the same rate on the Moon as on Earth.

120092.q: What changes when a mass on a spring oscillates hanging vertically instead of horizontally without friction?
a: The oscillation is no longer harmonic
120092.e: The weight stretches the spring further and shifts the equilibrium position downwards. Around this new equilibrium position, the same linear restoring force still acts.
120092.m: With a mass on a spring, gravity only shifts the equilibrium position.

120093.q: Why is the formula T = 2π·√(m/D) no longer exact for a heavy spring?
a: The spring partly oscillates with its own mass
A heavy spring has no spring constant
A heavy spring does not oscillate harmonically
120093.e: The formula assumes a massless spring. With a heavy spring, the coils move too, so the period is slightly longer than calculated.
120093.m: A heavy spring partly oscillates along with the mass.

120094.q: A body oscillates on a spring. How does the period change if it hangs from two such springs in parallel instead?
a: It drops to about 71 per cent
120094.e: In parallel, the spring constant doubles. Since T is proportional to 1/√D, the period drops by a factor of 1/√2 ≈ 0.71.
120094.m: Stiffer springs make a mass on a spring oscillate faster.

120095.q: How does the period of an ideal mass on a spring change if you double the amplitude?
120095.e: In a harmonic oscillation the period does not depend on the amplitude (isochronism). With a larger amplitude, the body simply moves correspondingly faster.
120095.m: The period of an ideal mass on a spring does not depend on the amplitude.

120096.q: A body of 1 kg oscillates on a spring with D = 100 N/m and an amplitude of 10 cm. What is its maximum speed?
120096.e: v_max = A·ω with ω = √(D/m) = √(100 N/m / 1 kg) = 10 s⁻¹. So v_max = 0.1 m · 10 s⁻¹ = 1 m/s.
120096.m: The maximum speed is the amplitude times the angular frequency.

120097.q: What is the formula for the period of a simple pendulum at small displacements?
120097.e: For small angles, the simple pendulum has T = 2π·√(l/g). The mass of the bob does not appear in the formula.
120097.m: The period of a simple pendulum depends on its length and the gravitational acceleration.

120098.q: What is the period of a simple pendulum 2.5 m long (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?

120099.q: By what factor is the period of a simple pendulum on the Moon (g equals 1.62 m/s²) longer than on Earth (9.81 m/s²)?
120099.e: The period is proportional to 1/√g. The factor is √(9.81 / 1.62) ≈ √6.06 ≈ 2.5.
120099.m: With weaker gravity, a simple pendulum swings more slowly.

120100.q: Why does the formula T = 2π·√(l/g) only apply to small displacements?
a: Because only there is sin φ roughly equal to φ
Because otherwise there is no air resistance
120100.e: The restoring force is m·g·sin φ. Only at small angles (below about 10°) can you replace sin φ with φ and get a linear force law.
120100.m: The simple pendulum is only harmonic for small swings.

120101.q: How does the actual period of a simple pendulum at a 60° displacement compare with the small-angle formula?
120101.e: At large angles, sin φ is smaller than φ, so the restoring force is weaker than in the approximation. At 60° the period is about 7 per cent longer.
120101.m: Large swings make a simple pendulum a little slower.

120102.q: A simple pendulum 0.80 m long has a period of 1.80 s. What value of g does this give?
120102.e: From T = 2π·√(l/g), g = 4π²·l/T² = 4π² · 0.80 m / 3.24 s² ≈ 9.75 m/s².
120102.m: A simple pendulum can be used to measure the gravitational acceleration.

120103.q: What is assumed for the idealised simple (mathematical) pendulum?
a: A point mass on a massless, unstretchable string
An extended body on a rod
A mass sitting on a spring
A string with evenly distributed mass
120103.e: The mathematical pendulum is a model: all the mass sits in one point, and the string has no mass and does not stretch. Real pendulums are described more accurately as physical pendulums.
120103.m: The mathematical pendulum is a simplified model.

120104.q: How does the period of a simple pendulum change in a lift that is accelerating upwards?
120104.e: When accelerating upwards, the effective gravitational acceleration g + a is greater. According to T = 2π·√(l/g), the period therefore becomes smaller.
120104.m: A greater effective gravity makes a simple pendulum swing faster.

120105.q: Which scientist built the first accurate pendulum clock around 1656?
120105.e: Galileo had observed the regularity of the pendulum’s swing, but Christiaan Huygens used it to build the first practical pendulum clock in 1656. It was much more accurate than earlier clocks.
120105.m: Huygens made the pendulum the timekeeper of clocks.

120106.q: What is meant by the period of an oscillation?
a: The time for one complete back-and-forth movement
The time from the start until it stops
The time from the equilibrium position to the turning point
The time for half an oscillation
120106.e: The period T is the time after which the state of motion repeats exactly for the first time. It is the reciprocal of the frequency.
120106.m: The period is the duration of one whole oscillation.

120107.q: Why do experiments usually measure the time for ten oscillations and divide by ten?
a: The error from reaction time is spread out
Because the pendulum only swings evenly after ten oscillations
Because stopwatches only show whole seconds
120107.e: Starting and stopping creates an error due to reaction time. If you measure many periods at once, this error only counts for a tenth per period.
120107.m: Measuring many oscillations at once makes the result more accurate.

120108.q: What is the period of a 440 Hz tuning fork?
120108.m: The higher the frequency, the shorter the period.

120109.q: A pendulum makes exactly 20 swings in 36 s. What is its frequency?
120109.e: The period is T = 36 s / 20 = 1.8 s. The frequency is f = 1/T = 1/1.8 s ≈ 0.56 Hz.
120109.m: The frequency is the reciprocal of the period.

120110.q: Why does a pendulum clock with a metal rod run slow in hot summer weather?
a: The rod expands and the period becomes longer
The air becomes thinner and slows it more
The mass of the pendulum increases
120110.e: Heat makes the pendulum rod expand. A longer pendulum swings more slowly, so the clock counts too few swings and runs slow.
120110.m: Heat lengthens the pendulum and makes the clock run slow.

120111.q: A pendulum clock is running fast. How do you correct it?
120111.e: A clock that runs fast is swinging too quickly. If you move the bob down, the pendulum becomes longer and the period greater.
120111.m: A longer pendulum slows down a clock that runs fast.

120112.q: Two pendulums with periods of 2.0 s and 2.1 s start in step at the same time. After how long are they first in step again?
120112.e: The faster pendulum must make exactly one more swing: n · 2.0 s = (n−1) · 2.1 s gives n = 21. That is 21 · 2.0 s = 42 s.
120112.m: Two slightly different pendulums come back into step periodically.

120113.q: A pendulum takes 0.8 s to go from one turning point to the other. What is its period?
120113.e: From one turning point to the opposite one is only half an oscillation. For the whole period the pendulum also has to come back: 2 · 0.8 s = 1.6 s.
120113.m: A whole period includes the way there and back.

120114.q: How does the amplitude decrease when the friction force is proportional to the velocity?
120114.e: With velocity-proportional damping, for example in oil, the amplitude decreases according to A(t) = A₀·e^(-δt). In equal time intervals it shrinks by the same factor each time.
120114.m: With damping in liquids, the amplitude decreases exponentially.

120115.q: How does the amplitude decrease when a constant sliding friction force acts as a brake?
120115.e: With a constant friction force, the amplitude decreases by the same amount every half oscillation. So the turning points move closer together in equal steps.
120115.m: Dry friction makes the amplitude shrink evenly.

120116.q: What is the damping case called in which a displaced system returns to equilibrium fastest without overshooting?
120116.e: With critical damping, the damping is just strong enough that no oscillation occurs. At the same time, the system returns faster than with even stronger damping.
120116.m: Critical damping brings a system to rest fastest.

120117.q: What happens when a damped oscillation is overdamped?
a: The system creeps slowly back to equilibrium without oscillating
The system oscillates more and more strongly
The system keeps oscillating the same for ever
The system jumps straight to equilibrium
120117.e: When overdamped, the damping is very strong. The body returns without overshooting, but much more slowly than with critical damping.
120117.m: With very strong damping, a system creeps back slowly.

120118.q: What does the logarithmic decrement of a damped oscillation indicate?
a: The logarithm of the ratio of two successive amplitudes
The number of oscillations until it stops
120118.e: The logarithmic decrement Λ = ln(Aₙ / Aₙ₊₁) is a measure of damping per period. With exponential damping it is constant.
120118.m: The logarithmic decrement measures the damping per oscillation.

120119.q: The amplitude of a damped oscillation falls to 80 per cent each period. What percentage of the starting amplitude is left after five periods?
120119.e: After each period you multiply by 0.8: 0.8⁵ ≈ 0.328. So about 33 per cent is left.
120119.m: With exponential damping, the amplitude is multiplied by the same factor every period.

120120.q: How does the frequency of a weakly damped oscillation compare with the undamped one?
a: It is exactly twice as high
120120.e: The damped angular frequency is ω_d = √(ω₀²−δ²). Because of the damping δ, it is slightly smaller than the natural angular frequency ω₀.
120120.m: Damping slows an oscillation down a little.

120121.q: What does a high quality factor of an oscillator mean?
a: It has a very low frequency
120121.e: The quality factor roughly indicates how many oscillations a system makes before most of its energy is used up. A high quality factor means little damping and a sharp resonance.
120121.m: An oscillator with a high quality factor rings on for a long time.

120122.q: At what frequency does a driven system oscillate after the transient phase?
a: At the difference between the two frequencies
120122.e: Once the natural oscillation has died away through damping, the system follows the rhythm of the driver. Only the amplitude depends on how close this is to the natural frequency.
120122.m: A driven oscillator takes on the rhythm of the driver.

120123.q: At resonance, by how much is the oscillator out of phase with the driver?
120123.e: At resonance, the oscillator lags a quarter period behind the driver. This way the driving force always acts in the direction of motion and supplies the most energy.
120123.m: At resonance, the driver is a quarter period ahead of the oscillator.

120124.q: How does an oscillator move when the driving frequency is far above its natural frequency?
a: In antiphase with a small amplitude
In phase with a large amplitude
In phase with an infinite amplitude
120124.e: At a very high driving frequency, the inert mass can hardly follow. The amplitude becomes small, and the phase difference approaches 180°.
120124.m: Driving too fast hardly moves an oscillator.

120125.q: How does an oscillator move when the driving frequency is far below its natural frequency?
a: Almost in phase with about the driver’s amplitude
In antiphase with a very small amplitude
120125.e: With very slow driving, the oscillator follows the driver with practically no delay. Its amplitude roughly matches the displacement set by the driver.
120125.m: With slow driving, the oscillator moves almost in step.

120126.q: How does stronger damping change the resonance curve of a driven oscillation?
a: The peak becomes lower and wider
The peak becomes higher and narrower
The peak disappears towards higher frequencies
120126.e: Damping takes energy from the system. The resonance peak is smaller, the curve becomes flatter and the maximum shifts slightly to lower frequencies.
120126.m: Strong damping makes the resonance curve flat and wide.

120127.q: What is the initial phase called in which the natural oscillation and the driven oscillation overlap?
120127.e: At first the system oscillates both at its natural frequency and in the rhythm of the driver. Only when the natural part has died away is the steady state reached.
120127.m: The transient phase comes before the steady driven oscillation.

120128.q: Which school apparatus with an eddy current brake is often used to study driven oscillations?
120128.e: Pohl’s wheel is a torsion pendulum driven by a motor. An adjustable eddy current brake makes it possible to study different levels of damping.
120128.m: Pohl’s wheel can be used to measure resonance curves.

120129.q: Why does a car’s rear-view mirror often vibrate strongly only at a certain engine speed?
a: The engine frequency matches its natural frequency there
Air resistance is greatest at this engine speed
The mirror gets warmer at this engine speed
120129.e: The engine drives the car periodically. If the driving frequency matches the natural frequency of the mirror, resonance with a large amplitude occurs.
120129.m: Parts vibrate especially strongly when the engine matches their natural frequency.

120130.q: What is meant by a resonance disaster?
a: The destruction of a weakly damped system by driving it at its natural frequency
A building collapsing under its own excessive weight
A body breaking from a single force
An oscillation dying away due to friction
120130.e: If a system is pushed again and again exactly in time with its natural frequency, the amplitude grows strongly. If the damping is too low, the system can be destroyed.
120130.m: In a resonance disaster, a system is destroyed by oscillating along.

120131.q: Why should soldiers not march in step across bridges?
a: The regular rhythm could set the bridge into resonance
Marching in step makes the bridge heavier
Marching in step makes you slip more easily
The noise could snap the bridge cables
120131.e: If the rhythm of the steps matches the natural frequency of the bridge, the oscillation builds up. In 1831 a suspension bridge in England collapsed under marching soldiers for this reason.
120131.m: On bridges, soldiers break step to avoid resonance.

120132.q: What happened to the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the USA in 1940, shortly after it opened?
a: It swung more and more strongly in the wind and collapsed
It was rammed by a ship and broke
It sank into the river in an earthquake
It burned down after a lightning strike
120132.e: Even a moderate wind set the slender suspension bridge into ever larger twisting oscillations until it broke. Since then, bridges have been tested in wind tunnels for how they oscillate.
120132.m: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge shows how dangerous oscillations that build up can be.

120133.q: Why was London’s Millennium Bridge closed shortly after it opened in 2000?
a: Pedestrians made it sway strongly from side to side
A ship had damaged a pier
A storm had torn the cables
120133.e: The bridge began to sway sideways, and pedestrians unconsciously adjusted their steps to this movement. This made the swaying even stronger.
120133.m: Pedestrians can also set a bridge into resonance.

120134.q: In theory, what happens if a completely undamped oscillator is driven exactly at its natural frequency?
120134.e: Without damping, no energy is lost, while the driver keeps adding energy. So in the model the amplitude grows without limit.
120134.m: Without damping, resonance has no upper limit.

120135.q: Why does a washing machine briefly shake especially hard as the spin speeds up?
a: The drum speed passes through the machine’s natural frequency
The drum turns backwards at that moment
120135.e: Unevenly distributed laundry drives the machine at the rotation frequency. As it speeds up, this briefly comes into the range of the natural frequency; afterwards it is above it and the shaking eases.
120135.m: Passing through its natural frequency makes a machine shake hard for a moment.

120136.q: What measure prevents a machine from setting a component into resonance?
a: Shifting the component’s natural frequency by stiffening it
Making the component as smooth as possible
Only increasing the mass of the machine
120136.e: Stiffening increases the spring constant and so the natural frequency. If this is far from the driving frequency, no resonance can occur.
120136.m: A shifted natural frequency protects against resonance.

120137.q: Why does a car need shock absorbers as well as springs?
a: They damp the spring oscillations so that they do not build up
They lift the car over bumps
They replace the brakes on bumpy roads
120137.e: Without damping, the car would keep bouncing for a long time after every bump, and matching bumps could build the oscillation up by resonance. Shock absorbers turn the oscillation energy into heat.
120137.m: Damping stops oscillations from building up.

120138.q: In which year did the first Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse?
120138.e: The suspension bridge collapsed on 7 November 1940. The collapse was filmed and is one of the best-known examples of bridge oscillations.
120138.m: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed in 1940.

120139.q: In which US state was the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
120139.e: The bridge spanned the Tacoma Narrows strait in Puget Sound in the state of Washington.
120139.m: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge was in the state of Washington.

120140.q: How long after it opened did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse?
120140.e: The bridge opened on 1 July 1940 and collapsed on 7 November 1940, just over four months later.
120140.m: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge lasted only a few months.

120141.q: What nickname did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge get because of its oscillations?
120141.e: Even during construction, the road deck moved up and down strongly in the wind. So people called the bridge “Galloping Gertie”.
120141.m: Because of its wave-like movements, the bridge was called “Galloping Gertie”.

120142.q: At roughly what wind speed did the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse?
120142.e: On the day of the collapse, the wind was blowing at about 64 km/h (40 miles per hour). That is not a hurricane, but it shows how dangerous wind-driven oscillations can be.
120142.m: Even a moderately strong wind brought down the Tacoma bridge.

120143.q: Which mechanism is now seen as the main cause of the collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
a: Regular gusts of wind in time with the natural frequency
120143.e: The road deck and the wind affected each other: every twist changed the air forces so that they made the movement stronger. This self-excited oscillation is called aeroelastic flutter and is not simple forced resonance.
120143.m: The Tacoma collapse was a self-excited oscillation caused by wind.

120144.q: Which living creature died in the collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
120144.e: A journalist had to leave his car on the bridge, and his dog Tubby was inside. No people died.
120144.m: No person died in the Tacoma collapse.

120145.q: Which feature of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge made its strong oscillations more likely?
a: A very slender, flexible deck girder
A concrete deck that was too heavy
A span that was too short
120145.e: Instead of a deep, open truss girder, the bridge only had flat plate girders about 2.4 m deep. The narrow, flexible deck gave the wind a large surface to act on and was easy to twist.
120145.m: A deck that was too slender made the Tacoma bridge vulnerable.

120146.q: What form of oscillation did the deck of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge show shortly before the collapse?
a: A torsional oscillation around the long axis
An oscillation of the piers in the water
A sound vibration of the cables
120146.e: After a cable band on the northern main cable had slipped in the middle of the bridge, the deck twisted alternately to the left and right. This torsional oscillation finally destroyed the main span.
120146.m: The Tacoma bridge twisted until it broke.

120147.q: Which fictitious force causes the slow turning of the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum?
120147.e: In a rotating frame of reference such as the Earth, the Coriolis force acts on moving bodies. It deflects the pendulum very slightly sideways with every swing.
120147.m: The Coriolis force turns the plane of swing of the Foucault pendulum.

120148.q: What do you observe with a Foucault pendulum exactly at the equator?
a: The plane of swing does not turn
120148.e: The rate at which the plane of swing turns is proportional to the sine of the latitude. At the equator this is zero, so the plane does not turn.
120148.m: At the equator, the plane of a Foucault pendulum stays still.

120149.q: Roughly how long does the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum in Zurich (about 47.4° north) take for one full turn?
120149.e: The time for one turn is about 23.93 h / sin(latitude). With sin 47.4° ≈ 0.736 you get about 32.5 hours.
120149.m: The closer to the pole, the faster the plane of the pendulum turns.

120150.q: In which direction does the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum turn in the Northern Hemisphere, seen from above?
120150.e: Seen from above the North Pole, the Earth turns anticlockwise. So relative to the ground, the plane of the pendulum seems to move clockwise.
120150.m: In the Northern Hemisphere, the plane of the pendulum moves clockwise.

120151.q: How long was the wire of Foucault’s famous pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris?
120151.e: Foucault hung a 28 kg ball on a 67 m wire in the dome of the Panthéon.
120151.m: Foucault’s pendulum in the Panthéon was almost 70 metres long.

120152.q: Roughly what is the period of a simple pendulum 67 m long (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
120152.m: A very long pendulum swings very slowly.

120153.q: Why do Foucault pendulums usually have a long wire and a heavy bob?
a: So that air resistance and disturbances matter little and it swings for a long time
So that the Coriolis force disappears
So that the plane turns faster
So that the pendulum is quieter
120153.e: A heavy body has a lot of energy compared with the air friction and keeps swinging for a long time. A long wire makes the swing slow and disturbances at the suspension less effective.
120153.m: Long, heavy pendulums show the Earth’s rotation most clearly.

120154.q: Why are modern Foucault pendulums in museums often given electromagnetic pushes?
a: To make up for the energy lost through air friction
To fake the turning of the plane
To hold the plane of swing in place
To make the pendulum swing faster
120154.e: Without a drive, air resistance would bring the swinging to a stop after a few hours. An electromagnet gives a small push with every swing without setting the direction.
120154.m: A small drive keeps a Foucault pendulum moving all day.

120155.q: How is the natural angular frequency ω₀ related to the natural frequency f₀?
120155.e: In the circle model, one full oscillation corresponds to an angle of 2π. So the angular frequency is 2π times the frequency.
120155.m: The angular frequency is 2π times the frequency.

120156.q: What is the natural angular frequency of a mass on a spring?
120156.e: From the equation of motion m·ẍ = -D·x, it follows that ω₀² = D/m. A stiffer spring raises the natural angular frequency, a larger mass lowers it.
120156.m: A stiff spring and a small mass give a high natural angular frequency.

120157.q: What is the natural angular frequency of a simple pendulum at small displacements?
120157.e: For small angles, ẍ = -(g/l)·x. From this, ω₀ = √(g/l), regardless of the mass.
120157.m: For a simple pendulum, gravity and length determine the natural angular frequency.

120158.q: What is the natural angular frequency of a mass on a spring with D = 200 N/m and m = 0.5 kg?
120158.m: The natural angular frequency is the square root of spring constant divided by mass.

120159.q: An oscillator has a period of 0.5 s. What is its angular frequency?
120159.m: The angular frequency is 2π divided by the period.

120160.q: In which unit is the natural angular frequency usually given?
120160.e: The angular frequency gives the angle swept per second in the circle model. You write rad/s or simply s⁻¹.
120160.m: The angular frequency measures angle per time.

120161.q: What is the natural angular frequency of an electrical oscillating circuit made of a coil and a capacitor?
120161.e: In the oscillating circuit, energy swings back and forth between the magnetic field of the coil and the electric field of the capacitor. Thomson’s oscillation equation gives ω₀ = 1/√(L·C).
120161.m: Larger coils and capacitors lower the frequency of an oscillating circuit.

120162.q: What is the natural angular frequency of an oscillating circuit with L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF?
120162.m: The natural angular frequency of an oscillating circuit follows from inductance and capacitance.

120163.q: Roughly how heavy is the pendulum ball of the tuned mass damper in the Taipei 101 skyscraper?
120163.e: The gilded steel ball hangs between the 87th and 92nd floors and weighs about 660 tonnes. It reduces the swaying of the tower during typhoons and earthquakes.
120163.m: In Taipei 101, a huge pendulum ball slows down the swaying.

120164.q: How does a tuned mass damper in a building work?
a: An extra mass with the same natural frequency oscillates in antiphase
An extra mass holds the building rigidly in place
A motor pushes the building back
120164.e: The damper is tuned to the natural frequency of the building. It oscillates in antiphase and so draws oscillation energy from the building, which is often also turned into heat in dampers.
120164.m: A tuned mass damper swings against the building and calms it.

120165.q: What happens to the kinetic energy in a car’s hydraulic shock absorber?
a: It is stored in the battery
It is turned into potential energy
It passes into the steering wheel
120165.e: In the shock absorber, oil is forced through narrow valves. The internal friction of the oil turns the oscillation energy into heat.
120165.m: Shock absorbers turn oscillations into heat.

120166.q: Why does a car need shock absorbers as well as springs?
a: Otherwise it would keep bouncing for a long time after every bump
Otherwise the springs would be too soft
Otherwise the car could not brake
120166.e: The springs absorb bumps, but only store the energy. Without damping, the body would keep oscillating like a mass on a spring and the tyres would lose contact with the road.
120166.m: Springs absorb bumps, dampers stop the bouncing.

120167.q: What is the earthquake protection called in which a building stands on elastic bearings that pass on ground movements only in weakened form?
120167.e: With base isolation, rubber or sliding bearings separate the building from the ground. The natural frequency of the building is lowered a lot, so it is hardly affected by fast ground shocks.
120167.m: Elastic bearings decouple buildings from the shaking ground.

120168.q: What are the dumbbell-shaped weights hanging on high-voltage power lines for?
a: They damp oscillations of the conductor cables in the wind
They keep birds off the cables
120168.e: Wind makes the conductor cables oscillate, which tires the material over time. The dampers take up this oscillation energy.
120168.m: Dampers protect overhead lines from fluttering in the wind.

120169.q: What principle is contactless eddy current damping based on?
a: Induced currents create a braking magnetic field
Air is compressed in a cylinder
120169.e: When a piece of metal moves through a magnetic field, eddy currents form in it. According to Lenz’s law, their magnetic field opposes the motion and slows it down.
120169.m: Eddy currents slow down movements without contact.

120170.q: What are the spiral strakes on tall steel chimneys for?
a: They prevent regular vortex shedding and thus oscillations
They serve as ladders for chimney sweeps
120170.e: On round chimneys, the wind sheds vortices in a regular rhythm that make the chimney sway sideways. The strakes, named after Christopher Scruton, disturb this even rhythm.
120170.m: Spiral strakes on chimneys prevent wind-driven oscillations.

120171.q: At what frequency does the quartz in most wristwatches oscillate?
120171.e: Watch quartzes usually oscillate at 32,768 Hz. This frequency cannot be heard by humans and is easy to divide electronically.
120171.m: A watch quartz oscillates 32,768 times a second.

120172.q: Why is exactly 32,768 Hz chosen for watch quartzes?
a: Because 32,768 equals 2 to the power of 15
Because the quartz can only oscillate like this
Because this number can be divided by 60
Because it equals the speed of sound
120172.e: 32,768 is 2¹⁵. After halving 15 times in a simple binary counter, you get exactly one tick per second.
120172.m: A binary counter halves the quartz frequency down to one tick per second.

120173.q: Which effect makes it possible to set a quartz crystal oscillating with an electric voltage?
120173.e: In the piezoelectric effect, a deformation creates an electric voltage, and in reverse, a voltage deforms the crystal. So a circuit can drive the quartz and pick up its oscillation.
120173.m: Quartz deforms under voltage and produces voltage when deformed.

120174.q: Who discovered the direct piezoelectric effect in 1880?
120174.e: In 1880 the brothers Jacques and Pierre Curie showed that certain crystals such as quartz form electric charges on their surface under pressure.
120174.m: The Curie brothers discovered the piezoelectric effect.

120175.q: Which Swiss research institute developed the “Beta 21” quartz wristwatch movement in the 1960s?
a: The Centre Electronique Horloger in Neuchâtel
The Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen
120175.e: The Centre Electronique Horloger (CEH) was founded in Neuchâtel by the Swiss watch industry. The Beta 21 movement it produced came onto the market in 1970 in watches of several brands.
120175.m: The first Swiss quartz wristwatch movement was created in Neuchâtel.

120176.q: What is the slump of the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s and 1980s called?
120176.e: Cheap quartz watches, mainly from Japan and Hong Kong, pushed out many mechanical Swiss watches. The number of people working in the industry fell sharply.
120176.m: The quartz crisis shook the Swiss watch industry.

120177.q: Why does a quartz watch keep much better time than a simple mechanical watch?
a: The quartz has a very stable natural frequency and low damping
The quartz oscillates with a larger amplitude
The battery provides the time directly
120177.e: A quartz oscillator has a very high quality factor and a natural frequency that hardly varies. It also oscillates much faster than a balance wheel, so small disturbances matter less.
120177.m: The stable natural frequency of the quartz makes the watch accurate.

120178.q: What shape does the quartz oscillator in a wristwatch usually have?
a: The shape of a tiny tuning fork
120178.e: The quartz is shaped into a small tuning fork whose prongs vibrate against each other. This design is small, saves power and suits low frequencies.
120178.m: A tiny tuning fork vibrates inside a watch quartz.

120179.q: At what temperature does a typical tuning fork watch quartz run most accurately?
120179.e: The frequency of a tuning fork quartz depends on temperature in a parabola, with its peak at about 25 °C. On the wrist the temperature is close to this value.
120179.m: A watch quartz is tuned to room temperature.

120180.q: Which quantity stays constant over time in exponential population growth?
120180.e: In exponential growth, the population always grows by the same percentage per unit of time. The absolute increase therefore gets bigger with each generation.
120180.m: Exponential growth means a constant percentage increase.

120181.q: A population of 1,000 animals grows by 10 per cent every year. How many animals are there after 2 years?
120181.e: After one year there are 1,000 · 1.1 = 1,100 animals, after two years 1,100 · 1.1 = 1,210. The increase in the second year is bigger because it is based on the larger population.
120181.m: In exponential growth, you multiply by the same factor every year.

120182.q: Which differential equation describes exponential population growth?
120182.e: In exponential growth, the increase is proportional to the current population size N. The solution is N(t) = N0 · e to the power of (r · t).
120182.m: In exponential growth, the increase is proportional to the population size.

120183.q: A population grows exponentially with r = 0.07 per year. Roughly how long is its doubling time?
120183.e: The doubling time is ln 2 divided by r, so 0.693 divided by 0.07. That gives about 9.9 years.
120183.m: You get the doubling time by dividing ln 2 by the growth rate.

120184.q: What does exponential growth look like if you plot the logarithm of the population size against time?
120184.e: Taking the logarithm of N(t) = N0 · e to the power of (r · t) gives ln N = ln N0 + r · t. That is a straight line with gradient r.
120184.m: On a semi-logarithmic graph, exponential growth appears as a straight line.

120185.q: Under what conditions does a population grow approximately exponentially?
a: With plenty of resources and no density effects
When it reaches its carrying capacity
With very heavy pressure from predators
120185.e: Exponential growth requires food and space to be practically unlimited. This is the case, for example, when a habitat is newly colonised.
120185.m: Exponential growth only happens while resources are practically unlimited.

120186.q: In a population, the birth rate is 0.5 and the death rate 0.3 per individual per year. What is the growth rate r?
120186.e: The intrinsic growth rate is the difference between birth rate and death rate: 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 per year (without immigration and emigration).
120186.m: The growth rate r is the birth rate minus the death rate.

120187.q: Which animal multiplied almost exponentially in Australia after being released in 1859?
120187.e: In 1859, a settler in Victoria released a few wild rabbits. Without suitable predators, they spread across large parts of the continent within decades.
120187.m: Rabbits in Australia are a well-known example of explosive growth.

120188.q: Who formulated the logistic growth model in 1838?
120188.e: The Belgian mathematician Verhulst developed the logistic equation in 1838 to describe slowed population growth.
120188.m: The logistic growth model goes back to Verhulst.

120189.q: At what population size is the absolute increase per unit of time greatest in the logistic model?
a: At a quarter of the carrying capacity
120189.e: The increase r · N · (1 − N/K) is the product of a growing and a shrinking factor. Its maximum is at N = K/2.
120189.m: Logistically growing populations increase fastest at half the carrying capacity.

120190.q: In the logistic model, what is the largest population that a habitat can support permanently called?
120190.e: The carrying capacity K states how many individuals a habitat can feed permanently with its resources. Close to K, growth comes to a standstill.
120190.m: The carrying capacity K is the upper limit of a population.

120191.q: A population with r = 0.4 per year and K = 1,000 has 500 animals. What is its logistic increase per year?
120191.m: In the logistic model, the factor 1 minus N over K slows the increase.

120192.q: In the logistic model, what happens if a population is larger than its carrying capacity K?
120192.e: If N is larger than K, the factor (1 − N/K) becomes negative. The increase is then negative and the population shrinks back towards K.
120192.m: Above the carrying capacity, the logistic model predicts a decrease.

120193.q: What shape is the curve of population size over time in logistic growth?
120193.e: At first the population grows almost exponentially, then growth slows and the curve flattens out near the carrying capacity K. This creates an S-shape.
120193.m: Logistic growth produces an S-shaped curve.

120194.q: What does the logistic model take into account, unlike the exponential model?
a: The age structure of the population
120194.e: In the logistic model, the growth rate per individual falls the denser the population becomes. This represents competition for limited resources.
120194.m: The logistic model slows growth as density increases.

120195.q: What is the phase called in which a logistically growing population levels off around the carrying capacity?
120195.e: Near K, births and deaths are roughly in balance. The population hardly grows any more; it is saturated.
120195.m: In the saturation phase, the population stays close to its carrying capacity.

120196.q: How does logistic growth behave while the population is very small compared with the carrying capacity?
120196.e: If N is much smaller than K, the factor (1 − N/K) is close to 1. The equation then practically equals dN/dt = r · N.
120196.m: At low density, logistic growth hardly differs from exponential growth.

120197.q: What does the carrying capacity K of a habitat refer to?
a: The largest population size that can be supported permanently
The highest birth rate of a species
120197.e: K states how many individuals of a species a habitat can feed in the long term with its resources.
120197.m: The carrying capacity is the population size that a habitat can support permanently.

120199.q: Which factor typically limits a population in a density-dependent way?
a: A forest fire caused by lightning
120199.e: The more individuals have to share the food, the stronger the competition. Its effect therefore depends on density.
120199.m: Density-dependent factors act more strongly the denser a population is.

120200.q: Which factor typically acts on an insect population independently of density?
120200.e: A late frost kills a similar proportion of the animals, however dense the population is. Parasites and diseases, by contrast, spread more easily at high density.
120200.m: Weather extremes are usually density-independent factors.

120201.q: On St Matthew Island in Alaska, introduced reindeer multiplied strongly and then crashed. What is exceeding the carrying capacity called?
120201.e: The reindeer released in 1944 grew to about 6,000 animals and overgrazed the lichens. In the winter of 1963/64, the vast majority died.
120201.m: A population that greatly exceeds its carrying capacity can then crash.

120202.q: What can raise the carrying capacity of a habitat for a species?
120202.e: K depends on the resources of the habitat, not on properties of the population such as birth rate or r.
120202.m: The carrying capacity is determined by the supply of resources.

120203.q: How large is the increase of a logistically growing population that has exactly reached its carrying capacity?
120203.e: At N = K, the factor (1 − N/K) becomes zero. Births and deaths then balance each other out.
120203.m: At the carrying capacity, a population no longer grows on average.

120204.q: What is the braking factor (1 − N/K) for a population with N = 750 and a carrying capacity of K = 1,000?
120204.e: 1 − 750/1,000 = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25. The population therefore grows at only a quarter of its maximum per capita rate.
120204.m: The closer N is to K, the smaller the braking factor becomes.

120205.q: What does the letter K stand for in the K-strategy?
a: The carrying capacity of a habitat
120205.e: K stands for the carrying capacity, the largest number of individuals that a habitat can feed permanently. K-strategists usually live close to this limit. The r stands for the growth rate.
120205.m: K stands for the carrying capacity of a habitat.

120206.q: Which feature is typical of K-strategists?
a: Few offspring with intensive parental care
120206.e: K-strategists usually live close to the carrying capacity. They invest a lot in a few offspring, which therefore have a good chance of survival.
120206.m: K-strategists rely on a few well-cared-for offspring.

120207.q: Which animal is a typical r-strategist?
120207.e: Aphids multiply very quickly and can form huge colonies within a few weeks. The other species have only a few young that grow up slowly.
120207.m: Aphids are a textbook example of r-strategists.

120208.q: Which animal is a typical K-strategist?
120208.e: Elephants have a very long pregnancy, usually only one calf, and look after it for years. Their population fluctuates little.

120209.q: Which kind of habitat favours r-strategists?
a: Stable habitats close to carrying capacity
120209.e: After disturbances such as floods, resources are suddenly free. Whoever multiplies quickly can use them first.
120209.m: Rapidly changing habitats favour species with a high rate of reproduction.

120210.q: Which type of survivorship curve is typical of many r-strategists?
a: Type III with high mortality of the young
Type I with mortality in old age
Type IV with rising life expectancy
120210.e: In type III, most of the offspring die very early. Only a few reach adulthood, as in many fish and insects.
120210.m: r-strategists usually show a type III survivorship curve.

120211.q: Where do the letters r and K in the terms r-strategy and K-strategy come from?
a: From the names of two researchers
