120211.e: r is the growth rate and K the carrying capacity in the logistic equation. r-strategists maximise reproduction, K-strategists are adapted to life near the carrying capacity.
120211.m: The terms r-strategy and K-strategy refer to parameters of logistic growth.

120212.q: Which plant shows typical features of an r-strategy?
120212.e: Dandelions grow quickly, produce a great many light seeds and colonise open ground fast. Trees such as the yew grow slowly and live to a great age.
120212.m: Pioneer plants such as the dandelion often follow an r-strategy.

120213.q: What does the first Lotka-Volterra rule state?
a: Predator and prey numbers fluctuate periodically, with the predators lagging behind
Predators and prey always remain equally common
The predators fluctuate more and ahead of the prey
120213.e: In the model, predators increase when there is plenty of prey, after which the prey decreases, and then the predators too. This creates out-of-phase oscillations.
120213.m: According to the first rule, predator and prey numbers fluctuate periodically and out of step.

120214.q: What does the second Lotka-Volterra rule state?
a: The average values of both populations stay constant in the long term
The predators increase all the time
The fluctuations get stronger and stronger
The prey never reaches its average value
120214.e: Despite the oscillations, the sizes of the predator and prey populations averaged over a long time stay the same in the model.
120214.m: According to the second rule, the average numbers of predator and prey are preserved.

120215.q: What does the third Lotka-Volterra rule state if predators and prey are reduced by the same amount?
a: The prey recovers faster than the predators
120215.e: After an even reduction, the prey faces fewer enemies and can grow rapidly. The predators at first find little food.
120215.m: The third rule predicts that the prey recovers faster after a reduction.

120216.q: Which pair of animals is often used as an example of predator-prey cycles, based on fur trade records from Canada?
120216.e: The Hudson’s Bay Company recorded the number of furs traded over many decades. These records show regular fluctuations in hares and lynxes.
120216.m: The fur numbers of hares and lynxes are a classic example of population cycles.

120217.q: Roughly how long is one cycle in the population fluctuations of the snowshoe hare and Canada lynx?
120217.e: The populations reach a peak about every nine to eleven years. This is why people often speak of the ten-year cycle.
120217.m: The hare and lynx populations in Canada fluctuate in a roughly ten-year rhythm.

120218.q: Which observation inspired the mathematician Vito Volterra to develop his predator-prey model?
a: Fishing records from the Adriatic from the time of the First World War
120218.e: The biologist Umberto D’Ancona noticed that the proportion of predatory fish had risen during the war, when there was little fishing. Volterra looked for a mathematical explanation.
120218.m: Volterra’s model came from analysing fishing records.

120219.q: How does the prey population behave in the Lotka-Volterra model when there are no predators?
120219.e: The simple model assumes unlimited resources for the prey without predators. Its growth is therefore exponential.
120219.m: In the simple Lotka-Volterra model, prey grows without limit if there are no predators.

120220.q: In which decade did Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra independently develop their predator-prey equations?
120220.e: Lotka published his equations in 1925, Volterra in 1926. That is why they bear both names.
120220.m: The Lotka-Volterra equations date from the 1920s.

120221.q: Why do real predator-prey systems often not follow the Lotka-Volterra rules exactly?
a: Predators often use several prey species
120221.e: The model only includes one predator and one prey species. In nature, other prey animals, diseases, weather and limited food also play a role.
120221.m: The Lotka-Volterra rules only apply to a greatly simplified predator-prey system.

120223.q: Which Russian biologist demonstrated the competitive exclusion principle with laboratory experiments in 1934?
120223.e: Gause kept single-celled organisms in shared cultures and observed that one species completely displaced the other.
120223.m: Gause provided the first experimental evidence of competitive exclusion.

120224.q: What did Gause observe when he kept two species of paramecium together in one culture?
a: One species completely displaced the other
Both species grew better than alone
The species merged into a new species
120224.e: In separate cultures, both species grew well. Kept together, Paramecium aurelia displaced Paramecium caudatum because both used the same food.
120224.m: In Gause’s experiment, one paramecium species displaced the other.

120225.q: Why do a great many algal species live side by side in open water, even though they compete for the same few nutrients?
a: Conditions change constantly, so no species stays superior for long
Each algal species lives in its own lake
The species share their nutrients fairly
120225.e: This puzzle is called the paradox of the plankton. Light, temperature and nutrients change all the time, so the balance in which one species displaces all others is never reached.
120225.m: Changing conditions prevent one algal species from displacing all others.

120226.q: Which form of competition does the competitive exclusion principle deal with?
120226.e: The principle concerns competition between different species. Competition within a species is called intraspecific.
120226.m: Competition between different species is called interspecific.

120227.q: An animal defends its territory and so keeps competitors away from the food. Which form of competition is this?
a: Competition only through using up the same food
120227.e: Experts call this interference competition: one competitor actively denies the other access. In exploitation competition, both simply use up the same resource.
120227.m: In direct competition, an animal actively hinders its competitor.

120228.q: When can two competing species exist permanently in the same habitat?
a: When they eat exactly the same food
When one species grows twice as fast
When both species are the same size
120228.e: If species use different resources, competition within each species is stronger than between the species. This way each species limits itself before it displaces the other.
120228.m: Different niches make living together possible.

120229.q: Which condition must be met for competitive exclusion to happen at all?
a: A limited resource that is shared
120229.e: Competition only arises when a resource is scarce. If there is plenty of food or space, the species do not get in each other’s way.
120229.m: Without a scarce shared resource, there is no competition.

120230.q: What is meant by niche differentiation?
a: The evolutionary division of resources between species
120230.e: Because of competition, selection favours individuals that use slightly different resources. Over generations, this produces different ecological niches.
120230.m: Niche differentiation reduces competition between species through different use of resources.

120231.q: Several species of warbler in North America search for insects in the same conifers. How do they avoid strong competition?
a: They use different parts of the trees
They take turns feeding every other day
120231.e: A study from the 1950s showed that the species prefer to hunt at different heights and zones of the trees, for example at the top or close to the trunk.
120231.m: Even on the same tree, species can occupy separate niches.

120232.q: What is it called when competing species differ more where their ranges overlap than where they live apart?
120232.e: In Darwin’s finches, for example, the beak sizes of two species differ more on islands they share. This way they use seeds of different sizes.
120232.m: Character displacement is a visible result of niche differentiation.

120233.q: What is the niche called that a species actually occupies when competitors are present?
120233.e: The fundamental niche includes all conditions under which a species could live. Because of competition, the range actually used is usually smaller.
120233.m: The realised niche is limited by competitors.

120234.q: How does ecology understand the term “ecological niche”?
a: As all the conditions and resources a species uses
As the place where an animal builds its nest
As a hiding place from predators
As a territory that a species defends
120234.e: According to G. Evelyn Hutchinson, the niche is a multidimensional space of factors such as temperature, food and humidity. So it is not a place but the role of a species in the ecosystem.
120234.m: An ecological niche is not a place but the way a species uses its environment.

120235.q: What did Joseph Connell show with two species of barnacle on the rocky coast of Scotland?
a: The weaker species is pushed into the upper tidal zone
The stronger species lives only in fresh water
120235.e: Chthamalus could also live lower down, but there it is displaced by the stronger competitor Balanus. Higher up, Chthamalus survives because it tolerates drying out better.
120235.m: Connell’s barnacles show the difference between the possible and the actual niche.

120236.q: Birds of prey hunt mice by day, owls by night. Which form of niche differentiation is this?
120236.e: Both groups use similar prey but at different times of day. As a result, they compete less directly.
120236.m: Species can avoid competition by being active at different times.

120237.q: What are species with a very broad ecological niche called?
120237.e: Generalists such as the red fox use many food sources and habitats. Specialists depend on a few resources.
120237.m: Generalists have a broad niche, specialists a narrow one.

a: A group of spatially separate subpopulations linked by migration
All the species of an ecosystem
A population made up of two species
120238.e: Subpopulations in separate patches of habitat can die out and be founded again by newcomers. Together they form a metapopulation.
120238.m: A metapopulation consists of connected subpopulations.

120239.q: Why is exchange between subpopulations important for their survival?
a: Patches where they have died out can be recolonised
120239.e: If a subpopulation dies out, newcomers can recolonise the patch. They also bring new genetic diversity with them.

120240.q: In the Levins model, the equilibrium proportion of occupied patches is p = 1 − e/c. What is p when e = 0.2 and c = 0.5?
120240.e: e is the extinction rate and c the colonisation rate. p = 1 − 0.2/0.5 = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. So 60 per cent of the patches are occupied.
120240.m: In the Levins model, more patches are occupied when colonisation clearly outweighs extinction.

120241.q: What is a particular threat to metapopulations in Switzerland?
a: Too much dead wood in the forest
120241.e: Roads, settlements and intensive farming separate habitats. Then animals can no longer move between them and patches where they have died out stay empty.

120242.q: What is the effect called when newcomers save a small subpopulation from dying out?
120242.e: Immigrating individuals top up a shrinking population and bring new genetic diversity.
120242.m: The rescue effect protects small subpopulations through immigration.

120243.q: What is the metapopulation model called in which a large, stable main population supplies small subpopulations?
120243.e: The large main population practically never dies out. From it, smaller patches are colonised again and again.
120243.m: In the mainland-island model, one large population feeds many small ones.

120244.q: What is a subpopulation called that would die out without constant immigration?
120244.e: In a sink, more individuals die than are born. It only survives because animals keep arriving from source populations.
120244.m: Sinks only survive thanks to immigration from source populations.

120245.q: Why are wildlife bridges built over motorways in Switzerland?
a: To feed wild animals along motorways
To keep wild animals away from forests
120245.e: Motorways cut habitats into pieces. Bridges allow animals to move between subpopulations, making exchange and recolonisation possible.

120246.q: Which researchers published the theory of island biogeography in 1967?
a: Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson
120246.e: In their book “The Theory of Island Biogeography”, MacArthur and Wilson explained the number of species on islands with simple processes.
120246.m: Island biogeography was founded by MacArthur and Wilson.

120247.q: According to island biogeography, what determines the number of species on an island?
a: A balance between immigration and extinction
Only the age of the island
Only the height of the highest mountain
The number of people on the island
120247.e: New species arrive while others die out. Where both rates balance, a stable number of species is reached.
120247.m: On islands, the number of species settles as a balance between immigration and extinction.

120248.q: According to the theory, why do more species live on large islands than on small ones?
120248.e: Large islands offer more habitats and larger populations. Large populations die out by chance less often.
120248.m: Larger islands have lower extinction rates and therefore more species.

120249.q: What effect does a greater distance from the mainland have on an island?
120249.e: Distant islands are reached less often by animals, seeds or spores. As a result, fewer new species arrive per unit of time.

120250.q: The species-area relationship is S = c · A to the power of z. By what factor does the number of species increase with z = 0.3 if the area becomes ten times larger?
120250.e: The factor is 10 to the power of 0.3. That gives about 1.995, almost a doubling of the number of species.
120250.m: Ten times the area roughly doubles the number of species.

120251.q: What did Daniel Simberloff and Edward O. Wilson do on small mangrove islands in Florida in the 1960s?
a: They removed all arthropods and watched the recolonisation
120251.e: The islands were fumigated under tents so that no insects or spiders survived. Within about a year, the numbers of species were similar to before.
120251.m: The mangrove experiment confirmed island biogeography in the field.

120252.q: Which volcanic island, where a huge eruption in 1883 wiped out almost all life, is regarded as a field laboratory of recolonisation?
120252.e: After the eruption of 1883, researchers followed the return of plants and animals over decades.
120252.m: Krakatoa is a textbook example of the recolonisation of an island.

120253.q: What is the ongoing exchange of species called when the number of species on an island is in balance?
120253.e: Even in balance, species disappear and new ones arrive. Only their total number stays about the same.
120253.m: A stable balance of species includes constant species turnover.

120254.q: What is the so-called SLOSS debate in nature conservation about?
a: Whether one large or several small reserves are better
Whether species should be bred in zoos
Whether islands should be enlarged artificially
Whether invasive species should be fought
120254.e: SLOSS stands for “Single Large Or Several Small”. The debate arose from applying island biogeography to nature reserves.
120254.m: The SLOSS debate asks about the best size and number of nature reserves.

120255.q: Which part of an arch does the term “keystone species” come from?
120255.e: The keystone at the top of the arch holds all the other stones together. If it is removed, the arch collapses, like an ecosystem without its keystone species.
120255.m: A keystone species holds its ecosystem together like a keystone holds an arch.

120256.q: Robert Paine removed the starfish Pisaster from the rocky coast in the north-west of the USA. What happened?
a: Mussels spread and the number of species fell
120256.e: The starfish prefers to eat mussels. Without it, the mussels overgrew the rocks and pushed out many other species.
120256.m: A single predator can secure the diversity of a whole community.

a: Its influence is much greater than its abundance would suggest
It is the most common species in the ecosystem
120257.e: A keystone species can be rare and still shape the structure of a community. If it disappears, the ecosystem changes greatly.
120257.m: Keystone species have a disproportionately large influence on their ecosystem.

120258.q: Which animal, reintroduced in Switzerland from the middle of the 20th century, is regarded as an “ecosystem engineer” because it reshapes waters?
120258.e: Beavers dam streams and so create ponds, wetlands and dead wood. Many amphibians, insects and fish benefit from this.
120258.m: With its dams, the beaver changes whole landscapes.

120259.q: Why are African elephants regarded as a keystone species of the savannah?
a: They stop scrub spreading by eating and knocking over trees
They are the most common mammals
120259.e: Elephants keep open grasslands open. Without them, many savannahs would slowly turn into bush or woodland.
120259.m: Elephants shape the savannah through their feeding.

120260.q: Why are fig trees regarded as a key resource in many tropical forests?
a: They bear fruit even in times of shortage
120260.e: Because different fig trees fruit at different times, fruit-eating animals find food even when little else is ripe.
120260.m: Figs feed many animals when food is scarce.

120261.q: Which rodents are regarded as a keystone species of the North American prairie?
120261.e: Prairie dogs dig extensive burrow systems, loosen the soil and provide shelter for other animals. They are also prey for many predators.
120261.m: With their burrows, prairie dogs shape the prairie ecosystem.

120262.q: Why is the black woodpecker regarded as a keystone species in Swiss forests?
a: Its holes are used by many other species
It eats all the bark beetles in a forest
It spreads the seeds of the beech
It is the only forest bird
120262.e: Black woodpeckers carve out large nesting holes. Later, stock doves, Tengmalm’s owls, bats or wild bees, for example, move in.
120262.m: The black woodpecker’s holes provide homes for many other forest dwellers.

a: An indirect effect of a predator across several feeding levels
The decrease of energy at each feeding level
120263.e: A predator reduces the number of herbivores, so the plants increase. The effect therefore reaches across several levels of the food chain.
120263.m: In a trophic cascade, a predator acts indirectly all the way down to the plants.

120264.q: In which year were wolves first reintroduced into Yellowstone National Park?
120264.e: In 1995 and 1996, wolves from Canada were brought to the park after the species had been missing there for about 70 years.
120264.m: Wolves returned to Yellowstone National Park in 1995.

120265.q: Which hoofed animals were the main prey of the wolves reintroduced into Yellowstone National Park?
120265.e: Elk make up most of the prey. Fewer elk and more cautious behaviour can take pressure off the vegetation along the rivers.
120265.m: In Yellowstone, wolves mainly hunt elk.

120266.q: In a meadow, spiders eat grasshoppers and grasshoppers eat grasses. How does the amount of grass change if the spiders increase?
120266.e: More spiders eat more grasshoppers or make them more cautious. As a result, less grass is eaten and the amount of plants rises.
120266.m: In a three-level chain, the predator indirectly helps the plants.

120267.q: What is it called when an ecosystem is controlled by predators at the top of the food chain?
120267.e: In top-down control, predators determine the size of the lower levels. In bottom-up control, nutrients and plants limit the system.
120267.m: Top-down control starts from the predators.

120268.q: Why are predatory fish such as pike introduced in the biomanipulation of lakes?
a: So that zooplankton increases and eats more algae
So that the pike eat algae
So that more nutrients get into the water
So that the water gets warmer
120268.e: Pike eat small plankton-eating fish. Without these, the zooplankton that grazes on the algae increases, and the water becomes clearer.
120268.m: More predatory fish can lead to clearer lake water via the zooplankton.

120269.q: What does the “green world hypothesis” of 1960 state?
a: The world is green because predators limit the herbivores
Plants are green because they reflect red light
The Earth is getting greener because of climate change
Green plants are poisonous to animals
120269.e: Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin argued that herbivores do not strip the vegetation bare because they are themselves controlled by predators.
120269.m: According to the green world hypothesis, predators indirectly protect plants.

120270.q: Which effect on Swiss mountain forests is often expected from the return of wolves?
a: Less browsing of young trees by red deer and roe deer
More bark beetles in the spruces
Fewer avalanches because of less snow
More wild boar at high altitudes
120270.e: Wolves hunt red deer and roe deer and keep them on the move. As a result, the feeding pressure on young trees can fall in some places.
120270.m: Large predators can indirectly help forests to regenerate.

120271.q: What is the effect called when prey animals avoid certain areas out of fear of predators?
120271.e: Even the presence of predators changes where and for how long prey animals feed. This can take pressure off plants in dangerous places.
120271.m: The landscape of fear describes changes in behaviour caused by predator pressure.

a: An interaction that benefits both partners
A relationship that harms both partners
A relationship in which one partner is harmed
120272.e: In mutualism, both species involved benefit from each other, for example through food, protection or dispersal.

120273.q: How do ruminants such as cows benefit from the microorganisms in their rumen?
a: The microorganisms make vitamin D from light
120273.e: Vertebrates cannot digest cellulose themselves. Bacteria and single-celled organisms in the rumen break it down and in return get a warm habitat rich in food.
120273.m: Without the organisms in their rumen, cows could hardly make use of grass.

120274.q: What does the fungus receive from its partner plant in mycorrhiza?
120274.e: The plant passes part of its photosynthesis products to the fungus. In return, the fungus supplies it with water and minerals such as phosphate.
120274.m: In mycorrhiza, plant and fungus swap sugar for mineral nutrients.

120275.q: How do legumes such as clover or peas benefit from their root nodule bacteria?
a: The bacteria fix nitrogen from the air
120275.e: Root nodule bacteria convert nitrogen from the air into compounds the plant can use. In return they get sugar and a protected habitat.
120275.m: Root nodule bacteria make nitrogen from the air usable for plants.

120276.q: Which fish removes parasites from larger fish on coral reefs?
120276.e: The cleaner wrasse gets food, and the large fish are freed from parasites. At fixed cleaning stations, even predatory fish let themselves be treated.
120276.m: Cleaner fish and their customers both benefit from the cleaning.

120277.q: How do certain acacias in Central America benefit from the ants that live in their hollow thorns?
a: The ants defend them against herbivores
The ants supply them with water
120277.e: The acacia provides a home and food. The ants attack herbivores and even remove competing plants.
120277.m: Acacia and ant protect and feed each other.

120278.q: Which plant is pollinated by specialised moths whose caterpillars eat some of the seeds in return?
120278.e: The yucca moth places the pollen precisely on the stigma and lays eggs in the ovary at the same time. Both partners depend on each other.
120278.m: Yucca and yucca moth depend closely on each other.

120279.q: What is a mutualism called in which the partners cannot survive without each other?
120279.e: In obligate mutualism, the relationship is vital for at least one, often both partners. Facultative mutualism, by contrast, is useful but not essential.
120279.m: Obligate mutualism is vital for the partners’ survival.

120379.q: In which photoreceptors of the retina is rhodopsin the visual pigment?
120379.e: Rhodopsin is the visual pigment of the rods, which are responsible for seeing in dim light. The cones have other opsins for colour vision.
120379.m: Rhodopsin is the visual pigment of the rods.

120380.q: Which two components make up rhodopsin?
120380.e: Rhodopsin consists of the protein opsin and the light-sensitive molecule retinal bound to it. Only together can they absorb light and trigger a signal.
120380.m: Rhodopsin is made of the protein opsin and the pigment retinal.

120381.q: From which vitamin does the body make the retinal needed for vision?
120381.e: Retinal is the aldehyde form of vitamin A. A lack of vitamin A therefore leads to poor vision at dusk.
120381.m: The body needs vitamin A for the visual pigment.

120382.q: What happens to 11-cis-retinal when it absorbs a photon?
a: It is broken down into carbon dioxide
It splits into two amino acids
It binds a calcium ion tightly
120382.e: Absorbing light causes isomerisation from 11-cis to all-trans-retinal. This change of shape activates the opsin and starts the signalling cascade.

120383.q: What other name is commonly used for rhodopsin?
120383.e: In the dark, rhodopsin has a reddish purple colour and is therefore called visual purple. It bleaches in the light.
120383.m: Because of its colour, rhodopsin is also called visual purple.

120384.q: Why can we hardly see colours at night?
a: Because then almost only the rods work, and they cannot tell colours apart
Because the cones break down rhodopsin at night
Because the pupil closes at night
Because the lens becomes cloudy at night
120384.e: Cones need a lot of light. At dusk almost only the rods are working, with their single visual pigment rhodopsin. They only provide brightness, not colours.
120384.m: All cats are grey in the dark, because only the rods are working.

120385.q: Why does the eye need a few minutes to see well after going from light to dark?
a: The bleached rhodopsin first has to form again
The lens has to change shape
The cones first have to grow
The optic nerve has to cool down
120385.e: Bright light bleaches the rhodopsin of the rods. In the dark it is slowly rebuilt and the eyes become more sensitive. This is called dark adaptation.
120385.m: In the dark, the eye first has to rebuild visual purple.

120386.q: Why can you often see a faint star better at night if you look just to one side of it?
a: There are more rods at the edge of the retina
There are more rods in the centre of the retina
The lens is thicker at the edge of the retina
The star then shines more brightly
120386.e: In the centre of the retina, the yellow spot, there are almost only cones. The light-sensitive rods with rhodopsin sit mainly at the edge.
120386.m: The edge of the retina is more sensitive to faint light.

120387.q: How does the membrane potential of a rod change when exposed to light?
120387.e: When cGMP is broken down, sodium channels close and the cell becomes more negative. In the dark, by contrast, a dark current flows constantly.

120388.q: Which photoreceptors are found almost exclusively in the fovea centralis?
a: Rods and cones in equal parts
120388.e: In the fovea centralis the cones are packed most densely, and rods are largely absent. This makes it the place of the sharpest colour vision.
120388.m: The fovea centralis contains almost only cones.

120389.q: Why is visual acuity greatest in the fovea centralis?
a: Its cones are hardly linked together
Most of the blood vessels are there
The cornea is most strongly curved there
120389.e: In the fovea, almost every cone passes its signal along its own chain to a ganglion cell. This low convergence allows very fine resolution.
120389.m: Little linking of the cones makes the fovea especially sharp-sighted.

120391.q: In which area of the retina is the fovea centralis located?
a: In the macula, the yellow spot
120391.e: The fovea lies in the middle of the macula lutea, the yellow spot. The yellow colour comes from pigments stored there.
120391.m: The fovea centralis lies in the middle of the yellow spot.

120392.q: Which spot on the retina lies on the nose side of the fovea and contains no sensory cells at all?
120392.e: At the blind spot, the optic disc, the optic nerve leaves the eye. Because there are no photoreceptors there, a gap appears in the field of vision, which the brain fills in.
120392.m: The optic nerve leaves the eye at the blind spot.

120393.q: Roughly what is the diameter of the fovea centralis?
120393.e: The fovea centralis measures only around one and a half millimetres. Yet a large part of the visual information that the brain analyses comes from this small area.
120393.m: The fovea centralis is only about one and a half millimetres across.

120394.q: Why does light reach the sensory cells in the fovea particularly unhindered?
a: The inner layers of the retina are pushed to the side
The vitreous body is interrupted there
The sensory cells lie in front of the retina there
120394.e: Normally light has to pass through several layers of cells before it reaches the photoreceptors. In the fovea these layers are pushed aside, which creates a pit.
120394.m: In the fovea, the layers of the retina that get in the way are pushed aside.

120395.q: What are the quick jumps of the eye called that bring objects onto the fovea?
120395.e: Saccades are very fast, jerky eye movements. They direct a point of interest onto the spot of sharpest vision.
120395.m: With saccades, the gaze jumps from target to target.

120396.q: Which condition, common in old age, mainly affects central vision?
120396.e: In age-related macular degeneration, cells in the area of the yellow spot die. Reading and recognising faces become difficult, while side vision is usually preserved.
120396.m: Macular degeneration mainly destroys central vision.

120397.q: What is meant by accommodation of the eye?
a: Adjusting the lens's focusing power to the distance
Adjusting the pupil to the brightness
Moving both eyes towards the nose
120397.e: During accommodation, the lens of the eye changes its shape and therefore its focusing power. In this way near and distant objects are focused sharply on the retina.
120397.m: Accommodation is the eye focusing on different distances.

120398.q: Which muscle is responsible for accommodation?
120398.e: The ring-shaped ciliary muscle in the ciliary body changes the tension on the lens through the suspensory fibres. This changes the lens's curvature.
120398.m: The ciliary muscle focuses the eye.

120399.q: What happens when you look at something close up?
a: The ciliary muscle tightens and the lens becomes rounder
The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens becomes flatter
The cornea becomes flatter and thinner
The lens moves back towards the retina
120399.e: When the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory fibres slacken. The elastic lens takes on a rounder shape and bends the light more strongly.
120399.m: For close vision, the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes rounder.

120400.q: What are the fibres called from which the lens of the eye is suspended?
120400.e: The zonular fibres connect the ciliary body to the lens capsule. Their tension determines how flat the lens is.
120400.m: The lens of the eye hangs from the zonular fibres.

120401.q: What is the main cause of age-related long-sightedness?
120401.e: Over the years the lens becomes harder and can hardly become rounder any more. That is why many people need reading glasses from about the age of 45.
120401.m: Age-related long-sightedness happens because the lens becomes stiffer.

120402.q: What is the power of a lens with a focal length of 0.25 m?
120402.e: The power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres: 1 / 0.25 m gives 4 dioptres.
120402.m: The power in dioptres is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres.

120403.q: An eye has its far point at infinity and its near point at 0.1 m. What is its range of accommodation?
120403.e: The range of accommodation is 1/near point minus 1/far point: 1 / 0.1 m minus 0 gives 10 dioptres.
120403.m: The range of accommodation shows by how many dioptres the lens can increase its power.

120404.q: Which two reactions accompany accommodation when you look at something close up?
a: Convergence and narrowing of the pupils
Divergence and widening of the pupils
Convergence and widening of the pupils
120404.e: When looking at something close, both eyes turn inwards and the pupils become narrower. Together with accommodation this is called the near response.
120404.m: In near vision, accommodation, convergence and narrowing of the pupils work together.

120405.q: Which part of the autonomic nervous system triggers accommodation for near vision?
120405.e: The ciliary muscle is supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve. Activating them leads to adjustment for near vision.
120405.m: The parasympathetic nervous system controls the ciliary muscle.

a: A clouding of the lens of the eye
120406.e: In a cataract, the normally clear lens becomes increasingly cloudy. The light is scattered and the image looks blurred.
120406.m: In a cataract, the lens of the eye becomes cloudy.

120407.q: The German everyday name for a cataract is “grey star”. What is the medical term?
120407.e: In medicine the “grey star” is called a cataract. The word comes from Greek and means something like waterfall.
120407.m: The “grey star” is called a cataract.

120408.q: Which form of cataract is by far the most common?
120408.e: Most cataracts develop in later life due to changes in the lens proteins. This is called age-related cataract.
120408.m: Cataracts usually appear in old age.

120409.q: How is a cataract treated today?
a: The cloudy lens is replaced by an artificial lens
Eye drops make the lens clear again
The cornea is removed with a laser
120409.e: Medicines cannot reverse the clouding. During the operation the lens is removed and an intraocular lens is inserted.
120409.m: A cataract is treated with an artificial lens.

120410.q: How is a cataract operation usually carried out today?
a: As a day patient with local anaesthetic
Under general anaesthetic for many hours
120410.e: Cataract surgery is one of the most common operations of all. It usually takes less than half an hour, and you can go home afterwards.
120410.m: Cataract surgery is usually a short procedure without a hospital stay.

120411.q: Which radiation is considered a risk factor for cataracts?
120411.e: Years of exposure to UV light damage the proteins of the lens. Sunglasses with UV protection lower the risk.
120411.m: UV protection for the eyes helps prevent cataracts.

a: A clouding of the lens capsule after the operation
A second cataract in the other eye
A cataract that only causes trouble at night
Bleeding in the retina after the operation
120412.e: After cataract surgery, the rear lens capsule that is left behind can become cloudy. It is usually opened with an Nd:YAG laser without a hospital stay.
120412.m: A secondary cataract is a later clouding of the lens capsule.

120413.q: Which complaints are typical of an early cataract?
a: Double vision only when looking up
120413.e: The clouding of the lens scatters the light. Those affected see as if through fog and are strongly dazzled by headlights, for example.
120413.m: A cataract makes vision foggy and sensitive to glare.

120414.q: The German everyday name for glaucoma is “green star”. What is the medical term?
120414.e: The “green star” is called glaucoma. It covers a group of diseases with progressive damage to the optic nerve.

120415.q: Which structure is damaged in glaucoma?
120415.e: In glaucoma, nerve fibres of the optic nerve die. This leads to permanent gaps in the field of vision.
120415.m: In glaucoma, the optic nerve suffers.

120416.q: What is the most important risk factor for glaucoma?
a: Blood sugar that is too low
Reading a lot under artificial light
120416.e: Pressure inside the eye that stays too high presses on the head of the optic nerve. But there are also glaucomas with normal pressure.
120416.m: Raised pressure inside the eye is the main risk factor for glaucoma.

120417.q: Which examination is usual from about the age of 40 for the early detection of glaucoma?
a: Measuring the pressure inside the eye
120417.e: Eye doctors measure the pressure inside the eye and look at the optic nerve. In this way glaucoma can be detected before you notice anything yourself.
120417.m: From 40, it is worth having the pressure inside your eyes checked.

120418.q: The draining of which fluid is often disturbed in glaucoma?
120418.e: Aqueous humour is constantly produced in the eye and drains away again. If the drainage is disturbed, the pressure inside the eye rises.
120418.m: Blocked drainage of aqueous humour raises the pressure inside the eye.

120419.q: Why is chronic glaucoma often noticed only late?
a: The gaps begin painlessly at the edge of the field of vision
It goes away again from time to time
120419.e: In the common open-angle glaucoma, the gaps first appear in the outer field of vision and do not hurt. That is why check-ups from middle age onwards are important.
120419.m: Glaucoma creeps in unnoticed from the edge.

120420.q: Which form of glaucoma is an eye emergency?
120420.e: In acute angle closure, the drainage angle suddenly closes and the pressure rises sharply. Typical signs are pain, a rock-hard eyeball, worsening vision and nausea.
120420.m: An acute glaucoma attack must be treated immediately.

120421.q: How is open-angle glaucoma usually treated first?
120421.e: Eye drops lower the pressure by reducing the production of aqueous humour or improving its drainage. Nerve fibres that have already been lost, however, cannot be recovered.
120421.m: Glaucoma is usually treated with pressure-lowering drops.

120422.q: How is the common red-green colour blindness inherited?
120422.e: The genes for the red and green opsins lie on the X chromosome. The condition is inherited recessively.
120422.m: Red-green colour blindness is inherited X-linked recessive.

120423.q: For which job is normal colour vision usually a requirement?
120423.e: In the cockpit, coloured signals, lights and displays must be recognised reliably. Colour vision is therefore tested in the aviation medical check.
120423.m: Pilots must be able to tell colours apart reliably.

120424.q: Roughly how many men in Central Europe have red-green colour blindness?
120424.e: In Central Europe, about one in every eleven or twelve men is affected, while among women it is less than one per cent. The reason is inheritance via the X chromosome.
120424.m: Red-green colour blindness affects many more men than women.

120425.q: What does not work properly in red-green colour blindness?
a: One type of cone in the retina
120425.e: There are three types of cone for colour vision. In red-green colour blindness, the red or the green cone is missing or altered.
120425.m: In red-green colour blindness, one type of cone is affected.

120426.q: Why do women have red-green colour blindness much less often than men?
a: They have no Y chromosome on which the gene lies
120426.e: The gene lies on the X chromosome. Women have two of them, so a healthy X makes up for the altered one. Men have only one X.
120426.m: A second X chromosome usually protects women from red-green colour blindness.

120427.q: Which picture plates are often used to test for red-green colour blindness?
120427.e: Ishihara plates show numbers made of coloured dots. People with red-green colour blindness cannot make out certain numbers or see different ones.

120428.q: How can you help people with red-green colour blindness when making charts and maps?
a: Show information with shapes, patterns or text as well
120428.e: Red and green are hard to tell apart for those affected. If shapes, patterns or labels add to the colour, the information is readable for everyone.
120428.m: Good charts do not rely on colour alone.

120429.q: After which scientist is colour blindness also called Daltonism?
120429.e: In 1794 the English chemist John Dalton described his own colour vision deficiency. It is often called Daltonism after him.
120429.m: John Dalton was the first to describe his own colour blindness.

120430.q: Where is the organ of Corti?
a: In the cochlea of the inner ear
120430.e: The organ of Corti lies in the cochlea on the basilar membrane. It converts sound vibrations into nerve signals.
120430.m: The organ of Corti is the hearing organ in the cochlea.

120431.q: What job does the organ of Corti do in the inner ear?
a: It converts sound vibrations into nerve signals
It balances the pressure in the middle ear
120431.e: The hair cells sit in the organ of Corti. They are moved by sound vibrations and turn them into nerve signals for the auditory nerve.
120431.m: The organ of Corti turns sound into nerve signals.

120432.q: What are the sensory cells in the organ of Corti called?
120432.e: The hair cells carry fine sensory hairs. When these are bent by sound, a nerve signal is produced.
120432.m: The sensory cells for hearing are hair cells.

120433.q: Roughly how many turns does the human cochlea have?
120433.e: The human cochlea is a bony passage with around two and a half turns. Unrolled, it would be about three centimetres long.
120433.m: The human cochlea has about two and a half turns.

120434.q: Why can very loud noise lead to permanent hearing loss?
a: It damages the hair cells, which do not grow back
It makes the ear bones melt
120434.e: The hair cells in the inner ear are overloaded by noise and can die. In humans they do not grow back, so the hearing loss remains.
120434.m: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back in humans.

120435.q: Through which nerve do the signals from the organ of Corti reach the brain?
120435.e: The cochlear nerve is part of the eighth cranial nerve. It passes the hearing information on to the brainstem.
120435.m: The cochlear nerve carries the signals of the organ of Corti.

120437.q: Roughly what range of frequencies can a young person hear?
120437.e: Human hearing picks up about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second. With age, mainly the upper limit drops.
120437.m: Young people hear from about 20 hertz to 20 kilohertz.

120438.q: In which part of the ear are the hair cells for hearing?
120438.e: The hair cells sit in the organ of Corti in the cochlea of the inner ear. There, sound waves are converted into nerve signals.
120438.m: The sensory cells for hearing sit in the cochlea.

120439.q: What do the hair cells in the inner ear convert?
120439.e: Sound makes the fluid in the cochlea vibrate. The tiny hairs of the hair cells are bent, and the cells produce an electrical signal.
120439.m: Hair cells turn vibrations into nerve signals.

120440.q: Which sounds are picked up by the hair cells at the start of the cochlea, near the oval window?
120440.e: Each section of the cochlea is tuned to certain frequencies. High sounds are picked up at the start, low sounds at the tip of the cochlea.
120440.m: High sounds are heard at the start of the cochlea.

120441.q: What are the fine projections on the top of hair cells called?
120441.e: The stereocilia are arranged like steps and linked by fine tip links. When they are bent, ion channels open.
120441.m: The tiny hairs of hair cells are called stereocilia.

120442.q: How does the age-related loss of hair cells usually show itself first?
a: You hear high sounds less well
You hear low sounds less well
120442.e: The hair cells for high sounds are the first to be lost with age. That is why older people find it hard to hear high voices or birdsong.
120442.m: In old age, high sounds are the first to become harder to hear.

120443.q: Why does noise-induced hearing loss usually remain permanent in humans?
a: Destroyed hair cells do not grow back
120443.e: In mammals, destroyed hair cells of the cochlea are not replaced. Birds, on the other hand, can regenerate them, which is being researched intensively.
120443.m: Lost hair cells cannot be replaced in humans.

120444.q: Why is a hearing screening done for newborn babies?
a: So that a hearing problem is detected early
To check the shape of the ears
So that the child learns to speak faster
120444.e: If a hearing problem is discovered early, help can come quickly, for example with hearing aids. This is important for language development.
120444.m: Hearing problems detected early can be treated better.

120445.q: Which device can directly stimulate the auditory nerve in deafness caused by destroyed hair cells?
120445.e: A cochlear implant is placed in the cochlea. It converts sound into electrical pulses and uses them to stimulate the auditory nerve directly.
120445.m: A cochlear implant takes over the job of destroyed hair cells.

120446.q: How does a cochlear implant work?
a: It stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrical pulses
It amplifies sound in the ear canal
It mechanically replaces the ear bones
It transmits sound through the skull bone
120446.e: A cochlear implant converts sound into electrical signals, which stimulate the auditory nerve through electrodes in the cochlea. In this way the damaged hair cells are bypassed.
120446.m: A cochlear implant stimulates the auditory nerve electrically.

120447.q: Which condition must be met for a cochlear implant?
a: The hair cells must be healthy
The middle ear must be inflamed
120447.e: The implant takes over the work of the hair cells, not that of the nerve. Without a working auditory nerve, it cannot bring signals to the brain.
120447.m: A cochlear implant needs a working auditory nerve.

120448.q: Where is the electrode array of a cochlear implant inserted?
120448.e: During the operation, the thin electrode array is pushed into the cochlea. Its contacts lie along the fibres of the auditory nerve.
120448.m: The implant's electrodes lie in the cochlea.

120449.q: Who developed the multi-channel cochlear implant in Australia?
120449.e: In 1978 the Australian surgeon Graeme Clark fitted a multi-channel cochlear implant in Melbourne. This development shaped today's devices.
120449.m: Graeme Clark developed the multi-channel cochlear implant.

120450.q: How do the signals of a cochlear implant pass through the skin to the implant?
a: By induction through a coil held by a magnet
Through sound waves in the ear canal
Through light signals through the skull
120450.e: A transmitter coil behind the ear is held in place by a magnet over the implant. Data and energy pass through the skin by electromagnetic induction.
120450.m: In a cochlear implant, a coil transmits the signals through the skin.

120451.q: What makes a cochlear implant different from a hearing aid?
a: It bypasses the hair cells instead of amplifying sound
It is always set more quietly
120451.e: A hearing aid makes sound louder and still needs working hair cells. The implant stimulates the nerve directly and is suitable for severe hearing loss.
120451.m: Hearing aids amplify, cochlear implants replace the hair cells.

120452.q: Why are children born deaf given a cochlear implant as early as possible?
a: The hearing pathway matures in the first years of life
The operation is banned for adults
The cochlea closes up after birth
120452.e: In the first years of life the brain is especially good at learning to process sounds. If they are missing for too long, the hearing pathway develops less well.
120452.m: Early fitting makes use of the sensitive phase of hearing development.

120453.q: What job does the speech processor of a cochlear implant do?
a: It splits sound into frequency bands
It measures the pressure inside the eye
It creates sound in the middle ear
120453.e: The speech processor picks up sound with a microphone and divides it into frequency channels. Each channel controls a particular electrode.
120453.m: The speech processor shares the sound out among individual electrodes.

120454.e: The organ of balance lies in the labyrinth of the inner ear, right next to the cochlea. Both are filled with endolymph.
120454.m: The organ of balance is in the inner ear.

120455.q: How many semicircular canals does the vestibular organ have on each side?
120455.e: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals that are roughly at right angles to each other. In this way rotations in all directions can be detected.
120455.m: Each organ of balance has three semicircular canals.

120456.q: What do the semicircular canals in the inner ear detect?
a: The air pressure in the middle ear
120456.e: When you turn, the fluid in the semicircular canals lags behind a little and bends fine sensory hairs. In this way the organ of balance reports rotations to the brain.
120456.m: The semicircular canals report rotating movements of the head.

120457.q: Which parts of the vestibular organ detect gravity and straight-line acceleration?
120457.e: The macula organs in the utricle and saccule carry a membrane with tiny crystals. It shifts with linear acceleration or tilting.
120457.m: The utricle and saccule measure gravity and linear acceleration.

120458.q: What are the otoliths in the organ of balance made of?
120458.e: The ear stones are tiny crystals of calcium carbonate. Because they are heavier than their surroundings, they react to gravity.
120458.m: The ear stones are made of calcium carbonate.

120459.q: Why do you still feel dizzy for a moment after spinning quickly in a circle, even though you are already standing still?
a: The fluid in the semicircular canals keeps flowing
Blood briefly drains from the head
The eyes are dazzled by the light
120459.e: The fluid in the semicircular canals is sluggish. When you stop turning, it keeps moving for a moment and tricks the brain into sensing a rotation.
120459.m: After spinning, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps flowing.

120460.q: According to current thinking, what causes travel sickness?
a: Conflicting signals from the eyes and the organ of balance
Lack of oxygen in the vehicle
An inflammation of the middle ear
120460.e: If you read in a car, for example, your eyes report stillness but your organ of balance reports movement. This sensory conflict can cause nausea and dizziness.
120460.m: Travel sickness comes from a conflict between sight and balance.

a: Loose otoliths get into a semicircular canal
A clouding of the lens in the eye
120461.e: Loose ear stones move in the semicircular canal when you change position and trick the brain into sensing a rotation. With special positioning manoeuvres they can be moved back.
120461.m: In positional vertigo, stray ear stones disturb the semicircular canals.

120462.q: Which reflex keeps your gaze steady on a target when you move your head?
120462.e: When the organ of balance reports a head turn, the eyes immediately move just as fast in the opposite direction. This keeps the image on the retina stable.
120462.m: The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilises the gaze.

120463.q: What does adaptation mean in sensory physiology?
a: Adjusting sensitivity to the strength of a stimulus
Passing a stimulus on to the brain
120463.e: In adaptation, sensory systems change their sensitivity depending on how strong a lasting stimulus is. This keeps them useful in very different surroundings.
120463.m: Adaptation is a sense adjusting to the strength of a stimulus.

120464.q: Why are you dazzled when you step out of a dark room into sunlight?
a: The retina is still set for darkness
The lens of the eye briefly clouds over
The optic nerve is temporarily interrupted
120464.e: In the dark the retina is very sensitive and the pupil is wide. Until light adaptation is complete, the light seems unpleasantly glaring.
120464.m: After darkness the eye needs a moment for light adaptation.

120465.q: Which sensory cells of the retina allow you to see at dusk after a while?
120465.e: The rods are much more sensitive to light than the cones but cannot tell colours apart. During dark adaptation they take over after a few minutes.
120465.m: In the dark we see mainly with the rods.

120466.q: Which of the eye's ways of adapting to brightness happens fastest?
120466.e: The pupil narrows or widens within fractions of a second to seconds. Biochemical adjustments in the retina take much longer.
120466.m: The pupil is the fastest to adjust how much light gets in.

120467.q: Why do you hardly feel the clothes you are wearing after a short time?
a: The spinal cord blocks all stimuli
120467.e: Fast-adapting mechanoreceptors mainly report changes. When the pressure stays the same, their signals quickly become weaker.
120467.m: Fast-adapting touch cells mainly report changes.

120468.q: Which sensory receptors hardly adapt at all, which is seen as a protective function?
120468.e: Nociceptors keep reporting tissue damage even when it lasts a long time. In this way the warning stays until the cause is removed.

120469.q: Why can you no longer smell the scent in a room after a while?
a: The scent substances break down at once
120469.e: Olfactory cells and the smell pathway reduce their sensitivity when a smell lasts. Someone entering the room fresh, however, notices the smell clearly.
120469.m: The nose quickly gets used to smells that stay the same.

120470.q: What colour is the afterimage after you have stared at a red surface for a long time?
120470.e: The red-sensitive cones adapt while you stare and become less sensitive. On a white surface, the opposite colour then dominates.
120470.m: An afterimage appears in the opposite colour.

120471.q: What is corrected with a LASIK operation?
120471.e: LASIK stands for laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis. The laser reshapes the cornea so that you can see sharply without glasses; a cataract, by contrast, affects the lens.

120472.q: Which tissue is reshaped in LASIK?
120472.e: The cornea provides most of the eye's focusing power. If its curvature is changed, the focusing power changes permanently.
120472.m: In LASIK, the cornea is reshaped.

120473.q: Which laser is used to remove corneal tissue in LASIK?
120473.e: The excimer laser emits ultraviolet light that removes tissue very precisely and with almost no heat. This allows the cornea to be shaped to within fractions of a micrometre.
120473.m: In LASIK, the excimer laser removes corneal tissue.

120474.q: What is the femtosecond laser used for in femto-LASIK?
a: It measures the pressure inside the eye
120474.e: The femtosecond laser makes a precise cut in the cornea with extremely short pulses. This creates the lid (flap), which is folded back for the reshaping.
120474.m: In femto-LASIK, the femtosecond laser cuts the flap.

120475.q: In PRK the laser is used without a corneal flap. What disadvantage does it have compared with LASIK?
a: Healing takes longer and is more painful
It changes the colour of the eyes
It only works for a few weeks
120475.e: In PRK, the top layer of cells of the cornea is removed and first has to grow back. In return there is no flap, which is an advantage if the cornea is thin.
120475.m: With PRK the eye heals more slowly, but without a corneal flap.

120476.q: How is the cornea changed when short-sightedness is corrected by laser?
a: It is flattened in the middle
It is curved more strongly in the middle
120476.e: A short-sighted eye bends light too strongly. If the cornea becomes flatter in the centre, the focusing power falls and the image lands on the retina.
120476.m: For short-sightedness, the laser flattens the centre of the cornea.

a: A cornea that is too thin
120477.e: For LASIK, enough corneal tissue must remain so that the cornea stays stable. If the cornea is too thin or bulges forward in a cone shape, doctors advise against it.
120477.m: A cornea that is too thin rules out LASIK.

120478.q: What is laser coagulation of the retina often used for?
a: Removing the lens of the eye
120478.e: In diabetic retinopathy, abnormal blood vessels grow in the retina. Targeted laser spots can slow this growth and help prevent bleeding.
120478.m: Laser coagulation protects the retina in diabetes.

120479.q: Unlike light, what does a mechanical wave absolutely need?
120479.e: Mechanical waves happen because particles of a medium push against each other. In a vacuum there are no such particles, so sound, for example, cannot travel there.

120480.q: What does a mechanical wave carry over long distances?
120480.e: The particles only oscillate around their rest position and pass the motion on to their neighbours. So energy travels through the medium, while the particles themselves stay where they are.
120480.m: Waves carry energy, but not matter.

120481.q: A sound wave travels through air at 343 m/s. How fast do the individual air particles move back and forth?
a: Much more slowly, under 1 mm/s at speaking volume
Not at all, they stand completely still
120481.e: The particles only oscillate a tiny amount around their rest position. Their speed is called particle velocity. The speed of sound, on the other hand, describes how fast the wave travels.
120481.m: Particle velocity is the speed of the oscillating particles.

120482.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel in water?
120482.e: Water is much less compressible than air, so sound travels in it a good four times as fast. The value depends a little on temperature and salt content.
120482.m: Sound is about four times faster in water than in air.

120483.q: A rope has a mass per unit length of 0.01 kg/m and is tensioned with 100 N. How fast does a wave travel along it?
120483.e: For waves on a rope, c equals the square root of F divided by the mass per unit length. The square root of 100 N / 0.01 kg/m is the square root of 10,000, so 100 m/s.
120483.m: The tighter a rope is, the faster waves travel along it.

120484.q: How does the speed of sound in air change when the temperature rises?
120484.e: In warmer air the molecules move faster and pass on collisions more quickly. For every degree Celsius, the speed of sound rises by about 0.6 m/s.
120484.m: Sound is faster in warm air.

120485.q: On what paths do water particles move in a deep-water wave?
a: Only forwards in the direction of travel
120485.e: Water waves are a mixture of transverse and longitudinal motion. The particles move in circles whose radius decreases with depth.
120485.m: In deep water, water particles move in circles.

120486.q: How does the intensity of a spherical wave change when you double the distance from the source?
120486.e: The energy spreads over the surface of a sphere, which grows with the square of the radius. Double the distance means four times the area, so a quarter of the intensity.
120486.m: The intensity of a spherical wave decreases with the square of the distance.

120487.q: What must exist between the particles of a medium for a mechanical wave to travel?
120487.e: An oscillation is only passed on if neighbouring particles are coupled to each other by forces. You can picture it as a chain of springs and balls.
120487.m: Coupled particles pass on an oscillation as a wave.

120488.q: How do the particles oscillate in a transverse wave?
a: At right angles to the direction of travel
Parallel to the direction of travel
Only in a circle around the source
120488.e: In transverse waves, the displacement is across the direction of travel. An example is a wave on a rope that is being shaken.
120488.m: In transverse waves, the particles oscillate across the direction of travel.

120489.q: Why are there no transverse waves inside liquids and gases?
120489.e: For a sideways movement, a particle must pull its neighbour along sideways. This needs shear forces, which only solids can take.
120489.m: Transverse waves need a medium that transmits shear forces.

120490.q: Which property can only transverse waves have?
120490.e: In transverse waves, the direction of oscillation can lie in different planes. If it is limited to one plane, the wave is polarised.
120490.m: Only transverse waves can be polarised.

120491.q: What kind of wave travels along a plucked guitar string?
a: A surface wave in the wood
120491.e: The string is pulled sideways, but the disturbance travels along the string. So the movement is at right angles to the direction of travel.
120491.m: Transverse waves travel along a guitar string.

120492.q: Why is the Mexican wave in a stadium a model of a transverse wave?
a: People move up and down, the wave travels sideways
People run along in the direction of the wave
The wave travels through the air
120492.e: Each person stands up and sits down again but stays in their seat. The disturbance moves across the stands at right angles to this.
120492.m: In the Mexican wave only the movement travels, not the people.

120493.q: Which material properties determine the speed of transverse waves in a solid?
a: Mass and volume of the whole body
120493.e: For shear waves, c equals the square root of the shear modulus divided by the density. The stiffer against shear and the lighter the material, the faster the wave.
120493.m: Stiff, light solids carry shear waves quickly.

120494.q: What happens to a crest on a rope when it is reflected at a fixed end?
a: It comes back as a trough
It comes back as a crest
120494.e: At the fixed end, the wave undergoes a phase jump of half a period. So a crest comes back as a trough, while at a free end it comes back as a crest.
120494.m: At a fixed end, a crest is reflected as a trough.

120495.q: What is the highest point of a transverse wave called?
120495.e: In a transverse wave, the points displaced furthest upwards form the crests. The lowest points are called troughs.
120495.m: A transverse wave has crests and troughs.

120496.q: How do the particles oscillate in a longitudinal wave?
a: Parallel to the direction of travel
At right angles to the direction of travel
120496.e: In longitudinal waves, the particles move back and forth in the same direction in which the wave travels.
120496.m: In longitudinal waves, the particles oscillate in the direction of travel.

120497.q: Which material properties determine the speed of longitudinal waves in a thin rod?
120497.e: For longitudinal waves in a thin rod, c equals the square root of Young’s modulus divided by the density. Stiff, light materials carry such waves particularly fast.
120497.m: In a rod, the speed of longitudinal waves depends on Young’s modulus and density.

120498.q: What alternates along the direction of travel in a longitudinal wave?
120498.e: Where particles are pushed together, a compression forms; in between there is a rarefaction. For sound, this corresponds to higher and lower pressure.
120498.m: Longitudinal waves consist of compressions and rarefactions.

120499.q: How do you create a longitudinal wave on a long spring (slinky)?
a: By moving one end back and forth along its length
By twisting the spring around itself
120499.e: A push along the length squeezes coils together, and the compression travels through the spring. Shaking it sideways would create a transverse wave instead.
120499.m: A push along the length creates a longitudinal wave.

120500.q: In which states of matter can longitudinal waves travel?
120500.e: Longitudinal waves only need pressure forces, which every medium can transmit. That is why you can also hear underwater or through a wall.
120500.m: Longitudinal waves travel through solids, liquids and gases.

120501.q: In which of these substances is the speed of sound greatest?
120501.e: In steel, sound travels at about 5000 to 6000 m/s, much faster than in water or gases. The reason is the high stiffness of the metal.
120501.m: Sound is especially fast in metals.

120502.q: Why does your voice sound higher after breathing in helium?
a: Sound is faster in helium, so the resonances in the throat rise
The vocal cords vibrate much faster
120502.e: In helium, the speed of sound is almost three times as great as in air. This shifts the resonant frequencies of the mouth and throat upwards, while the basic frequency of the vocal cords stays almost the same.
120502.m: Helium changes the tone of the voice because sound travels faster in it.

120503.q: Which animals also communicate over long distances using infrasound?
120503.e: Elephants make low-frequency sounds below the limit of human hearing. Because they are damped very little, these carry several kilometres.

a: As the distance between two neighbouring points in the same phase
As the greatest displacement of the wave
As the time for one oscillation
As the distance the wave travels in one minute
120504.e: The wavelength is, for example, the distance from one crest to the next. It is written with the Greek letter lambda.
120504.m: The wavelength is the distance between two points in the same phase.

120505.q: What is the wavelength of a 686 Hz tone in air with c of 343 m/s?
120505.e: Wavelength equals c divided by f: 343 m/s / 686 Hz gives 0.5 m.
120505.m: The wavelength is the speed of travel divided by the frequency.

120506.q: A tone in air with c of 343 m/s has a wavelength of 0.343 m. What is its frequency?
120506.e: The frequency is c divided by the wavelength: 343 m/s / 0.343 m gives 1000 Hz.
120506.m: The frequency is the speed of travel divided by the wavelength.

120507.q: How does the wavelength change when the frequency is doubled at the same speed of travel?
120507.e: Because wavelength times frequency equals the constant speed, the wavelength must be half as large when the frequency doubles.
120507.m: At the same speed, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

120508.q: A dipper in a ripple tank vibrates 10 times a second, and neighbouring crests are 3 cm apart. How fast do the waves travel?
120508.e: c equals λ · f: 0.03 m · 10 Hz gives 0.3 m/s.
120508.m: The speed of travel is wavelength times frequency.

120509.q: What is the wavelength of 5 MHz ultrasound in tissue with c of 1540 m/s?
120509.e: 1540 m/s divided by 5,000,000 Hz gives 0.000308 m, about 0.31 mm. This short wavelength allows detailed images.
120509.m: High ultrasound frequencies have very short wavelengths.

120510.q: What is the quantity 2π divided by the wavelength called?
120510.e: The angular wavenumber k tells you by what phase angle the wave changes per metre. It is the spatial counterpart of angular frequency.
120510.m: The angular wavenumber is two pi divided by the wavelength.

120511.q: A water wave travels at 2 m/s and has a period of 3 s. What is its wavelength?
120511.e: In one period the wave travels exactly one wavelength: 2 m/s · 3 s gives 6 m.
120511.m: In one period, a wave travels exactly one wavelength.

120512.q: Roughly what is the wavelength of a 20 Hz tone in air with c of 343 m/s?
120512.e: 343 m/s divided by 20 Hz gives about 17 m. So low notes have wavelengths the size of a house.
120512.m: Very low notes have wavelengths of many metres.

120513.q: What does the function y(x, t) of a wave describe?
a: The displacement at position x at time t
120513.e: A wave function gives a displacement for every position and every moment. This lets you calculate the shape of the wave at any time.
120513.m: The wave function gives the displacement at every position at every time.

120514.q: How do you calculate the phase velocity from the angular frequency ω and the angular wavenumber k?
120514.e: From ω equals 2πf and k equals 2π/λ, it follows that ω/k equals f times λ. That is the speed of travel.
120514.m: The phase velocity is the angular frequency divided by the angular wavenumber.

120515.q: A wave is described by y = 0.02 m · sin(2π · (5 s⁻¹ · t − 0.5 m⁻¹ · x)). How fast does it travel?
120515.e: From the equation you can read f equals 5 Hz and 1/λ equals 0.5 per metre, so λ equals 2 m. So c equals 5 Hz · 2 m, which is 10 m/s.
120515.m: The speed follows from the frequency and wavelength in a wave equation.

120516.q: In which direction does a wave of the form y = A · sin(ωt−kx) travel?
a: At right angles to the x axis
120516.e: A fixed phase requires x to get larger as time increases. So a minus sign between the terms means travel in the positive x direction.
120516.m: A minus between ωt and kx means travel in the positive x direction.

120517.q: How does the speed of a wave on a guitar string change when you tighten the string?
120517.e: The wave speed on a string grows with the tension. With the same length, the frequency therefore rises and the note becomes higher.
120517.m: A tighter string carries waves faster and sounds higher.

120518.q: Which property of the wave equation allows solutions simply to be added?
120518.e: With a linear equation, the sum of two solutions is again a solution. That is why waves can overlap without disturbing each other.
120518.m: Because the wave equation is linear, waves overlap without disturbing each other.

120519.q: According to d’Alembert, what does every solution of the one-dimensional wave equation consist of?
a: Two wave shapes travelling in opposite directions
A wave that keeps getting faster
A wave that only travels to the right
120519.e: In 1747 d’Alembert showed that every solution can be written as the sum of a shape travelling right and a shape travelling left. Both keep their shape as they travel.
120519.m: Every solution of the wave equation consists of two waves travelling in opposite directions.

120520.q: What phase difference do two points on a wave have that are half a wavelength apart?
120520.e: A whole wavelength corresponds to a phase of 2π. So half a wavelength corresponds to π, and the points oscillate exactly opposite to each other.
120520.m: Points half a wavelength apart oscillate in antiphase.

120521.q: When do two coherent waves reinforce each other most in interference?
a: When the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths
When the path difference is half a wavelength
When one wave is twice as fast
120521.e: With a path difference of 0, λ, 2λ and so on, crest meets crest and trough meets trough. This is called constructive interference.
120521.m: Constructive interference happens when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.

120522.q: At what path difference do two equally strong, coherent waves cancel each other out?
a: At an odd multiple of half a wavelength
At a whole number of wavelengths
At a multiple of two wavelengths
120522.e: At λ/2, 3λ/2 and so on, a crest meets a trough. The displacements then cancel each other out.
120522.m: Waves cancel out at a path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths.

120523.q: What principle do headphones with active noise cancelling work on?
120523.e: Microphones pick up the surrounding noise, and the loudspeaker produces a sound wave in antiphase. The two waves largely cancel each other out.
120523.m: Active noise cancelling wipes out noise with anti-noise.

120524.q: Two tuning forks sound at the same time at 440 Hz and 444 Hz. What is the beat frequency?
120524.e: The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies: 444 Hz minus 440 Hz gives 4 Hz. You hear the volume swell and fade four times a second.
120524.m: The beat frequency is the difference between two close frequencies.

120525.q: What condition must waves meet to produce an interference pattern that is stable over time?
a: They must come from different media
120525.e: Coherent waves have a fixed phase relationship to each other. Only then do the places of reinforcement and cancellation stay in the same spot.

120526.q: Two loudspeakers in phase send out a tone with a wavelength of 1 m. What do you hear at a place with a path difference of 0.5 m?
a: A tone at twice the frequency
120526.e: A path difference of 0.5 m is exactly half a wavelength. There, higher pressure meets lower pressure, and the tone becomes very quiet.
120526.m: At a path difference of half a wavelength it becomes quiet.

120527.q: What shape are the lines of cancellation when two point sources in a ripple tank vibrate in phase?
120527.e: On every nodal line, the difference in distance to the two sources is constant. Curves with a constant difference in distance to two points are hyperbolas.
120527.m: With two point sources, the cancellations lie on hyperbolas.

120528.q: What happens to the energy at places where waves cancel out through interference?
a: It is redistributed to places of reinforcement
It is completely turned into light
It flows back to the source and stops it
120528.e: Interference does not break the law of conservation of energy. What is missing at the nodes appears in addition at the places of constructive overlap.
120528.m: Interference redistributes energy but does not destroy it.

120529.q: What is meant by the diffraction of a wave?
a: The wave spreading into the shadow area behind obstacles
The change of direction at a boundary due to a change in speed
Being thrown back by a wall
The decrease in amplitude due to friction
120529.e: When a wave meets an edge or an opening, it also spreads into areas that geometrically lie in shadow. This behaviour is called diffraction.
120529.m: Through diffraction, waves reach the shadow area.

120530.q: When is diffraction at a slit especially strong?
a: When the slit width is about the same as the wavelength
When the slit is much wider than the wavelength
When the wave is very fast
When the amplitude is very large
120530.e: If the slit is comparable to the wavelength or smaller, the wave spreads out almost in a circle behind it. With very wide openings it stays largely straight.
120530.m: Diffraction is strong when openings are about the size of the wavelength.

120531.q: Why can you hear a person around the corner of a house but not see them?
a: Sound waves are much longer than light waves and are diffracted more
Sound is never reflected by walls
120531.e: Audible sound has wavelengths from centimetres to metres, similar in size to doors and corners. Light has wavelengths below a micrometre and is hardly diffracted by such obstacles.
120531.m: Because of its long wavelength, sound is diffracted around corners.

120532.q: Light with a wavelength of 600 nm falls on a grating with 500 lines per millimetre. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
120532.e: The grating spacing is 1 mm / 500, so 2 µm. With sin α equals λ / g, you get 0.6 µm / 2 µm equals 0.3, and the angle is about 17.5°.
120532.m: With a grating, the first maximum is where the sine of the angle is wavelength divided by grating spacing.

120533.q: Why are there still waves in the harbour basin behind a narrow harbour entrance?
a: The water waves are diffracted at the opening
The harbour water oscillates by itself
The waves are created by the seabed
The ships make all the waves
120533.e: The opening acts like a slit behind which the waves spread out like a fan. That is why the entrance is designed so that as little energy as possible gets into the basin.
120533.m: Harbour entrances diffract incoming waves into the basin.

120534.q: Water waves with a wavelength of 0.1 m meet a slit 0.2 m wide. At what angle is the first minimum?
120534.e: For the first minimum, sin α equals λ / b: 0.1 m / 0.2 m gives 0.5. The matching angle is 30°.
120534.m: The first diffraction minimum depends on the ratio of wavelength to slit width.

120535.q: What is the basic difference between refraction and diffraction?
a: Refraction is caused by a change in speed at a boundary
Refraction only exists in a vacuum
120535.e: In refraction, the wave changes direction when it passes into another medium, because its speed changes. Diffraction, on the other hand, happens at edges and openings within the same medium.
120535.m: Refraction is caused by a change in the speed of travel.

120536.q: What appears on a screen behind a single slit when waves are diffracted?
a: A wide central maximum with weaker side maxima
Only a sharp line the width of the slit
120536.e: Behind the slit, partial waves from different parts of the opening overlap. A bright centre forms, with alternating dark and weaker bright bands.
120536.m: A single slit produces a central maximum with side maxima.

a: Every point on a wavefront is the source of a wavelet
Every wave has exactly one frequency
Waves only travel in straight lines
Waves lose their energy at obstacles
120537.e: According to Huygens, every point on a wavefront sends out spherical wavelets. From these, the further spreading of the wave can be constructed.
120537.m: Every point on a wavefront sends out wavelets.

120538.q: According to Huygens, how is the new wavefront formed?
a: As the envelope of all the wavelets
As the average of the wavelengths
As the line joining the troughs
As the mirror image of the old front
120538.e: You draw small circles around many points of the old front and draw a common tangent. This envelope is the new wavefront.
120538.m: The new wavefront is the envelope of the wavelets.

120539.q: Which country did Christiaan Huygens come from?
120539.e: Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch physicist, mathematician and astronomer of the 17th century. For a time he also worked in Paris.
120539.m: Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch scientist.

120540.q: In which work did Huygens publish his wave theory?
120540.e: Huygens set out his wave theory of light in the “Traité de la lumière”, published in 1690. In “Opticks”, Newton instead put forward a particle idea.
120540.m: Huygens described his wave theory in the “Traité de la lumière”.

120541.q: Who extended the principle by taking the interference of the wavelets into account?
120541.e: Fresnel added that the wavelets overlap and reinforce or cancel each other. This gave the Huygens-Fresnel principle, which can be used to calculate diffraction patterns.
120541.m: The Huygens-Fresnel principle takes the interference of wavelets into account.

120542.q: Which law can be derived using wavelets that travel more slowly in the second medium?
120542.e: When a front meets the boundary at an angle, the wavelets start one after another and travel shorter distances in the second medium. So the new front is bent, as the law of refraction describes.
120542.m: Wavelets can explain the law of refraction.

120543.q: A water wave travelling at 0.4 m/s meets a zone with 0.2 m/s at 30°. Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
120543.e: sin α₂ equals sin α₁ · c₂ / c₁: 0.5 · 0.2 / 0.4 gives 0.25. The matching angle is about 14.5°.
120543.m: When a wave slows down, it bends towards the normal.

120544.q: According to Huygens, what forms behind a very narrow slit that a plane wave hits?
a: A plane wave of the same width
120544.e: If the slit is very narrow, it acts like a single point from which only one wavelet starts. So a circular wave spreads out behind it.
120544.m: A very narrow slit acts like a point source.

120545.q: How does a standing wave form?
a: By the overlap of two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions
By a wave that is suddenly stopped
By two waves of different frequencies in the same direction
120545.e: When two equally strong waves of the same frequency travel against each other, for example after a reflection, a pattern of oscillation forms that stays in place.
120545.m: Standing waves form from two waves travelling in opposite directions.

120546.q: How far apart are two neighbouring nodes of a standing wave?
120546.e: Nodes are where the two waves cancel each other out all the time. These places repeat every λ/2.
120546.m: Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart.

120547.q: A string fixed at both ends is 0.65 m long, and the wave speed is 286 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
120547.e: For the fundamental, half a wavelength fits on the string, so λ equals 1.3 m. So f equals 286 m/s / 1.3 m, which is 220 Hz.
