121210.e: Measles is extremely contagious and spreads through the air. That is why herd protection needs a very high share of immune people.
121210.m: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all.

121211.q: Why does tetanus not have a meaningful basic reproduction number?
a: Tetanus is not passed from person to person
Tetanus is only spread by mosquitoes
121211.e: Tetanus spores get into wounds from the environment, for example from soil. As no person infects another, there is no herd immunity; everyone has to protect themselves by vaccination.
121211.m: Only your own vaccination protects you against tetanus.

121212.q: How is the effective reproduction number R related to R0 when a share s of the population is still susceptible?
a: R equals R0 divided by s
121212.e: The fewer people are still susceptible, the fewer infections succeed. With R0 equal to 3 and s equal to 0.5, R becomes 1.5.
121212.m: The effective reproduction number is R0 times the share of susceptible people.

121213.q: An infection has an R0 of 3. Without countermeasures, how many new infections arise from a single case in the fourth generation of infection?
121213.e: Each generation triples the number: 3, 9, 27, 81. In the fourth generation, there are therefore 3 to the power of 4, which is 81 new cases.
121213.m: If R0 is greater than 1, case numbers grow exponentially.

121214.q: Which value of the effective reproduction number means that an epidemic is dying down?
121214.e: If each case infects fewer than one other person on average, the number of new infections falls from generation to generation. At exactly 1, it stays roughly constant.
121214.m: An epidemic dies down when R is below 1.

121215.q: Which three quantities determine R0 in a simple model?
a: Contact rate, probability of transmission and length of infectiousness
Vaccination rate, death rate and age
121215.e: R0 is roughly the product of the number of contacts per day, the probability of infection per contact and the number of infectious days. Measures such as keeping a distance or isolation reduce these factors.
121215.m: R0 depends on contacts, transmission and how long someone is infectious.

121216.q: A disease has an R0 of 5 and the vaccine protects 90 % of those vaccinated. Roughly what vaccination rate is needed for herd protection?
121216.e: The threshold is 1 minus 1/5, which is 0.8. Because only 90 % of those vaccinated are protected, you need 0.8 divided by 0.9, which is around 0.89 or 89 %.
121216.m: If a vaccine is not fully effective, a higher vaccination rate is needed.

121217.q: What does the vaccination coverage rate describe?
a: The share of a population group that has received a certain vaccination
The number of vaccine doses made per year
How effective a vaccine is in the laboratory
The number of vaccination centres per canton
121217.e: The vaccination coverage rate shows what percentage of a group is vaccinated. It is often recorded separately by age and vaccine dose.
121217.m: The vaccination coverage rate is the share of vaccinated people in a group.

121218.q: At a school, 552 of 600 young people have had two doses of measles vaccine. What is the vaccination coverage rate?
121218.e: 552 divided by 600 gives 0.92. The vaccination coverage rate is therefore 92 %.
121218.m: The coverage rate is calculated as vaccinated people divided by the total number.

121219.q: What two-dose vaccination coverage rate does the WHO recommend to eliminate measles?
121219.e: Because measles is so contagious, at least 95 % of people need to be immune. Only then can chains of infection be reliably broken.

121220.q: In which age groups does Switzerland regularly record vaccination coverage in the cantons?
121220.e: The Swiss vaccination coverage monitoring checks the vaccination records of 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds. The data are published by the Federal Office of Public Health.
121220.m: In Switzerland, vaccination coverage is recorded for 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds.

121221.q: Why does a high vaccination coverage rate also protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
a: Because germs can hardly form chains of infection any more
Because vaccinated people breathe out antibodies
Because unvaccinated people then have fewer contacts
121221.e: If almost everyone is immune, a germ rarely meets susceptible people. In this way babies or people with weak immune systems are protected indirectly; this is called herd protection.
121221.m: High vaccination coverage also protects unvaccinated people indirectly.

121222.q: Why can measles outbreaks happen despite a high national vaccination coverage rate?
a: Unvaccinated people are often clustered in certain groups or regions
The measles vaccine only protects for one year
Measles is only spread by vaccinated people
Measles viruses only survive in cities
121222.e: Averages hide local gaps in vaccination. Where unvaccinated people cluster, for example in certain communities, the virus can spread.
121222.m: Local vaccination gaps allow outbreaks despite good averages.

121223.q: In a municipality, 85 % of children are vaccinated, and the vaccine works in 95 % of those vaccinated. What share of the children is protected as a result?
121223.e: Protected are 0.85 times 0.95, which is 0.8075. That is around 81 % of all children.
121223.m: Only the share of vaccinated people with an effective immune response is protected.

121224.q: What does the vaccination record show when vaccination coverage is surveyed?
a: Which vaccinations are documented and with how many doses
How high the current antibody level is
Which diseases the child has already had
What blood group the child has
121224.e: The surveys analyse the entries in the vaccination record. They count the documented vaccinations and doses, not measured antibodies.
121224.m: Vaccination coverage rates are based on documented vaccinations.

121225.q: From what age does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend the yearly flu vaccination to everyone as a risk group?
121225.e: Older people have a much higher risk of severe flu and complications. That is why the flu vaccination is recommended to them every autumn.
121225.m: From 65, the flu vaccination is recommended every year.

121226.q: In the Swiss vaccination schedule, what are the vaccinations called that are recommended for everyone to protect personal and public health?
121226.e: The schedule distinguishes between basic vaccinations, supplementary vaccinations and vaccinations for risk groups. Basic vaccinations are recommended for the whole population, for example against measles or tetanus.
121226.m: Basic vaccinations are recommended for everyone.

121227.q: Against which three diseases does the MMR vaccination protect, which the Swiss vaccination schedule recommends for young children?
121227.e: MMR stands for measles, mumps and rubella. The schedule recommends two doses in early childhood so that reliable protection exists as early as possible.
121227.m: The MMR vaccination protects against measles, mumps and rubella.

121228.q: Apart from diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough, against which diseases does the six-in-one vaccination for babies protect?
a: Polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b and hepatitis B
121228.e: The hexavalent vaccine protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib and hepatitis B. It is given several times in the first year of life.
121228.m: The six-in-one vaccination also covers polio, Hib and hepatitis B.

121229.q: Why does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend vaccinating babies in their first months of life?
a: Diseases such as whooping cough are especially dangerous for babies
Babies tolerate vaccinations better than adults
Later on vaccinations no longer work at all
Babies are protected against everything from birth
121229.e: Some infections, such as whooping cough, are particularly severe in babies and can be life-threatening. That is why protection should be built up as early as possible.
121229.m: Early vaccinations protect babies from dangerous diseases.

121230.q: At what age does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend the hepatitis B vaccination if it was not given in infancy?
121230.e: The hepatitis B vaccination is preferably given in infancy. If it is missing, it should be caught up in young people between 11 and 15.
121230.m: Young people catch up on a missing hepatitis B vaccination at 11 to 15.

121231.q: Is there a general duty to be vaccinated in Switzerland?
a: No, vaccinations are voluntary in principle
Yes, but only in French-speaking Switzerland
Yes, for all children before kindergarten
121231.e: Vaccinations are voluntary in Switzerland. The law only allows the cantons, in exceptional cases, to make a vaccination compulsory for groups at risk or certain jobs.
121231.m: In Switzerland, vaccinations are voluntary in principle.

121232.q: In the Swiss vaccination schedule, what are vaccinations called that offer individual protection but are not counted as basic for everyone?
121232.e: Supplementary vaccinations mainly protect the vaccinated person against particular risks. Doctors give information about them, and the decision is an individual one.
121232.m: Supplementary vaccinations offer extra personal protection.

121233.q: What kind of body is the EKIF, the Federal Commission for Vaccination?
a: An extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation
A commission of the National Council
A private foundation of the pharmaceutical industry
121233.e: Extra-parliamentary commissions advise the Federal Council and the administration with outside expertise. The EKIF is such a commission for all questions about vaccinations.
121233.m: The EKIF is an extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation.

121234.q: What is the main job of the EKIF?
a: It draws up vaccination recommendations and advises the FOPH and the Federal Council
It approves vaccines for the market
It produces vaccines for the army
It imposes fines for missing vaccinations
121234.e: The EKIF assesses scientific data and draws up vaccination recommendations together with the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH). Approving vaccines, by contrast, is the job of another federal authority.
121234.m: The EKIF draws up vaccination recommendations.

121235.q: Which authority, not the EKIF, is responsible for approving vaccines in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences
The Federal Office for the Environment
121235.e: Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness and grants approval. Only afterwards does the EKIF decide whether and for whom a vaccination is recommended.

121236.q: Who chooses the members of the EKIF?
121236.e: The EKIF is set up by the Federal Council. Its members are experts from medicine and healthcare.
121236.m: The Federal Council chooses the members of the EKIF.

121237.q: What is the German counterpart of the EKIF, based at the Robert Koch Institute, called?
121237.e: In Germany, STIKO publishes the vaccination recommendations. It has a similar role to the EKIF in Switzerland.

121238.q: What role do recommendations from the FOPH and the EKIF play in the cost of a vaccination in Switzerland?
a: Recommended vaccinations are usually paid for by basic health insurance
Recommended vaccinations always have to be paid for yourself
They have no influence on costs
121238.e: For many recommended vaccinations, compulsory health insurance covers the costs if they are listed in the health care benefits ordinance. Travel vaccinations are usually not covered.
121238.m: Recommended vaccinations are usually covered by basic health insurance.

121239.q: What kinds of data does the EKIF take into account for a new vaccination recommendation?
a: Burden of disease, effectiveness, safety and costs
Only the recommendations from the USA
121239.e: The commission weighs up how common and severe a disease is and how well and safely the vaccine works. Practicality and cost-effectiveness are also included.
121239.m: Vaccination recommendations are based on weighing up many data.

121240.q: Which organisation in the USA draws up vaccination recommendations in a similar way to the EKIF?
121240.e: ACIP advises the US health authority CDC on vaccination recommendations. The FDA approves vaccines, much like Swissmedic, and the NIH fund research.
121240.m: In the USA, ACIP recommends vaccinations and the FDA approves them.

121241.q: Roughly how high was the death rate for the severe form of smallpox, variola major?
121241.e: About one in three people who fell ill died of variola major. Many survivors were left with scars or went blind.
121241.m: The severe form of smallpox killed about one in three people who caught it.

121242.q: Who carried out the first vaccination with cowpox against smallpox in 1796?
121242.e: The English country doctor Edward Jenner vaccinated the boy James Phipps with material from cowpox. Afterwards the boy was protected against real smallpox.
121242.m: In 1796 Edward Jenner vaccinated with cowpox for the first time.

121243.q: Where does the word “vaccine” come from?
121243.e: The term recalls Jenner's vaccination with cowpox. “Vaccinia” was the name for cowpox.
121243.m: Vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.

121244.q: What was the older method called in which people were inoculated with material from real smallpox pustules?
121244.e: In variolation, material from smallpox patients was put into small cuts in the skin. This usually led to milder illness, but it was risky and could infect others.
121244.m: Variolation used real smallpox germs and was dangerous.

121245.q: In which year did the World Health Organization officially declare smallpox eradicated?
121245.e: After the last natural case in Somalia in 1977, the World Health Assembly confirmed the eradication on 8 May 1980. It was the first human disease to be eradicated.
121245.m: Smallpox has been considered eradicated since 1980.

121246.q: Which strategy was decisive in the smallpox eradication programme?
a: Surveillance and ring vaccination around every case
Building smallpox hospitals in every town
121246.e: Instead of vaccinating everyone, each case was tracked down and the contacts around it were vaccinated in a targeted way. This strategy is called “surveillance and containment”.
121246.m: Smallpox was eradicated with surveillance and ring vaccination.

121247.q: Which feature of smallpox made its eradication possible?
a: The virus had no animal reservoir
The virus was not very contagious
The virus only lived in mosquitoes
121247.e: Smallpox only infected humans, and sick people were easy to recognise by the pustules. In addition, there was a stable, effective vaccine with long protection.
121247.m: Without an animal reservoir, the smallpox virus could be eradicated.

121248.q: Which simple instrument made vaccinating against smallpox much easier from the late 1960s?
a: The glass syringe with a plunger
121248.e: The bifurcated needle held a drop of vaccine between its two prongs. It was cheap, saved vaccine and could be learned quickly even by non-specialists.
121248.m: The bifurcated needle helped with smallpox vaccination worldwide.

121249.q: Which other infectious disease was eradicated after smallpox, though it is an animal disease?
121249.e: Rinderpest was declared eradicated in 2011 by the World Organisation for Animal Health and the FAO. It is so far the only animal disease to have been eradicated.

121250.q: Which cells does the poliovirus damage in polio?
a: Motor nerve cells in the spinal cord
121250.e: The poliovirus can destroy the motor nerve cells in the front horn of the spinal cord. The muscles they supply then stop working, and floppy paralysis results.
121250.m: Polio destroys motor nerve cells in the spinal cord.

121251.q: How is the poliovirus mainly transmitted?
a: Faecal-oral, through dirty hands, water or food
121251.e: Polioviruses are enteroviruses and multiply in the gut. They are shed in the stool and passed on through contaminated water or hands.

121252.q: Roughly what share of infections with polioviruses lead to paralysis?
121252.e: The great majority of infections cause no symptoms or only mild ones. Fewer than one per cent lead to paralysis, which is why the virus can spread unnoticed.

121253.q: Who developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, approved in 1955?
121253.e: Jonas Salk inactivated the polioviruses with formaldehyde. His vaccine (IPV) is injected and is also used in Switzerland today.
121253.m: Jonas Salk developed the injected inactivated polio vaccine.

121254.q: What risk does Sabin's oral live polio vaccine carry?
a: Rarely, disease-causing vaccine viruses can develop from it
It often causes allergies to sugar
It does not protect against polio at all
It has to be repeated every year
121254.e: The weakened vaccine viruses are shed and can change in poorly vaccinated populations. In this way, circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses rarely arise.
121254.m: The oral polio vaccine can rarely give rise to disease-causing vaccine viruses.

121255.q: In which two countries was wild polio still endemic in 2025?
121255.e: Thanks to the global polio initiative, the wild virus has almost disappeared. As of 2025, it is only endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
121255.m: Wild polio is only endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

121256.q: Which types of wild poliovirus are already considered eradicated?
121256.e: Wild poliovirus type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019. Only type 1 is still circulating.
121256.m: Only wild poliovirus type 1 is still circulating.

121257.q: Which device kept polio patients with paralysed breathing muscles alive in the 1950s?
121257.e: The iron lung creates low pressure in a closed tank so that the chest rises. In this way patients could breathe despite paralysed breathing muscles.
121257.m: The iron lung helped polio patients breathe using low pressure.

121258.q: When was the WHO European Region certified polio-free?
121258.e: The WHO European Region, which includes Switzerland, was declared free of wild polio in June 2002. But the virus can still be brought in, so vaccination continues.
121258.m: Europe has been certified polio-free since 2002.

121259.q: What is the aim of contact tracing?
a: Finding contacts of infected people and breaking chains of infection
Developing new vaccines in the laboratory
Counting the number of hospital beds
121259.e: In contact tracing, people who have had contact with an infected person are identified. They are informed, tested or sent into quarantine before they infect others.
121259.m: Contact tracing breaks chains of infection.

121260.q: What is the difference between isolation and quarantine?
a: Isolation is for sick people, quarantine for people who may have been infected
Isolation is for animals, quarantine for humans
Isolation always lasts longer than a year
121260.e: People who are confirmed to be infected stay in isolation. Quarantine concerns healthy contacts who could have been infected and are therefore kept apart as a precaution.
121260.m: Isolation is for the sick, quarantine for those who may have been infected.

121261.q: What is it called when tracers find out where an infected person caught the infection themselves?
121261.e: Backward tracing looks for the source of infection, such as an event. In this way superspreading events and further cases from the same source are found.
121261.m: Backward tracing looks for the source of an infection.

121262.q: What is the first known infected person in an outbreak called?
121262.e: The index case is the starting point of the investigation. Contacts are traced from there.
121262.m: The index case stands at the start of contact tracing.

121263.q: Who was mainly responsible for contact tracing in Switzerland during the Covid-19 pandemic?
121263.e: Carrying out disease control is largely the job of the cantons. The cantonal medical services organised the contact tracing.
121263.m: In Switzerland, the cantons organise contact tracing.

121264.q: Which technology did the SwissCovid app use to record encounters?
121264.e: The app exchanged anonymous keys with nearby devices via Bluetooth. No locations were stored, and the matching took place in a decentralised way on the phone.
121264.m: The SwissCovid app used Bluetooth instead of location data.

121265.q: Which universities played a leading role in developing the decentralised DP-3T protocol for the SwissCovid app?
a: University of Basel and University of Bern
University of Geneva and University of Fribourg
121265.e: DP-3T stands for Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing. It was developed by an international team led by EPFL and ETH Zurich.
121265.m: The DP-3T protocol comes from EPFL and ETH Zurich.

121266.q: Why does infection before symptoms start make contact tracing harder?
a: Infected people infect others before they know they are ill
Tests do not work at all before symptoms
121266.e: With presymptomatic transmission, tracing often starts too late. That is why testing and informing quickly are crucial.
121266.m: Presymptomatic transmission makes contact tracing harder.

121267.q: For how long are contacts usually monitored in the case of Ebola?
121267.e: The incubation period of Ebola is up to 21 days. Anyone who develops no symptoms during this time is considered not infected.
121267.m: With Ebola, contacts are watched for 21 days.

121268.q: What is the law of refraction for passing from medium 1 into medium 2?
a: n1 · sin α = n2 · sin β
n1 · cos α = n2 · cos β
n1 / sin α = n2 / sin β
121268.e: The product of the refractive index and the sine of the angle to the normal stays the same across the boundary. From this you can work out the angle of refraction.
121268.m: In the law of refraction, the product of refractive index and sine of the angle stays the same.

121269.q: Light passes at 45° from air (n equals 1.00) into water (n equals 1.33). Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
121269.e: sin β equals sin 45° / 1.33 equals 0.707 / 1.33 equals 0.532. So β is about 32°.
121269.m: When light enters water, the angle to the normal gets smaller.

121270.q: Light passes at 50° from air into glass with n equal to 1.60. Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
121270.e: sin β equals sin 50° / 1.60 equals 0.766 / 1.60 equals 0.479. The arcsine of this is about 28.6°.
121270.m: The greater the refractive index, the more strongly light is bent towards the normal.

121271.q: A ray of light hits a plastic from air at 60° and travels inside it at 35° to the normal. Roughly what is the refractive index of the plastic?
121271.e: n equals sin 60° / sin 35° equals 0.866 / 0.574, about 1.51. Here n for air is taken as 1.
121271.m: The refractive index can be found from the angles of incidence and refraction.

121272.q: A ray in glass (n equals 1.50) meets the boundary with air at 25° to the normal. Roughly at what angle does it come out?
121272.e: sin β equals 1.50 · sin 25° equals 1.50 · 0.423 equals 0.634. So β is about 39.3°.
121272.m: When light passes out into air, the angle to the normal gets bigger.

121273.q: The law of refraction is named after which scientist, who found it around 1621?
121273.e: The Dutch mathematician Willebrord van Roijen Snell formulated the law around 1621. René Descartes published it independently in 1637.
121273.m: The law of refraction is named after Snell.

121274.q: From what are the angles of incidence and refraction measured in the law of refraction?
a: From the optical axis of a lens
121274.e: The angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray hits. So a ray that just grazes the surface has almost 90°.
121274.m: In optics, angles are measured from the normal.

121275.q: Light passes at 40° from water (n equals 1.33) into glass (n equals 1.50). Roughly what is the angle of refraction?
121275.e: sin β equals 1.33 · sin 40° / 1.50 equals 1.33 · 0.643 / 1.50 equals 0.570. So β is about 34.7°.
121275.m: The law of refraction applies to any pair of media.

121276.q: Which principle explains the law of refraction as the path with the shortest travel time?
121276.e: According to Fermat, light between two points takes a path for which the travel time is extreme, usually minimal. Because light is slower in the denser medium, the path bends at the boundary.
121276.m: Light takes the path with the shortest travel time.

121277.q: How is the refractive index n of a medium defined?
a: Speed of light in a vacuum divided by speed of light in the medium
Density of the medium divided by density of water
Wavelength in the medium times frequency
Angle of incidence divided by angle of refraction
121277.e: n equals c / v. The slower light is in the medium, the greater the refractive index.
121277.m: The refractive index compares the speed of light in a vacuum with that in the medium.

121278.q: How fast is light in glass with n equal to 1.5?
121278.e: v equals c / n equals 3.0 · 10⁸ m/s / 1.5 equals 2.0 · 10⁸ m/s. So light in glass is a third slower.
121278.m: In glass, light is about a third slower than in a vacuum.

121279.q: Which substance has a refractive index of about 1.31, slightly less than liquid water?
121279.e: Frozen water has a lower density than liquid water and a refractive index of about 1.31. Diamond, flint glass and sapphire are much higher.
121279.m: Ice refracts light slightly less than liquid water.

121280.q: Why does the refractive index of air change slightly with the weather?
a: It depends on the air density, so on pressure and temperature
It depends on the wind direction
It depends on the time of day
It depends on the colour of the sky
121280.e: The denser a gas is, the more molecules interact with the light and the greater the refractive index. Warm air has a lower density and refracts light slightly less.
121280.m: The refractive index of gases depends on their density.

121281.q: What is the refractive index of a vacuum?
121281.e: In a vacuum the speed of light is c, so n equals c / c equals 1. For visible light, practically all substances have a refractive index greater than 1.
121281.m: A vacuum has a refractive index of 1.

121282.q: Roughly what is the refractive index of air under normal conditions?
121282.e: Air refracts light only very slightly; its refractive index is about 1.0003. So in many calculations it is taken as 1.
121282.m: Air has almost the same refractive index as a vacuum.

121283.q: In a medium, the speed of light is 2.25 · 10⁸ m/s. What is its refractive index?
121283.e: n equals c / v equals 3.0 · 10⁸ / 2.25 · 10⁸ equals 1.33. That matches the value for water.
121283.m: The refractive index is calculated from the ratio of the speeds of light.

121284.q: Red light has a wavelength of 600 nm in air. What is the wavelength in water (n equals 1.33)?
121284.e: The frequency stays the same at the boundary, but the speed drops. So λ equals 600 nm / 1.33, which gives about 451 nm.
121284.m: When light enters a medium, the frequency stays the same and the wavelength gets shorter.

121285.q: Which of two media is called optically denser?
a: The one with the greater refractive index
The one with the greater mass per volume
The one with the higher temperature
The one with the darker colour
121285.e: Optically denser means that light is slower in it and the refractive index is greater. This is not directly connected with mass density.
121285.m: Optically denser means a greater refractive index.

121286.q: How is a ray of light refracted when it passes into an optically denser medium?
121286.e: In the optically denser medium, the sine of the angle of refraction is smaller than that of the angle of incidence. So the ray bends towards the normal.
121286.m: Entering an optically denser medium, light bends towards the normal.

121287.q: Which substance is optically denser than water, even though it floats on water?
121287.e: Cooking oil has a refractive index of about 1.47, so it is optically denser than water. But its mass density is lower, so it floats on top.
121287.m: Optical density and mass density are different quantities.

121288.q: Why does a stick held at an angle in water look bent at the surface?
a: Light from the stick is refracted as it leaves the water
The stick becomes soft in the water
The water reflects the stick completely
121288.e: Light from the part under water is bent away from the normal as it passes into the optically less dense air. The eye extends the rays in straight lines, so the stick seems raised.
121288.m: Refraction makes objects under water appear higher.

121289.q: A pool is 2.0 m deep (n of water equals 1.33). Roughly how deep does it appear if you look straight down into it?
121289.e: When looking almost straight down, the apparent depth is roughly the real depth / n. So 2.0 m / 1.33 is about 1.5 m.
121289.m: From above, water looks less deep than it is.

121290.q: Which phenomenon occurs because hot air above a road is optically less dense than cooler air above it?
121290.e: In the air layers with falling refractive index, light is bent more and more away from the normal and finally turned upwards. So the road seems to shine as if it were wet.
121290.m: A mirage is caused by air layers of different optical density.

121291.q: Light travels at 2.0 · 10⁸ m/s in substance A and at 2.25 · 10⁸ m/s in substance B. Which statement is true?
a: A is optically denser than B
B is optically denser than A
You cannot say without the mass density
121291.e: The optically denser substance is the one in which light is slower. A has n equals 1.5, B has n equals 1.33.
121291.m: The slower the light, the optically denser the substance.

121292.q: How is light refracted when it passes from glass into air?
a: Not at all, whatever the angle
121292.e: Air is optically less dense than glass. So the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence, and the ray bends away from the normal.
121292.m: Entering an optically less dense medium, light bends away from the normal.

121293.q: Under what condition does total internal reflection occur?
a: Light passes into the optically less dense medium and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
Light passes into the optically denser medium at any angle
Light hits a boundary at right angles
121293.e: Only when passing into the optically less dense medium can the angle of refraction reach 90°. If the critical angle is exceeded, there is no refracted ray any more, and all the light is reflected.
121293.m: Total internal reflection only happens when light passes into an optically less dense medium.

121294.q: How do you calculate the critical angle for total internal reflection when passing from medium 1 into the less dense medium 2?
a: tan θ equals n1 minus n2
121294.e: At the critical angle, the angle of refraction is 90°, so sin 90° equals 1. From n1 · sin θ equals n2, it follows that sin θ equals n2 / n1.
121294.m: At the critical angle, the refracted ray runs along the boundary.

121295.q: What is the critical angle for total internal reflection for glass (n equals 1.50) against air?
121295.e: sin θ equals 1 / 1.50 equals 0.667. The arcsine of this is about 41.8°.
121295.m: Glass against air has a critical angle of about 42°.

121296.q: What is the critical angle for total internal reflection for flint glass (n equals 1.70) against air?
121296.e: sin θ equals 1 / 1.70 equals 0.588. The arcsine of this is about 36.0°.
121296.m: The greater the refractive index, the smaller the critical angle.

121297.q: Why does a cut diamond sparkle so strongly?
a: Its small critical angle of about 24° leads to frequent total internal reflection
It absorbs all colours except white
121297.e: Because of its high refractive index, sin θ is very small, and θ is only about 24.4°. Light is often totally reflected inside and comes out again through the upper facets.
121297.m: Diamonds sparkle because of their small critical angle.

121298.q: What is the critical angle for total internal reflection of glass (n equals 1.50) against water (n equals 1.33)?
121298.e: sin θ equals 1.33 / 1.50 equals 0.887. The arcsine gives about 62.5°.
121298.m: The more similar the refractive indices, the larger the critical angle.

121299.q: A substance has a critical angle of 40° against air. Roughly what is its refractive index?
121299.e: From sin θ equals 1 / n, n equals 1 / sin 40° equals 1 / 0.643. That gives about 1.56.
121299.m: The refractive index can be calculated from the critical angle.

121300.q: Why do the reversing prisms in binoculars redirect light without any mirror coating?
a: The light hits at 45°, which is more than the critical angle of glass
Glass absorbs light coming in at an angle
The light is scattered by dust particles
121300.e: In a right-angled prism, light hits the long side at 45°. Since 45° is greater than the critical angle of glass against air, the light is totally reflected with almost no loss.
121300.m: Prisms in binoculars use total internal reflection.

121301.q: What share of the light is reflected in total internal reflection at a clean boundary?
a: About 90 %, as with an aluminium mirror
121301.e: In total internal reflection there is no refracted ray, and the energy is reflected almost completely. Ordinary metal mirrors usually only reach about 90 to 95 %.
121301.m: Total internal reflection sends back practically all the light.

121302.q: What is the lens equation for thin lenses with focal length f, object distance g and image distance b?
121302.e: The lens equation links the three distances through their reciprocals. It applies to thin lenses with rays close to the axis.
121302.m: In the lens equation, you add the reciprocals of the object distance and the image distance.

121303.q: A converging lens has f equal to 10 cm, and the object is 30 cm away. What is the image distance?
121303.e: 1/b equals 1/10 minus 1/30 equals 2/30, so b equals 15 cm. The image forms behind the lens.
121303.m: The image distance comes from the rearranged lens equation.

121304.q: A converging lens has f equal to 20 cm, and the object is 25 cm in front of the lens. Where does the image form?
121304.e: 1/b equals 1/20 minus 1/25 equals 1/100, so b equals 100 cm. If the object is just outside f, the image is far away.
121304.m: Near the focal length, the image is very far behind the lens.

121305.q: Where does the image form if the object is exactly at the focal point of a converging lens?
a: At infinity, the rays run parallel
Exactly at the other focal point
121305.e: With g equal to f, 1/b becomes 0, so b is infinitely large. Behind the lens, the rays run parallel.
121305.m: An object at the focal point gives parallel light.

121306.q: A converging lens has f equal to 10 cm, and the object is 5 cm in front of it. What image distance does the lens equation give?
121306.e: 1/b equals 1/10 minus 1/5 equals -1/10, so b equals -10 cm. The negative sign shows an image on the object side.
121306.m: A negative image distance means an image on the object side.

121307.q: What is the power of a lens with a focal length of 25 cm?
121307.e: The power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres: 1 / 0.25 m equals 4 dioptres.
121307.m: The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres.

121308.q: How does the image distance change when an object outside the focal length moves closer to a converging lens?
121308.e: If g gets smaller, 1/g gets larger and 1/b, which equals 1/f minus 1/g, gets smaller. That is why with a camera, for example, the lens must be moved further from the sensor for close-up subjects.
121308.m: Closer objects are imaged further behind the lens.

121309.q: An object is 60 cm in front of a lens, and the sharp image forms 30 cm behind it. What is the focal length?
121309.e: 1/f equals 1/60 + 1/30 equals 3/60 equals 1/20, so f equals 20 cm.
121309.m: The focal length can be found from the object and image distances.

121310.q: A converging lens with f equal to 15 cm produces a sharp image 60 cm behind the lens. How far in front of the lens is the object?
121310.e: 1/g equals 1/15 minus 1/60 equals 3/60 equals 1/20, so g equals 20 cm.
121310.m: The lens equation can be solved for any of the three quantities.

a: Image size divided by object size
Focal length divided by image distance
121311.e: Magnification tells you how large the image is compared with the object. It also equals the ratio of image distance to object distance.
121311.m: Magnification compares image size and object size.

121312.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a lens, and the image forms 15 cm behind it. What is the magnification?
121312.e: The size of the magnification is b / g equals 15 cm / 30 cm equals 0.5. The image is half as large as the object.
121312.m: If the image distance is smaller than the object distance, the image is reduced.

121313.q: An object 2 cm tall is 12 cm in front of a converging lens with f equal to 8 cm. How tall is the image?
121313.e: 1/b equals 1/8 minus 1/12 equals 1/24, so b equals 24 cm. The image is 24 / 12 equals 2 times as large, so 4 cm tall.
121313.m: Image size is object size times magnification.

121314.q: A house front 3 m tall is to fill exactly the 24 mm tall sensor of a camera. What magnification is needed?
121314.e: The magnification is image size divided by object size, so 24 mm / 3000 mm equals 0.008. That corresponds to 1 : 125.
121314.m: For magnification, both sizes must be in the same unit.

121315.q: A slide is 24 mm tall and is projected onto a screen with a magnification of 50. How tall is the image?
121315.e: 24 mm times 50 gives 1200 mm, which is 1.2 m. For this, the screen is 50 times as far from the lens as the slide.

121316.q: A camera with f equal to 50 mm photographs a person 1.8 m tall at a distance of 10 m. Roughly how tall is the image on the sensor?
121316.e: The image distance, at 50.25 mm, is almost equal to f. The magnification is about 50.25 mm / 10,000 mm equals 0.005, so 1800 mm times 0.005 equals about 9 mm.
121316.m: For distant subjects, the magnification is very small.

121317.q: Under the usual sign convention, what does a negative magnification mean?
a: The image is virtual and upright
The image is smaller than zero
121317.e: With β equal to -b / g, real images give a negative value. The minus sign shows that the image is inverted.
121317.m: A negative magnification shows an inverted image.

121318.q: An object is 40 cm in front of a converging lens with f equal to 10 cm. What is the size of the magnification?
121318.e: 1/b equals 1/10 minus 1/40 equals 3/40, so b equals 13.3 cm. The magnification is 13.3 / 40 equals 1/3.
121318.m: If the object is well beyond 2f, the image is much smaller.

121319.q: How does a ray parallel to the axis travel after passing through a thin converging lens?
a: Through the focal point on the image side
Back through the centre of the lens
Parallel to the plane of the lens
121319.e: The parallel ray is refracted by the lens so that it passes through the focal point on the other side. It is one of the three construction rays.
121319.m: The parallel ray becomes a focal ray.

121320.q: How does the central ray pass through a thin lens?
121320.e: At its centre, a thin lens behaves like a thin plate with parallel sides. So the ray goes through practically without being refracted.
121320.m: The central ray goes through the lens without being refracted.

121321.q: How does a ray travel after a converging lens if it first passed through the focal point on the object side?
a: Through the centre of the lens
Through the focal point on the image side
121321.e: The focal ray is the reverse of the parallel ray. After the lens it runs parallel to the axis.
121321.m: The focal ray becomes a parallel ray.

121322.q: What is the minimum number of the special rays needed to construct an image point?
121322.e: The image point lies where the rays cross. Two rays are enough for this; the third serves as a check.
121322.m: Two construction rays are enough for an image point.

121323.q: Where does the image form if an object is between one and two focal lengths from a converging lens?
a: Beyond twice the focal length, enlarged and inverted
Between f and 2f, reduced and upright
In front of the lens, enlarged and upright
At the focal point, the same size
121323.e: The construction shows that the rays cross far behind the lens. The image is real, inverted and larger than the object, as in a projector.
121323.m: Between f and 2f, an enlarged, inverted image forms.

121324.q: Where does the image form if an object is further than twice the focal length from a converging lens?
a: Between f and 2f, reduced and inverted
In front of the lens, upright
121324.e: The rays cross between one and two focal lengths. The image is real, inverted and reduced, as in a camera.

121325.q: How does a ray parallel to the axis travel after a diverging lens?
a: As if it came from the focal point in front of the lens
Through the focal point behind the lens
121325.e: The diverging lens bends the ray away from the axis. If you extend it backwards, it passes through the virtual focal point on the side where the light comes in.
121325.m: With diverging lenses, the parallel ray seems to come from the focal point.

121326.q: Where do you draw the refraction when constructing rays for a thin lens?
a: At the centre plane of the lens
121326.e: For thin lenses, the two refractions are simplified into a single bend. This lies in the centre plane, also called the principal plane.
121326.m: For thin lenses, the rays are bent at the centre plane.

a: The light rays actually cross and the image can be caught on a screen
The rays only seem to come from one point
It only forms in a mirror
It is always the same size as the object
121327.e: In a real image, the light rays really meet at the image points. So it can be made visible on a screen, film or sensor.
121327.m: A real image can be caught on a screen.

121328.q: Which way round is the real image formed by a single converging lens?
a: Inverted, so upside down and reversed left to right
Upright and the right way round
Upright and reversed left to right
121328.e: The rays cross on their way through the lens. Top becomes bottom and left becomes right.
121328.m: The real image of a converging lens is upside down.

121329.q: Which device produces a real image?
a: A diverging lens on its own
121329.e: The projector casts a real image onto the screen. A magnifying glass, a flat mirror and a diverging lens give virtual images.
121329.m: A projector produces a real image on the screen.

121330.q: What kind of image forms on the retina of the human eye?
a: No image at all, only dots of colour
121330.e: The cornea and lens act like a converging lens and produce a real, inverted image on the retina. The brain processes it so that we see the world upright.
121330.m: An inverted, real image forms on the retina.

121331.q: Which device produces a real image without any lens at all?
121331.e: Through a small hole, only a narrow beam of light falls from each point of the object. This creates an inverted, real image on the back wall.
121331.m: A pinhole camera also produces a real image.

121332.q: When does a converging lens produce a real image?
a: When the object is further away than the focal length
When the object is within the focal length
When the object is right on the lens
Never, converging lenses only produce virtual images
121332.e: Only for g greater than f does the lens equation give a positive image distance. Then the rays really cross behind the lens.
121332.m: A real image forms when the object is outside the focal length.

121333.q: A converging lens with f equal to 12 cm produces a sharp real image on a screen 36 cm behind the lens. How far away is the object?
121333.e: 1/g equals 1/12 minus 1/36 equals 2/36, so g equals 18 cm.
121333.m: The object distance can be found from the focal length and image distance.

121334.q: Which curved mirror can produce a real image?
a: None, mirrors never produce real images
121334.e: A concave mirror focuses light like a converging lens. If the object is outside its focal length, a real image forms in front of the mirror.
121334.m: A concave mirror can produce real images.

a: The rays only seem to come from it, and it cannot be caught on a screen
It only forms on a screen
The rays cross behind the lens
121335.e: In a virtual image, only the backward extensions of the rays cross. The eye sees it, but a screen at that position stays dark.
121335.m: A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen.

121336.q: What properties does the image in a flat mirror have?
a: Virtual, upright and the same size
Real, inverted and the same size
121336.e: The mirror image seems to stand as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. It is upright and the same size, but front and back are swapped.
121336.m: A flat mirror shows a virtual image of the same size.

121337.q: Where must an object be for a converging lens used as a magnifying glass to produce an enlarged virtual image?
a: Exactly at twice the focal length
121337.e: Within the focal length, the rays spread apart after the lens. The eye sees an upright, enlarged virtual image on the object side.
121337.m: A magnifying glass needs the object within the focal length.

121338.q: What image does a curved traffic mirror at a blind exit show?
a: A virtual, inverted image of the same size
121338.e: A convex mirror spreads light like a diverging lens. The image is virtual, upright and reduced, but in return you can see a large area.
121338.m: A convex mirror shows a reduced, virtual image with a wide field of view.

121339.q: What is the magnification of a magnifying glass with a focal length of 5 cm, based on the near point distance of 25 cm?
121339.e: For a magnifying glass, the magnification is roughly V equals 25 cm / f. With f equal to 5 cm, that gives 5 times magnification.
121339.m: The shorter the focal length, the more a magnifying glass enlarges.

121340.q: A magnifying glass with f equal to 4 cm is 3 cm in front of a stamp. How far in front of the lens is the virtual image?
121340.e: 1/b equals 1/4 minus 1/3 equals -1/12, so b equals -12 cm. The image is 12 cm in front of the lens and 12 / 3 equals 4 times as large.
121340.m: A virtual image lies on the same side as the object.

121341.q: A person stands 2 m in front of a flat mirror. How far away from them is their mirror image?
121341.e: The virtual image is 2 m behind the mirror. Together with the 2 m in front of the mirror, that gives a distance of 4 m.
121341.m: The mirror image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

121342.q: A diverging lens with f equal to -10 cm images an object 10 cm away. Where is the virtual image?
a: 5 cm in front of the lens
20 cm in front of the lens
121342.e: 1/b equals -1/10 minus 1/10 equals -2/10, so b equals -5 cm. The image is 5 cm in front of the lens on the object side.
121342.m: With diverging lenses, the image lies between the lens and the focal point.

121343.q: What is spherical aberration in a converging lens?
a: Rays at the edge are refracted more strongly than rays near the axis
Different colours have different focal lengths
The image is distorted at the edge like a cushion
The lens lets no light through
121343.e: With spherical lens surfaces, edge rays meet closer to the lens than rays near the axis. Instead of a sharp focal point, a blurred spot forms.
121343.m: With spherical aberration, edge rays have a different focal point.

121344.q: How can spherical aberration be reduced simply?
a: By stopping down, using a smaller aperture
By making the image on the screen darker
121344.e: An aperture blocks the troublesome edge rays. The image becomes sharper, but also dimmer.

121345.q: Which lens shape largely avoids spherical aberration?
121345.e: Aspherical lenses have a surface that differs from the shape of a sphere. This brings all the rays together at one point.

121346.q: What is the lens error called in which straight lines at the edge of the image appear curved?
121346.e: In distortion, the magnification changes from the centre to the edge. Depending on the direction, barrel or pincushion distortion appears.
121346.m: Distortion bends straight lines at the edge of the image.

121347.q: What is the image error called in which light coming in at an angle images a point like a comet with a tail?
121347.e: With beams coming in at an angle, the ring zones of the lens have different magnifications. This turns the image point into a comet-like spot.
121347.m: Coma makes points look like comets.

121348.q: What is the error called in which oblique beams of light image a point as two separate lines at different distances?
121348.e: In the astigmatism of oblique beams, two planes at right angles to each other have different focal lengths. Instead of a point, two focal lines form.
121348.m: Astigmatism creates two focal lines instead of one image point.

121349.q: Which lens error means that the centre and edge of the image cannot both be sharp at the same time on a flat sensor?
121349.e: The sharp image points lie on a curved surface instead of a plane. A flat sensor can only touch this surface at one place.
121349.m: With field curvature, the sharp image lies on a curved surface.

121350.q: What is the lens error called in which a simple lens creates coloured fringes around objects?
121350.e: Glass refracts blue light more strongly than red. So the colours have different focal lengths and coloured edges appear. Achromatic lenses reduce this error.

121351.q: What causes chromatic aberration in lenses?
a: The refractive index depends on the wavelength
The lens is not ground into a spherical shape
The light is scattered by dust
121351.e: Because glass refracts different colours by different amounts, a lens has a slightly different focal length for each colour. This dependence is called dispersion.
121351.m: Chromatic aberration is caused by dispersion.

121352.q: Which light has the shortest focal length with a simple glass converging lens?
121352.e: Short-wavelength light has a greater refractive index in glass and is refracted more strongly. So its focal point is closer to the lens than that of red light.
121352.m: Blue light is refracted more strongly than red.

121353.q: How can you recognise chromatic aberration in a photo?
a: By coloured fringes at high-contrast edges
By a dark edge to the image
121353.e: Because the colours are not imaged exactly on top of each other, purple or green edges appear at light-dark boundaries. These are called colour fringes.
121353.m: Colour fringes at edges reveal chromatic aberration.

121354.q: How does an achromat reduce the colour errors of a lens?
a: It combines two lenses made of different types of glass
It consists of two identical converging lenses
It filters out all colours except green
It replaces the lens with an aperture
121354.e: A converging lens made of crown glass is combined with a diverging lens made of flint glass. Because the glasses split light into colours by different amounts, the colour errors largely cancel out while the focusing effect remains.
121354.m: An achromat combines two types of glass.

121355.q: What does it mean if a lens glass has low dispersion?
a: It hardly splits light into colours
It does not refract light at all
It lets no UV light through
121355.e: Dispersion means that the refractive index depends on the wavelength. If it is low, all colours are refracted almost equally, and hardly any colour fringes appear.
121355.m: Glass with low dispersion produces hardly any colour fringes.

121356.q: Why do reflecting telescopes have no chromatic aberration in the main mirror?
a: Reflection is the same for all wavelengths
Mirrors only let white light through
121356.e: According to the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, whatever the colour. This is one reason why Isaac Newton built a reflecting telescope in 1668.
121356.m: Mirrors image all colours in the same way.

121357.q: For a biconvex lens with two equal radii R, f equals R / (2(n−1)). With R equal to 10 cm, n is 1.50 for red and 1.52 for blue. Roughly how big is the difference in focal length?
121357.e: For red, f equals 10 cm / 1.00, so 10.0 cm. For blue, it is 10 cm / 1.04, about 9.6 cm. The difference is about 0.4 cm.
121357.m: Even small differences in refractive index noticeably shift the focal point.

121358.q: Which lens of the same shape shows stronger colour errors?
a: A lens made of glass with strong dispersion
A lens made of glass with weak dispersion
A lens made of especially hard glass
A lens with an anti-reflective coating
121358.e: The more a glass refracts the colours differently, the further apart the focal points of the colours are. That is why high-quality lenses use special low-dispersion glass.
121358.m: Strong dispersion means strong colour errors.

121359.q: Which phenomenon, like chromatic aberration, is based on dispersion?
a: The splitting of white light into colours by a prism
121359.e: In a prism, each colour is refracted slightly differently, creating a spectrum. The same effect causes colour errors in lenses.
121359.m: Prisms split white light through dispersion.

121360.q: What physical effect is light guiding in an optical fibre based on?
a: Total internal reflection at the boundary between core and cladding
121360.e: The light hits the boundary with the cladding at shallow angles. Because the critical angle is exceeded, it stays trapped in the core.
121360.m: Optical fibres guide light by total internal reflection.

121361.q: What condition must the core of an optical fibre meet compared with the cladding?
a: The core has a greater refractive index
The core has a smaller refractive index
Both have exactly the same refractive index
The core must be made of metal
121361.e: Total internal reflection only happens when light passes into an optically less dense medium. So the cladding must have a slightly smaller refractive index than the core.
121361.m: The core of an optical fibre is optically denser than the cladding.

121362.q: An optical fibre has a core with n equal to 1.48 and cladding with n equal to 1.46. Roughly what is the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary?
121362.e: sin θ equals 1.46 / 1.48 equals 0.986. The arcsine of this is about 80.6°.
121362.m: In optical fibres, the critical angle is close to 90°.

121363.q: What are optical fibres used for in medicine?
a: For endoscopes, used to look inside the body
121363.e: In an endoscope, optical fibres carry light into the body and the image back. This makes it possible, for example, to examine the stomach without a major operation.
121363.m: Endoscopes use optical fibres for light and image.

121364.q: How long does a light signal take to travel through 100 km of optical fibre with n equal to 1.5?
121364.e: In glass, v equals 3 · 10⁸ / 1.5 equals 2 · 10⁸ m/s. The travel time is 100,000 m / 2 · 10⁸ m/s equals 0.0005 s.
121364.m: In optical fibres, light travels at about 200,000 kilometres per second.

121365.q: What advantage does data transmission with optical fibres have over copper cables?
a: It is not affected by electromagnetic interference
It needs no amplifiers over any distance
The fibres also conduct electric current
The fibres can be bent as sharply as you like
121365.e: Light in the fibre is not disturbed by electric and magnetic fields. In addition, the losses are low and the bandwidth is very large.
121365.m: Optical fibres are not affected by electromagnetic interference.

121366.q: Which wavelength is used especially often for data transmission over long optical fibre links?
a: About 10 nm in the X-ray range
121366.e: At about 1550 nm, the losses in silica glass are lowest. That is why long-distance links use this infrared light.
121366.m: Long-distance networks transmit data with infrared light around 1550 nm.

121367.q: Which type of optical fibre has a core so thin, about 9 µm, that only one light path can travel?
121367.e: In single-mode fibre there are no light paths of different lengths. Pulses hardly spread out, so it is suitable for high data rates over long distances.
121367.m: Single-mode fibres are suitable for long distances.

121368.q: Which federal office is responsible for nature and landscape protection in Switzerland?
121368.e: The FOEN implements the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage in the area of nature and landscape. Monument preservation and townscapes, by contrast, are mainly the responsibility of the Federal Office of Culture.
121368.m: At federal level, the FOEN looks after nature and landscape.

121369.q: According to the Federal Constitution (Art. 78), who is basically responsible for protecting nature and cultural heritage?
121369.e: Art. 78 para. 1 of the Constitution states that the cantons are responsible for protecting nature and cultural heritage. When carrying out its own tasks, the Confederation takes this into account and can support such efforts.
121369.m: In Switzerland, protecting nature and cultural heritage is mainly a matter for the cantons.

121370.q: What does Art. 3 of the Nature and Cultural Heritage Act (NHG) oblige the Confederation to do when carrying out its own tasks, such as building railway lines?
a: To spare the native landscape and townscape
To leave every project to the municipalities
Only to build projects approved in a popular vote
121370.e: For federal tasks such as railways, national roads or licences, the Confederation must spare natural and cultural monuments as well as landscapes and townscapes. Where the general interest prevails, it must preserve them undiminished.
121370.m: The Confederation, too, must take landscape and townscape into account in its building projects.

121371.q: What does the federal inventory ISOS list?
a: Townscapes worth protecting, such as villages and old towns
Historic transport routes such as mule tracks
121371.e: The ISOS is the federal inventory of Swiss townscapes worth protecting that are of national importance. Historic transport routes are listed in the IVS.
121371.m: The ISOS protects valuable townscapes such as villages and old towns.

121372.q: Which commission produces expert reports when a federal project could seriously harm a site in a federal inventory under the NHG?
a: Federal Commission for the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage
121372.e: The commission (ENHK) assesses interventions in sites listed in the federal inventories. Its report is an important basis for the decision of the responsible authority.
121372.m: The ENHK advises the authorities on interventions in protected landscapes.

121373.q: Under the NHG, what applies to the bank vegetation (reeds, rushes, riverside woodland) along waters?
a: In principle, it must not be removed.
It must be removed every five years.
It is only protected in forests.
121373.e: Art. 21 NHG states that bank vegetation must not be cleared, buried or killed off in any other way. Exceptions are only possible for projects that can only be built there.
121373.m: The vegetation along lakes and rivers is protected by law.

121374.q: Which habitats does the Confederation designate under Art. 18a NHG?
121374.e: Under Art. 18a NHG, the Federal Council designates biotopes of national importance, such as floodplains, bogs, amphibian breeding sites and dry meadows and pastures. Their protection and maintenance are regulated by the cantons.
121374.m: Biotopes of national importance are designated by the Confederation and protected by the cantons.

121375.q: What does the NHG mean by “Heimatschutz” (protection of cultural heritage)?
a: Protecting townscapes, historic sites and cultural monuments
121375.e: Besides nature and landscape, the NHG also protects the native landscape and townscape, historic sites and natural and cultural monuments. So “Heimatschutz” means preserving the cultural heritage.
121375.m: Heritage protection preserves townscapes and cultural monuments.

121376.q: What does the federal inventory IVS list?
a: Historic transport routes such as old pass routes
121376.e: The IVS is the federal inventory of historic transport routes in Switzerland. It includes, for example, old pass routes and mule tracks.
121376.m: The IVS preserves the traces of old transport routes.

121377.q: Which department is the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) part of?
121377.e: The FOEN belongs to the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications. The offices for transport, energy and spatial development are also based there.
121377.m: The FOEN is an office in the environment and transport department DETEC.

121378.q: Which office did the FOEN emerge from in 2006, together with the Federal Office for Water and Geology?
a: SAEFL (Federal Office for the Environment, Forests and Landscape)
121378.e: The Swiss Agency for the Environment, Forests and Landscape (SAEFL, German BUWAL) was merged with parts of the Federal Office for Water and Geology in 2006 to form the FOEN. Since then, the FOEN has also been in charge of flood protection.
121378.m: The FOEN was created in 2006 from the SAEFL and the Federal Office for Water and Geology.

121379.q: Which law of 1983 is the central basis for protection against air pollution, noise and waste?
121379.e: The Environmental Protection Act (USG) of 7 October 1983 came into force in 1985. Among other things, it regulates air pollution control, noise protection, waste and contaminated sites.
121379.m: The Environmental Protection Act regulates air, noise and waste.

121380.q: Which principle in the Environmental Protection Act requires pollution to be limited early, before damage has been proven?
121380.e: According to Art. 1 para. 2 USG, effects that could become harmful or a nuisance must be limited early as a precaution. So you do not wait until damage occurs.
121380.m: The precautionary principle acts before damage occurs.

121381.q: Which principle states that whoever causes environmental pollution bears the costs?
121381.e: Art. 2 USG states that whoever causes measures under this law bears the costs of them. One example is waste charges by volume, such as the rubbish bag with a fee.
121381.m: Whoever pollutes the environment should also pay for it.

121382.q: Who mainly implements the Environmental Protection Act in Switzerland?
121382.e: The Confederation passes laws and ordinances, and the FOEN provides implementation guides. But it is mostly the cantons that have to implement and check the rules.
121382.m: Environmental protection is mainly implemented by the cantons.

121383.q: Which task is NOT one of the FOEN’s responsibilities?
121383.e: The FOEN deals with forests, water, biodiversity, natural hazards, air and noise, among other things. In Switzerland, medicines are approved by Swissmedic.
121383.m: The FOEN looks after nature, forests, water and natural hazards.

121384.q: Which federal office was responsible for environmental protection from 1971, before the SAEFL?
121384.e: The Federal Office for Environmental Protection was created in 1971. In 1989 it was merged with the Federal Office of Forestry and Landscape Protection to form the SAEFL (BUWAL).
121384.m: The Federal Office for Environmental Protection was a forerunner of today’s FOEN.

121385.q: In which law was the right of environmental organisations to appeal first laid down?
121385.e: Art. 12 NHG gave nationwide nature and heritage conservation organisations the right to appeal for the first time. A similar rule was later added to the Environmental Protection Act.
121385.m: The organisations’ right of appeal originated in the Nature and Cultural Heritage Act.

121386.q: Which environmental organisation is one of those allowed to lodge appeals as an organisation in Switzerland?
121386.e: Pro Natura is a nationwide nature conservation organisation and has been designated by the Federal Council as entitled to appeal. WWF Switzerland and the Swiss Foundation for Landscape Conservation are also among them.
121386.m: As an environmental organisation, Pro Natura is allowed to lodge appeals.

121387.q: Who decides which environmental organisations may exercise the right of appeal?
a: The FOEN alone, without an ordinance
121387.e: The entitled organisations are named by the Federal Council in an ordinance. They include, for example, Pro Natura, WWF Switzerland and the Swiss Foundation for Landscape Conservation.
121387.m: The Federal Council decides in an ordinance which organisations may appeal.

121388.q: In 2008, how did voters decide on the popular initiative that wanted to severely restrict the organisations’ right of appeal?
121388.e: The initiative was rejected on 30 November 2008 by about two thirds of voters and by all cantons. The organisations’ right of appeal remained in place.
121388.m: The organisations’ right of appeal was clearly confirmed at the ballot box in 2008.

121389.q: What is the main purpose of the organisations’ right of appeal?
a: Nature, which cannot defend itself, gets a voice in the proceedings.
Organisations can use it to levy taxes.
Organisations can use it to approve building projects themselves.
It replaces the people’s right to vote.
121389.e: For many building projects, nobody who stands up for nature and landscape is personally affected. The right of appeal allows a court to check whether environmental law is being applied correctly.
121389.m: The organisations’ right of appeal gives nature and landscape a voice in court.

121390.q: Apart from the NHG, which other law regulates appeals by environmental organisations in Art. 55, for example for installations requiring an environmental impact assessment?
121390.e: Art. 55 USG gives environmental organisations a right to appeal against decisions on installations that require an environmental impact assessment. This complements Art. 12 NHG.
121390.m: The Environmental Protection Act also includes a right of appeal for organisations.

121391.q: Since the change in the law in 2007, who usually pays the costs of the proceedings if an environmental organisation loses its appeal?
a: Nobody, the proceedings are always free
121391.e: The revision tightened the rules: organisations that lose pay the costs of the proceedings like other parties. The circle of organisations entitled to appeal was also narrowed.
121391.m: Whoever loses an appeal usually has to pay the costs.

121392.q: Which requirement regarding its area of activity applies to an environmental organisation that wants to lodge an appeal?
a: It must be active throughout Switzerland.
It only needs to be active in one municipality.
It must be funded by the state.
121392.e: Art. 12 NHG requires the organisation to be active throughout Switzerland and to pursue purely non-profit aims. Local associations are therefore not entitled to appeal.
121392.m: Only environmental organisations active throughout Switzerland may lodge such appeals.

121393.q: Which popular initiative put the article on protecting moorland into the Federal Constitution in 1987?
121393.e: The Rothenthurm Initiative was accepted by the people and the cantons on 6 December 1987. It is named after the moorland landscape near Rothenthurm in the canton of Schwyz.
121393.m: Thanks to the Rothenthurm Initiative of 1987, moorland protection is in the constitution.

121394.q: Which project triggered the Rothenthurm Initiative?
a: A reservoir for a hydropower plant
121394.e: The Military Department planned a training ground in a valuable moorland landscape near Rothenthurm. The population fought back with a federal popular initiative.
121394.m: A planned army training ground triggered the Rothenthurm Initiative.

121395.q: At which legal level is the protection of moorland laid down in Switzerland?
121395.e: Since the Rothenthurm Initiative, moorland protection has been in the Federal Constitution. Moors of national importance may hardly be changed.
121395.m: Moorland protection is in the Federal Constitution.

121396.q: What is basically forbidden in Swiss moors of national importance?
a: Buildings and interventions that conflict with the purpose of protection
121396.e: The constitution forbids installations and changes to the ground in protected moors that conflict with their protection. Some buildings already put up that conflicted with protection even had to be removed.
121396.m: Harmful interventions are forbidden in protected moors.

121397.q: What is a moorland landscape in the sense of the moorland protection article?
a: A near-natural landscape strongly shaped by moors
121397.e: Besides the moors, moorland landscapes also include the surrounding forests, pastures and settlement structures that form a whole with them. They are protected in a separate federal ordinance.
121397.m: A moorland landscape protects the moors together with their surroundings.

121398.q: Which federal ordinance was the first to implement the moorland protection article in 1991?
121398.e: After the Rothenthurm Initiative was accepted, the Raised Bog Ordinance came into force in 1991. Ordinances for fens and moorland landscapes followed later.
121398.m: The Raised Bog Ordinance of 1991 was the first step in putting moorland protection into practice.

121399.q: How does a fen differ from a raised bog?
a: It is fed by mineral-rich groundwater or water from slopes.
It consists only of open water.
121399.e: Fens are connected with groundwater, spring water or water running down slopes and are therefore richer in nutrients than raised bogs. Many are used as litter meadows.
121399.m: Fens get water from the ground, raised bogs from the rain.

121400.q: Why are moors important for climate protection?
a: Their peat stores large amounts of carbon.
They lock nitrogen from the air into rock.
121400.e: In wet, oxygen-poor peat, plant remains are hardly broken down, so the carbon stays stored. If a moor is drained, the peat decomposes and releases CO2.
121400.m: Intact moors store carbon in their peat.

121401.q: According to the federal concept, what does the Ecological Infrastructure consist of?
121401.e: The Ecological Infrastructure is a nationwide network of valuable core areas and connecting areas that link them. This lets species move around and populations mix.
121401.m: The Ecological Infrastructure links core areas through connecting areas.

121402.q: In which strategy of 2012 did the Federal Council set the goal of building up an Ecological Infrastructure?
121402.e: The Swiss Biodiversity Strategy was adopted in 2012 and made concrete with an action plan in 2017. The Ecological Infrastructure is one of its main goals.
121402.m: The Swiss Biodiversity Strategy calls for an Ecological Infrastructure.

121403.q: Why are connecting areas needed between nature reserves?
a: Isolated populations are more prone to inbreeding and dying out.
They serve as a reserve of building land.
They prevent any movement of animals.
121403.e: Small, isolated populations lose genetic diversity and die out more easily. Corridors and stepping stones allow movement and recolonisation.
121403.m: Connections protect species from dying out on isolated islands.

121404.q: What is the structure called that allows wild animals to cross a motorway safely?
121404.e: Wildlife bridges are wide bridges covered in vegetation over transport routes. They restore broken wildlife corridors and are part of the Ecological Infrastructure.
121404.m: Wildlife bridges link habitats across motorways.

121405.q: How can natural gardens, parks and green roofs in towns contribute to the Ecological Infrastructure?
a: They can serve as connecting elements for animals and plants.
They are of no importance for species.
They prevent all insects from spreading.
121405.e: Habitats can also be created in built-up areas with native plants, small structures and green spaces. As stepping stones, they link green spaces inside and outside settlements.
121405.m: Natural green spaces in villages and towns improve connections.

121406.q: What is meant by habitat fragmentation?
a: Cutting habitats into small, isolated pieces
121406.e: Roads, railway lines and settlements split up habitats. Animals can then hardly move around, and the remaining areas are often too small for stable populations.
121406.m: Fragmentation cuts up habitats and isolates animal populations.

121407.q: Who is mainly responsible for nature conservation and the protection of biotopes in Switzerland?
121407.e: According to the Federal Constitution, protecting nature and cultural heritage is a matter for the cantons. The Confederation sets principles, protects biotopes of national importance and supports the cantons financially.
121407.m: In Switzerland, the cantons are mainly responsible for nature conservation.

a: Small habitats that serve species as a stopover when moving
Stone slabs in a garden path
121408.e: Stepping stones are smaller natural areas such as hedges, ponds or flower meadows. They link larger habitats even when these do not border each other directly.
121408.m: Stepping-stone biotopes help species to get from one habitat to the next.

121409.q: Which principle is at the heart of the Spatial Planning Act of 1979?
a: The separation of building zones from non-building zones
121409.e: The Spatial Planning Act requires land to be used economically. Outside building zones, only what fits the zone or can only be built in that place may in principle be built.
121409.m: The Spatial Planning Act separates building zones from non-building zones.

121410.q: When did voters accept the first revision of the Spatial Planning Act (RPG 1)?
121410.e: On 3 March 2013, the revision was accepted with about 63 per cent voting yes. It is meant to slow down urban sprawl and reduce oversized building zones.
121410.m: The first revision of the Spatial Planning Act was accepted in 2013.

121411.q: Under the revised Spatial Planning Act, what must municipalities with building zones that are too large do?
a: They must reduce their building zones
They must create more building zones
121411.e: Building zones may only match the expected need over the next 15 years. Municipalities with too much building land must therefore rezone areas out of it.
121411.m: Building zones that are too large must be reduced.

121412.q: What is the added value levy when land is rezoned for building?
a: Part of the gain in the land’s value goes to the public
A fee for building permits in the forest
A bonus for farmers who give up land
121412.e: When land becomes building land, its value rises sharply. At least 20 per cent of this planning gain must be handed over, for example to compensate for land being rezoned out.
121412.m: The added value levy takes part of the gain in value when land is rezoned for building.

121413.q: Which planning tool is binding on landowners?
121413.e: The structure plan is only binding on the authorities. The land use plan, for example the municipality’s zoning plan, sets out plot by plot how a piece of land may be used.
121413.m: The land use plan sets out what is allowed on a plot.

121414.q: Who must approve the cantonal structure plan?
121414.e: The cantons draw up the structure plan, and the Federal Council approves it. This ensures that federal requirements are met.
121414.m: Cantonal structure plans need the approval of the Federal Council.

121415.q: Which initiative, accepted in 2012, limits the share of second homes in a municipality to 20 per cent?
121415.e: The initiative launched by Franz Weber was narrowly accepted on 11 March 2012. It mainly affects tourist municipalities in the Alps.
121415.m: The Second Homes Initiative limits second homes to 20 per cent.

121416.q: Which areas does the sectoral plan for crop rotation areas safeguard?
a: The best farmland for feeding people in times of crisis
121416.e: Crop rotation areas are the most valuable agricultural soils. The Confederation requires the cantons to keep a minimum amount of them so that supplies are secure in a crisis.
121416.m: Crop rotation areas protect Switzerland’s best farmland.

121417.q: What applies in the core zone of a nature discovery park?
a: Nature may develop freely, and visitors stay on marked paths.
New buildings are particularly welcome there.
The forest must be cleared there regularly.
121417.e: In the core zone, there is no use of the land, so that nature can develop freely. In the transition zone, nature experiences and environmental education are possible.
121417.m: In the core zone of a nature discovery park, nature comes first.

121418.q: Who awards parks the label “Park of national importance”?
121418.e: The FOEN awards the label at the request of the canton if the requirements are met. The park then also receives financial support.
121418.m: The park label is awarded by the Confederation.

121419.q: Who must agree to a park of national importance before it can be created?
121419.e: Parks are created on the initiative of the region. The municipalities must agree to the charter, often at the municipal assembly or in a ballot.
121419.m: A park is only created if the municipalities of the region agree.

121420.q: What is the main aim of a regional nature park?
a: To preserve nature and landscape and strengthen the region’s sustainable economy
To cut down the forest completely
121420.e: Regional nature parks are partly inhabited rural areas. They are meant to enhance nature and landscape while promoting a sustainably run economy.
121420.m: Regional nature parks combine nature conservation with sustainable regional development.

121421.q: Which park is regarded as Switzerland’s first nature discovery park?
121421.e: Wildnispark Zürich Sihlwald was the first park to receive the nature discovery park label. It lies near the city of Zurich and has a core zone where the forest may develop freely.
121421.m: The Sihlwald near Zurich was Switzerland’s first nature discovery park.

121422.q: Which planned national park in the area of the Grisons and Ticino failed in municipal votes in 2016?
121422.e: Parc Adula around the Rheinwaldhorn was rejected by several of the municipalities involved in 2016. As a result, Switzerland’s second national park did not come about.
121422.m: The Parc Adula national park project failed in 2016.

121423.q: What must every park of national importance set out in a charter?
a: The aims and measures for the park’s development
The entrance prices for all visitors
The names of all animal species
121423.e: The charter is a contract between the park municipalities and the body running the park. It sets out the aims and measures for the ten-year operating phase.
121423.m: The charter describes how a park should develop.

121424.q: By which law is the Swiss National Park in the Engadine governed?
a: By its own National Park Act
121424.e: The Swiss National Park, founded in 1914, has its own legal basis in the National Park Act of 1980. The Parks Ordinance governs the newer parks.
121424.m: The Swiss National Park has its own law.

121425.q: In which year was the Bern Convention on the protection of European animals and plants concluded?
121425.e: The Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats was signed in Bern on 19 September 1979. It came into force in 1982.
121425.m: The Bern Convention was signed in Bern in 1979.

121426.q: What does the Bern Convention allow states to do regarding individual species when they ratify it?
a: Make reservations to exclude certain species
Move their own species into Appendix II
Hunt all species in Appendix II
Trade in protected species without a permit
121426.e: When signing or ratifying, states can declare reservations for certain species. For these species, the protection obligations then do not apply or apply only in part.
121426.m: Under the Bern Convention, states can make reservations for individual species.
