121427.q: What is the network of protected areas called that states build up under the Bern Convention?
121427.e: In the Emerald Network, the contracting states report areas of special value for the species and habitats of the convention. In the EU, Natura 2000 fulfils this role.
121427.m: The Emerald Network brings together protected areas of the Bern Convention.

121428.q: Which change regarding the wolf did the Standing Committee of the Bern Convention decide in December 2024?
a: It downgraded it from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
It removed it from the convention completely.
It classified it as an invasive species.
121428.e: The wolf was moved from Appendix II (strictly protected species) to Appendix III (protected species). The change came into force in March 2025 and makes it easier to control numbers.
121428.m: Since 2025, the wolf has only been protected, no longer strictly protected, under the Bern Convention.

121429.q: What do the appendices of the Bern Convention contain?
a: Lists of protected plant and animal species
Lists of the world’s national parks
121429.e: Appendix I lists strictly protected plants, Appendix II strictly protected animals and Appendix III protected animals. Appendix IV lists banned means of capture and killing.
121429.m: The appendices of the Bern Convention list the protected species.

121430.q: Which proposal did Switzerland make under the Bern Convention in 2018 that did not win a majority at the time?
a: To lower the protection status of the wolf
To give the bear strict protection
121430.e: Switzerland proposed downgrading the wolf from strictly protected to protected status. Only a similar proposal by the EU was accepted in 2024.
121430.m: Switzerland was already pushing for a lower protection status for the wolf in 2018.

121431.q: Apart from protecting individual species, what aim does the Bern Convention pursue?
121431.e: The convention aims to conserve wild plants and animals and their habitats. Endangered and migratory species are given particular attention.
121431.m: The Bern Convention protects species and their habitats.

121432.q: What kind of agreement is the Bern Convention?
a: A law of the canton of Bern
121432.e: The Bern Convention is an international agreement that states join by ratification. The contracting states commit themselves to putting its requirements into their own law.
121432.m: The Bern Convention is an international treaty between states.

121433.q: Which habitats does the Ramsar Convention protect?
121433.e: The Ramsar Convention is the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance. Originally, the protection of water birds and waders was the main focus.

121434.q: In which country was the Ramsar Convention signed in 1971?
121434.e: The convention is named after the town of Ramsar on the Caspian Sea in Iran. It was concluded there on 2 February 1971.
121434.m: The Ramsar Convention is named after a town in Iran.

121435.q: In which Swiss town is the secretariat of the Ramsar Convention based?
121435.e: The Ramsar secretariat is based in Gland in the canton of Vaud, in the same building as the IUCN. This links Switzerland closely with the convention.
121435.m: The secretariat of the Ramsar Convention is in Gland on Lake Geneva.

121436.q: Which day has been set as World Wetlands Day?
121436.e: World Wetlands Day commemorates the signing of the Ramsar Convention on 2 February 1971. Since 2021 it has also been an official UN day.
121436.m: World Wetlands Day is on 2 February.

121437.q: Which group of animals was a particular focus when the Ramsar Convention was founded?
121437.e: The full name refers to wetlands “especially as waterfowl habitat”. Many migratory birds depend on a chain of wetlands.
121437.m: Migratory birds need wetlands as resting places.

121438.q: Which area on Lake Maggiore is a Swiss Ramsar site?
121438.e: The Bolle di Magadino are a river delta with floodplain woodland and reeds at the mouth of the Ticino and Verzasca rivers. They are an important resting place for migratory birds.
121438.m: The Bolle di Magadino in Ticino are a Ramsar site.

121439.q: Why are moors, as wetlands, also important for climate protection?
a: They store large amounts of carbon in peat
They cool the air with ice
They filter fine dust from cities
121439.e: In wet moors, dead plants are hardly broken down and are stored as peat. If moors are drained, the carbon gets into the air as CO2.
121439.m: Intact moors are important carbon stores.

121440.q: Which Swiss Ramsar site lies at the mouth of the Rhône where it flows into Lake Geneva?
121440.e: Les Grangettes near Noville in the canton of Vaud are an area of reeds and floodplain on the Rhône delta. It is an important breeding and resting place for water birds.
121440.m: Les Grangettes on the Rhône delta are a Ramsar site.

121441.q: What does the Forest Act mean by clearance (deforestation)?
a: Using forest land for another purpose, permanently or temporarily
121441.e: According to Art. 4 of the Forest Act, clearance is any use of forest land for another purpose, for example for a road or a building. Normal timber harvesting in the forest is not clearance.
121441.m: Clearance turns forest into something else, permanently or temporarily.

121442.q: What is the basic rule of the Forest Act on clearance?
a: Clearance is forbidden; exceptions need a permit.
Clearance is only forbidden in building zones.
Clearance is only allowed in winter.
121442.e: Art. 5 of the Forest Act forbids clearance in principle. An exceptional permit is only given if important reasons outweigh the interest in preserving the forest.
121442.m: In Switzerland, forest may in principle not be cleared.

121443.q: What usually has to be provided when a clearance has been permitted?
a: Replacement by planting new forest in the same area
A fine paid to the municipality
121443.e: Art. 7 of the Forest Act basically requires equivalent replacement in the same area. In areas where forest cover is increasing, a measure for nature and landscape can be provided instead.
121443.m: Forest that has been cleared usually has to be replaced by new forest.

121444.q: Which federal law of 1876 laid the foundation for preserving forests in Switzerland?
121444.e: After major floods in the 1860s, which were partly blamed on clear-cutting, the Confederation passed the Forest Police Act for the high mountains in 1876. For the first time, it required the area of forest to be preserved.
121444.m: The Forest Police Act of 1876 protected the Swiss forest for the first time.

121445.q: What does the forest distance rule regulate?
a: The minimum distance between buildings and the edge of the forest
121445.e: Art. 17 of the Forest Act requires buildings to keep a suitable distance from the edge of the forest. The cantons set the exact distance; it protects forest and buildings from each other.
121445.m: The forest distance rule keeps buildings away from the edge of the forest.

121446.q: Which event led to stricter forest protection in Switzerland in the 19th century?
121446.e: Overused, bare mountain slopes could hold back little water. After the floods of the 1860s, the forest was recognised as protection against natural hazards.
121446.m: Deforestation led to floods and therefore to forest protection.

121447.q: Which function of the forest is particularly important in the Alps and one reason for the ban on clearance?
a: Protection against avalanches, rockfall and debris flows
121447.e: Protection forests hold back snow, stones and soil and protect settlements and transport routes. Almost half of the Swiss forest fulfils such a protective function.
121447.m: Protection forests keep villages and roads safe from natural hazards.

121448.q: Which three functions of the forest does the Federal Constitution name?
121448.e: The forest article of the Federal Constitution requires the forest to protect against natural hazards, supply timber and serve recreation.
121448.m: The forest is meant to protect, to be useful and to serve recreation.

a: The amount of water left in a river after water has been taken out
The water in an empty reservoir
The waste water from a sewage works
121449.e: According to the Waters Protection Act, residual water is the flow that remains in the river below a point where water is taken out, for example for a hydropower plant. It safeguards life in the river.
121449.m: Residual water is the water that must stay in the river after some is taken out.

121450.q: Which law of 1991 sets the minimum residual flows?
121450.e: The Waters Protection Act of 24 January 1991 regulates the minimum residual flows in Art. 31. It was accepted in a popular vote in 1992.
121450.m: The minimum residual flows are set out in the Waters Protection Act.

121451.q: Why is the minimum residual flow based on a river’s flow in dry periods?
a: Because fish and small creatures need enough water precisely then
Because power plants produce the most electricity then
Because the river is warmest and most acidic then
Because floods are most frequent then
121451.e: The law links residual water to the low flow that a river reaches on almost every day. This leaves enough water for life in the river even in dry periods.
121451.m: Residual water is based on a river’s low flow.

121452.q: A stream has a Q347 of 80 litres per second. What is the minimum residual flow under Art. 31 of the Waters Protection Act (50 l/s for the first 60 l/s, plus 8 l/s for every further 10 l/s)?
121452.e: For the first 60 l/s, 50 l/s apply. The remaining 20 l/s are two lots of 10 l/s, so 2 times 8 l/s; in total 50 + 16 makes 66 l/s.
121452.m: The minimum residual flow rises in steps with the flow Q347.

121453.q: When do existing hydropower plants usually have to comply fully with the new residual flow rules?
121453.e: The minimum residual flows apply to new uses of water and when licences are renewed. Until then, existing plants only have to be improved as far as this is reasonable without compensation.
121453.m: Stricter residual flow rules apply when licences are renewed.

121454.q: What is the phenomenon called when a storage power plant makes the flow below its outlet rise and fall sharply and quickly?
121454.e: When the turbines run, the water level rises quickly (surge); when they stop, it falls fast (low flow). Fish and small creatures can be stranded; since 2011 the Waters Protection Act has required this to be remedied.
121454.m: Hydropeaking means artificial changes in water level below power plants.

121455.q: Which interests mainly conflict when the residual flow is set?
a: Electricity production from hydropower and protecting river habitats
121455.e: More residual water means less water for the turbines and therefore less electricity. Too little residual water harms fish, floodplains and the look of the landscape.
121455.m: Setting the residual flow means weighing electricity production against protecting waters.

121456.q: How was the Waters Protection Act of 1991, with its residual flow rules, brought into force?
a: Voters accepted it in a referendum in 1992
The Federal Council brought it into force without parliament
The cantons adopted it one by one
It was never brought into force
121456.e: A referendum was called against the law. On 17 May 1992, the people accepted it and at the same time rejected a stricter initiative on protecting waters.
121456.m: The Waters Protection Act was accepted by the people in 1992.

121457.q: In which law is the environmental impact assessment (EIA) laid down in Switzerland?
121457.e: Art. 10a of the Environmental Protection Act requires an EIA for installations that could seriously burden the environment. The details are set out in the EIA Ordinance of 1988.
121457.m: The EIA is regulated in the Environmental Protection Act.

121458.q: For which projects is an environmental impact assessment required?
a: For installations that could seriously burden the environment
121458.e: The types of installation that need an EIA are listed in the annex to the EIA Ordinance. They include, for example, national roads, large power plants, landfills and shopping centres.
121458.m: Only projects with serious environmental effects need an EIA.

121459.q: Who writes the environmental impact report?
121459.e: In the report, the developer must show how the project affects the environment. The environmental protection office checks the report and gives an assessment.
121459.m: The developer writes the environmental impact report.

121460.q: Who assesses the environmental impact report from an expert point of view?
a: The environmental protection office of the canton or the Confederation
121460.e: Depending on the procedure, the cantonal environmental protection office or the FOEN assesses the report. The deciding authority takes this assessment into account when deciding on the permit.
121460.m: Expert offices check the environmental report before a decision is made.

121461.q: Within which procedure is the environmental impact assessment carried out?
a: Within the permit procedure for the project
121461.e: The EIA is not a procedure of its own but part of the relevant permit procedure, such as the building permit or plan approval procedure. This way the environment is considered early on.
121461.m: The EIA takes place as part of the project permit.

121462.q: What is the basic aim of an EIA?
a: To check whether a project complies with environmental rules
121462.e: The EIA clarifies whether a project complies with environmental law, for example on air, noise, waters and nature. It helps to set measures to reduce the burden.
121462.m: The EIA checks whether a project is compatible with environmental law.

121463.q: What does international law require if a large building project could seriously burden the environment of a neighbouring country?
a: The neighbouring country must be informed and consulted
Only the law of the country where it is built applies
The neighbouring country must help pay
121463.e: The UNECE Espoo Convention of 1991 obliges states to inform and consult neighbouring countries if a project could have serious cross-border environmental effects. Switzerland is a contracting state.
121463.m: If there are cross-border effects, the neighbouring country is consulted.

121464.q: What is the advantage of the EIA taking place before construction?
a: Environmental damage can be avoided already at the planning stage.
A building permit is no longer needed.
121464.e: Environmental problems are easier and cheaper to solve during planning than after construction. This matches the precautionary principle of the Environmental Protection Act.
121464.m: An early check prevents environmental damage before it happens.

121465.q: How did voters decide on 10 February 2019 on the Urban Sprawl Initiative, which wanted to freeze the total area of building zones?
121465.e: The Young Greens’ initiative demanded that new building zones only be created if areas of the same size were rezoned out. It was rejected by about 64 per cent of voters.
121465.m: The Urban Sprawl Initiative was rejected in 2019.

121466.q: A river has a Q347 of 100 litres per second. What is the minimum residual flow under Art. 31 of the Waters Protection Act (50 l/s for the first 60 l/s, plus 8 l/s for every further 10 l/s)?
121466.e: For the first 60 l/s, 50 l/s apply. The other 40 l/s are four lots of 10 l/s, so 4 times 8 l/s; that gives 50 + 32, which makes 82 l/s.
121466.m: With a larger Q347, more residual water must also stay in the river.

121467.q: What does a state at least commit itself to when it joins the Ramsar Convention?
a: To put at least one wetland on the Ramsar List
To ban hunting of water birds completely
To abolish its own water authority
121467.e: Under Art. 2 of the convention, every contracting state designates at least one wetland of international importance when joining. It also commits itself to the wise use of all wetlands.
121467.m: Every Ramsar state must name at least one wetland of international importance.

121567.q: Which feature do prokaryotes lack, unlike eukaryotes?
a: A nucleus with a nuclear envelope
121567.e: In prokaryotes, the DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm without being surrounded by a nuclear envelope. A cell membrane, ribosomes and cytoplasm, on the other hand, are found in all cells.

121568.q: Which two domains of life belong to the prokaryotes?
121568.e: In Carl Woese's three-domain system, bacteria and archaea are prokaryotic, and the eukaryotes form the third domain. Viruses are not considered living things with their own cells.
121568.m: Bacteria and archaea are the two groups of prokaryotes.

121569.q: What is the region in a bacterium's cytoplasm called where the ring-shaped chromosome lies?
121569.e: The nucleoid is a nuclear region without a membrane in which the bacterial chromosome is tightly packed. The nucleolus, by contrast, is part of the nucleus of eukaryotes.
121569.m: Bacterial DNA lies in the nucleoid without an envelope.

121570.q: Which type of ribosome do prokaryotes have?
121570.e: Prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes, while eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Many antibiotics use this difference and specifically block the 70S ribosomes.

121571.q: What substance is the cell wall of most bacteria mainly made of?
121571.e: Murein, also called peptidoglycan, is a network of sugar chains and short peptides. Cellulose is found in plant cell walls, chitin in fungi and insects.
121571.m: The bacterial cell wall is made of murein.

121572.q: What are the long, rotating structures that many bacteria use to move called?
121572.e: Bacterial flagella are turned like a propeller by a motor in the cell envelope. Cilia and pseudopodia, by contrast, are found in eukaryotic cells.

121573.q: What are the small, usually ring-shaped DNA molecules called that bacteria can have in addition to their chromosome?
121573.e: Plasmids copy themselves independently of the chromosome and often carry useful extra genes. Plastids, by contrast, are organelles of plant cells.
121573.m: Plasmids are small rings of DNA in bacteria.

121574.q: After which Danish doctor is the staining method named that divides bacteria into two groups by the structure of their cell wall?
121574.e: Hans Christian Gram developed the stain in 1884. Bacteria with a thick cell wall layer stain blue-violet, those with a thin layer and an outer membrane stain red.
121574.m: Gram staining distinguishes bacteria by their cell wall.

121575.q: What is the reproductive cycle of a phage called in which the host cell bursts after new phages have formed?
121575.e: In the lytic cycle, the bacterium immediately produces new phages until the cell is dissolved and releases them. Lysis means dissolving.
121575.m: In the lytic cycle, the bacterial cell is destroyed.

121576.q: What is the phage DNA called that is built into the bacterial chromosome in the lysogenic cycle?
121576.e: The prophage is copied along with every cell division without killing the bacterium. Only under stress can it be cut out and trigger the production of new phages.
121576.m: A built-in phage is called a prophage.

121577.q: What is the protein shell called that surrounds the genetic material of a phage?
121577.e: The capsid consists of many identical protein building blocks. In typical phages such as T4, it sits as a head on a tail with fibres.
121577.m: The capsid protects a virus's genetic material.

121578.q: What did Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase prove with bacteriophages in 1952?
a: That DNA is the genetic material
That proteins are the genetic material
That viruses have their own cells
121578.e: They labelled the DNA with radioactive phosphorus and the proteins with radioactive sulphur. Only the labelled DNA got into the bacteria.
121578.m: The Hershey-Chase experiment proved that DNA carries genetic information.

121579.q: What would people like to use bacteriophages for more often in medicine?
121579.e: Phages attack particular bacteria specifically, including those against which antibiotics no longer work. This phage therapy has a long tradition, especially in Georgia.
121579.m: Phages are a hope against resistant bacteria.

121580.q: Why are bacteriophages basically harmless to humans?
a: They do not survive in water
They are bigger than human cells
They are digested by the stomach at once
121580.e: Phages use their tail fibres to recognise very specific surface structures of bacteria. They cannot dock onto human cells.

121581.q: What does the Greek part “phage” in “bacteriophage” mean?
121581.e: Phagein means to eat or devour in Greek. A bacteriophage is therefore literally a bacteria eater.

121582.q: What is the transfer of bacterial genes from one cell to another with the help of phages called?
121582.e: In transduction, phages accidentally package pieces of bacterial DNA and carry them into the next bacterium. In transformation, by contrast, a bacterium takes up free DNA from its surroundings.
121582.m: In transduction, phages carry bacterial genes.

121583.q: What is the transfer of plasmids between two bacteria through direct cell contact via a pilus called?
121583.e: In conjugation, a donor bacterium forms a bridge to the recipient and transfers a copy of the plasmid. In this way resistance genes spread quickly, even between different species.
121583.m: Conjugation transfers plasmids through direct contact.

121584.q: Which enzyme makes many bacteria resistant to penicillins by splitting the active substance?
121584.e: Beta-lactamases destroy the penicillin molecule before it can work. That is why penicillins are often combined with inhibitors such as clavulanic acid.

121585.q: What is the approach called that looks at antibiotic resistance in humans, animals and the environment together?
121585.e: Resistant bacteria move back and forth between people, farm animals, food and water. That is why, in the One Health approach, human and veterinary medicine, farming and environmental protection work together.
121585.m: Resistance is best fought with the One Health approach.

121586.q: Which evolutionary process explains why resistant bacteria increase during antibiotic treatment?
121586.e: The antibiotic kills sensitive bacteria, while resistant ones survive and multiply. In this way resistance spreads through the bacterial population.

121587.q: What is meant by horizontal gene transfer in bacteria?
a: Genes are exchanged between existing cells
Genes are only passed on to daughter cells
121587.e: In horizontal gene transfer, genes pass not through division but sideways from one bacterium to another. This can even happen between different bacterial species.
121587.m: Horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance genes between bacteria.

121588.q: When is a germ described as multi-resistant?
a: When it is resistant to several classes of antibiotics
When disinfectants do not affect it
121588.e: Multi-resistant germs no longer respond to several groups of antibiotics. This makes treatment difficult and expensive.
121588.m: Multi-resistant germs defy several groups of antibiotics.

121589.q: What is the main aim of the Swiss Strategy on Antibiotic Resistance (StAR)?
a: To keep antibiotics effective in the long term
To sell antibiotics without a prescription
121589.e: The StAR strategy was adopted by the Federal Council in 2015. It includes measures in human and veterinary medicine and in farming so that antibiotics remain effective.
121589.m: Switzerland fights antibiotic resistance with the StAR strategy.

121590.q: Which behaviour by patients encourages antibiotic resistance to develop?
a: Stopping or changing the course without talking to the doctor
Telling the doctor about side effects
121590.e: Anyone who stops antibiotics on their own, takes the wrong dose or later takes leftover tablets themselves exposes bacteria to the drug unnecessarily or insufficiently. This helps resistant germs survive.
121590.m: Take antibiotics exactly as the doctor prescribes.

121591.q: Which aminopenicillin is very often prescribed today, for example for middle ear infections?
121591.e: Amoxicillin is a penicillin with a wider range of action that is well absorbed from the gut. Ciprofloxacin, doxycycline and clarithromycin belong to other classes of antibiotics.
121591.m: Amoxicillin is a commonly used penicillin.

121592.q: What did Alexander Fleming observe in 1928 that led to the discovery of penicillin?
a: A mould stopped bacteria growing in a culture dish
121592.e: Fleming noticed that no bacteria grew around a mould of the genus Penicillium. The mould produced a substance that he called penicillin.

121593.q: Why was penicillin only used as a medicine more than ten years after its discovery?
a: It was difficult to make it pure and in large amounts
It was banned at the time
At first it only worked on plants
Nobody had recognised bacteria as germs
121593.e: Only around 1940 did Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in Oxford manage to purify penicillin and show its healing effect. For this they received the Nobel Prize with Fleming in 1945.
121593.m: Florey and Chain turned penicillin into a medicine.

121594.q: How does penicillin act on bacteria?
a: It blocks the building of the cell wall
It dissolves the cell membrane at once
121594.e: Penicillin blocks enzymes that cross-link the network of sugar chains and peptides in the cell wall. Growing bacteria therefore become unstable and burst.
121594.m: Penicillin disrupts the building of the bacterial cell wall.

121595.q: Which ring structure in the molecule is crucial for penicillin's effect?
121595.e: The strained four-membered beta-lactam ring binds to the enzymes that build the cell wall and blocks them. Cephalosporins also have this ring.
121595.m: Penicillins belong to the beta-lactam antibiotics.

121596.q: Against which bacteria does penicillin G mainly work?
121596.e: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick cell wall layer that is easy to reach. In gram-negative bacteria, an outer membrane protects the thin cell wall layer.
121596.m: Penicillin G works especially well against gram-positive germs.

121597.q: Why is penicillin G usually injected rather than swallowed?
a: It is destroyed by stomach acid
It does not dissolve in water
It is stored straight away by the liver
121597.e: Penicillin G is sensitive to acid and would be largely broken down in the stomach. Penicillin V is more stable in acid and can be taken as a tablet.

121598.q: Which unwanted reaction to penicillin is the best known?
121598.e: Penicillin allergies are among the most common drug allergies and range from skin rashes to anaphylactic shock. Discoloured teeth, by contrast, are typical of tetracyclines.

121599.q: What do staphylococci typically look like under the microscope?
a: Spheres in clusters like bunches of grapes
121599.e: Staphylé is the Greek word for a bunch of grapes. Spherical bacteria in chains, by contrast, are streptococci.
121599.m: Staphylococci lie together like bunches of grapes.

121600.q: Where does Staphylococcus aureus live in many healthy people without making them ill?
121600.e: Around 20 to 30 per cent of people carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nose, some of them permanently. It only becomes dangerous when it gets into the body, for example through wounds.
121600.m: Many healthy people carry staphylococci in their nose.

121601.q: Which measure is most important in hospital to prevent MRSA from being passed on?
a: Taking the temperature of all visitors
121601.e: MRSA is mainly carried from patient to patient on the hands of staff. Hand disinfection breaks this route most effectively.
121601.m: Hand disinfection stops MRSA from spreading.

121602.q: What does the “R” in the abbreviation MRSA stand for?
121602.e: MRSA means methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. These bacteria are not affected by methicillin and related antibiotics such as penicillins.
121602.m: MRSA is resistant to methicillin and related antibiotics.

121603.q: Why are MRSA infections harder to treat than ordinary staphylococcal infections?
a: Many common antibiotics no longer work
121603.e: The usual beta-lactam antibiotics fail against MRSA. Doctors have to switch to a few reserve drugs such as vancomycin, which can have more side effects.
121603.m: Many common antibiotics do not work against MRSA.

121604.q: What does decolonisation mean for MRSA carriers?
a: The bacteria are removed from the skin and mucous membranes
The person is moved to another country
The bacteria are grown in the laboratory
The person is given a vaccine against MRSA
121604.e: Nasal ointments and antiseptic washes, for example, are used for several days. The aim is that the person no longer carries the bacteria and passes them on.

121605.q: In which decade was MRSA first described, shortly after methicillin was introduced?
121605.e: Methicillin came onto the market in 1959, and resistant strains were already described in Great Britain in 1961. This shows how quickly bacteria adapt.
121605.m: MRSA appeared as early as the 1960s.

121606.e: Prions contain no genetic material but are proteins with an abnormal three-dimensional folding. This makes them fundamentally different from viruses and bacteria.
121606.m: Prions are disease-causing proteins without genetic material.

121607.q: Who coined the term prion and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1997?
121607.e: In 1982 the American Stanley Prusiner described prions as protein-like infectious particles. His theory was controversial for a long time.

121608.q: Which animal disease, which also concerned Switzerland in the 1990s, is caused by prions?
121608.e: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, known as mad cow disease, also occurred in Swiss cattle. The other diseases are caused by viruses.
121608.m: BSE is a prion disease of cattle.

121609.q: Which human disease is caused by prions?
121609.e: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease quickly destroys nerve tissue in the brain and is fatal. One variant has been linked to eating beef contaminated with BSE.
121609.m: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease.

121610.q: How do prions multiply in the body?
a: They make normal proteins fold wrongly too
They build their genetic material into the DNA
They form spores in the nerve cells
121610.e: A misfolded prion protein acts like a template and changes the shape of healthy proteins. This creates a chain reaction, and the faulty proteins build up as deposits.
121610.m: Prions multiply by refolding healthy proteins.

121611.q: Why do surgical instruments need special treatment if prions are suspected?
a: Prions survive many usual sterilisation methods
121611.e: Prions are very resistant to heat, radiation and many disinfectants. That is why especially strict cleaning rules apply to them.

121612.q: What is the prion disease of sheep and goats called?
121612.e: Scrapie has been known since the 18th century; sick animals often rub themselves against fences. Distemper, foot rot and mange have other causes.
121612.m: Scrapie is the prion disease of sheep.

121613.q: In which country did the prion disease kuru occur?
121613.e: Kuru affected the Fore people in the highlands of Papua New Guinea. It was passed on through ritual funeral customs and disappeared after these were given up.
121613.m: Kuru was a prion disease in Papua New Guinea.

121614.q: Which enzyme in retroviruses copies RNA into DNA?
121614.e: Reverse transcriptase reverses the usual flow of information from DNA to RNA. This is also where the name retrovirus comes from.
121614.m: Retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA.

121615.q: Which is the best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill?
121615.e: The human immunodeficiency virus is a retrovirus and, if untreated, can lead to the disease AIDS. Flu, measles and hepatitis A viruses are not retroviruses.
121615.m: HIV is one of the retroviruses.

121616.q: Which immune cells does HIV mainly attack?
121616.e: HIV docks onto the surface protein CD4, which is carried mainly by T helper cells. If these cells fail, the whole immune defence is weakened.
121616.m: HIV mainly destroys T helper cells.

121617.q: What is the DNA of a retrovirus called once it is built into the host cell's genome?
121617.e: The provirus stays permanently in the cell's genome and is copied with every division. That is why an HIV infection cannot yet be cured completely.
121617.m: Built-in retrovirus DNA is called a provirus.

121618.q: Which enzyme of a retrovirus builds the newly made viral DNA into the host genome?
121618.e: Integrase cuts open the host DNA and inserts the viral DNA. Integrase inhibitors are an important part of HIV treatment today.
121618.m: Integrase builds viral DNA into the genome.

121619.q: Why was the discovery of reverse transcriptase around 1970 so important?
a: It showed that genetic information can also flow from RNA to DNA
It showed that viruses have no genetic information
It proved that DNA is made of proteins
It led directly to a cure for AIDS
121619.e: People had assumed that information only flows from DNA to RNA. But retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA. The discoverers received the Nobel Prize in 1975.
121619.m: Retroviruses reverse the flow of information.

121620.q: What kind of genetic material do retroviruses carry in the virus particle?
121620.e: Each retrovirus particle contains two copies of single-stranded RNA. Only in the host cell is it turned into double-stranded DNA.
121620.m: Retroviruses carry their genetic material as RNA.

121621.q: What are endogenous retroviruses in the human genome?
a: Remains of old virus infections passed down for generations
Active viruses that make every person ill
Bacteria living in the cell nucleus
Genes that only appear during illness
121621.e: Millions of years ago, retroviruses built their DNA into the germ cells of our ancestors. These traces have been inherited ever since and are mostly inactive.
121621.m: Our genome contains many remains of old retroviruses.

121622.q: What is typical of a parasite?
a: It lives at the expense of a host
It lives only on dead material
121622.e: A parasite takes nutrients from its host and harms it, but usually does not kill it straight away. When both partners benefit, it is called symbiosis.
121622.m: A parasite lives at the expense of its host.

121623.q: Which of these organisms is an ectoparasite?
121623.e: Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host's body, like the tick on the skin. Tapeworm, roundworm and liver fluke live inside the body and are endoparasites.
121623.m: Ectoparasites live on the outside of their host.

121624.q: What is the host called in which a parasite reaches its adult stage?
121624.e: In the definitive host, the parasite becomes adult and reproduces. Only larval or young stages live in the intermediate host.
121624.m: A parasite becomes adult in the definitive host.

121625.q: Which animals are the typical intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm?
121625.e: Mice take in the worm eggs, and larvae grow in their liver. When a fox eats the mouse, the cycle is complete; humans can be infected as accidental hosts.
121625.m: Mice are the intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm.

121626.q: What is a relationship called in which one partner benefits and the other neither benefits nor is harmed?
121626.e: In commensalism, an animal might for example use another's food scraps without harming it. In parasitism, by contrast, the host is harmed.
121626.m: Commensals help themselves without harming their partner.

121627.q: Which native bird is a well-known brood parasite?
121627.e: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in other birds' nests. The host birds raise the cuckoo chick, often at the expense of their own young.
121627.m: The cuckoo has its young raised by other birds.

121628.q: Which bacterial disease is most often passed on by ticks in Switzerland?
121628.e: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria of the genus Borrelia and can be treated with antibiotics. There is a vaccine against TBE, which is also passed on by ticks but is caused by a virus.
121628.m: In Switzerland, ticks mainly pass on Lyme disease.

121629.q: Which animal is the definitive host of the parasite Toxoplasma gondii?
121629.e: Only in cats and other felines can Toxoplasma complete its full life cycle. Mice and also humans are intermediate hosts.
121629.m: Cats are the definitive hosts of Toxoplasma.

121630.q: Which mosquitoes pass the malaria parasites on to humans?
121630.e: Only females of the genus Anopheles pass on plasmodia when they suck blood. The tiger mosquito passes on other diseases, such as dengue.
121630.m: Malaria is spread by Anopheles mosquitoes.

121631.q: To which group of disease-causing organisms do plasmodia belong?
121631.e: Plasmodia are single-celled organisms with a nucleus, in other words eukaryotes. That is why antibiotics against bacteria do not help against malaria.
121631.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled organisms.

121632.q: Which species of Plasmodium causes the most dangerous form of malaria?
121632.e: Plasmodium falciparum causes falciparum malaria, which is often fatal if untreated. Infected blood cells stick together in small vessels, for example in the brain.
121632.m: Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous malaria parasite.

121633.q: Which blood cells do plasmodia attack in the human body?
121633.e: The parasites multiply in the red blood cells and make them burst. Many cells bursting at the same time leads to bouts of fever.
121633.m: Plasmodia multiply in red blood cells.

121634.q: Which organ do plasmodia travel to first after a mosquito bite?
121634.e: The parasites first multiply unnoticed in liver cells. Only after that do they get into the blood and cause the signs of illness.
121634.m: Plasmodia first multiply in the liver.

121635.q: For discovering which malaria drug did the Chinese researcher Tu Youyou receive the Nobel Prize in 2015?
121635.e: Tu Youyou obtained artemisinin from sweet wormwood, a plant used in traditional Chinese medicine. Combination therapies with artemisinin are standard today against falciparum malaria.
121635.m: Artemisinin is an important malaria drug from a plant.

121636.q: Which inherited blood disease, in its mild form with only one copy of the gene, partly protects against malaria?
121636.e: Carriers with one copy of the sickle cell gene are less likely to become seriously ill with falciparum malaria. That is why the gene is common in the malaria regions of Africa.
121636.m: The sickle cell gene gives some protection against malaria.

121637.q: What best protects travellers in malaria regions from infection?
a: Protection against mosquitoes and, depending on the region, preventive medicines
Having no contact with sick people
A single vaccination before the trip
121637.e: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites, not by water or direct contact. Mosquito nets, long clothing and insect repellent help, and in some regions tablets as well.
121637.m: Protection against mosquitoes is the main defence against malaria.

a: An infection caught in hospital or a care home
An infection that only affects animals
121638.e: Nosocomial comes from the Greek nosokomeion, hospital. It means infections that arise in connection with a stay or treatment in a healthcare facility.

121639.q: From when after admission to hospital is an infection usually considered nosocomial?
a: At the earliest about 48 hours after admission
121639.e: If an infection only appears after about 48 hours and was not present or incubating on admission, it is put down to the hospital. Earlier infections were usually brought in from home.
121639.m: After about 48 hours in hospital, a new infection counts as nosocomial.

121640.q: Which doctor reduced childbed fever in Vienna in 1847 through handwashing with chlorinated lime?
121640.e: Semmelweis realised that doctors were carrying disease material from corpses to patients. With a chlorinated lime solution, the death rate on his ward fell sharply.
121640.m: Ignaz Semmelweis is considered a pioneer of hand hygiene.

121641.q: Which medical device especially increases the risk of a urinary tract infection in hospital?
121641.e: Bacteria can get directly into the bladder through the catheter tube. That is why a urinary catheter should only stay in for as long as necessary.
121641.m: Urinary catheters encourage urinary tract infections.

121642.q: What is the Swiss national centre for infection prevention called, which records hospital infections?
121642.e: Swissnoso carries out surveillance of wound infections after operations and runs infection prevention programmes. Swissmedic, by contrast, is the authority for medicines.
121642.m: Swissnoso deals with hospital infections in Switzerland.

121643.q: According to the WHO, for how long should hands be rubbed with an alcohol-based disinfectant?
121643.e: The WHO recommends rubbing in the product for 20 to 30 seconds until the hands are dry. In this way every part of the hands is reached.
121643.m: Hand disinfection takes about half a minute.

121644.q: How many moments for hand hygiene does the WHO describe for healthcare staff?
121644.e: The moments are: before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings.
121644.m: The WHO names five moments for hand hygiene.

121645.q: What is the federal strategy for monitoring, preventing and fighting hospital infections called?
121645.e: The Federal Council adopted the NOSO strategy in 2016. It aims to reduce infections in hospitals and care homes in Switzerland.
121645.m: The NOSO strategy fights hospital infections in Switzerland.

121646.q: Why are patients in intensive care especially at risk of hospital infections?
a: They often have catheters, tubes and a weakened immune system
They always lie in single rooms
121646.e: Breathing tubes and venous catheters open direct routes into the body for germs. In addition, the defences of seriously ill people are often weakened.
121646.m: Intensive care patients have a high risk of infection.

121647.q: According to today's definition, what is sepsis?
a: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a misdirected response to an infection
Harmless reddening of the skin after an insect bite
121647.e: Since the Sepsis-3 definition of 2016, the focus is not on the infection itself but on the excessive and harmful reaction of the body. It can make organs such as the kidneys, lungs or circulation fail.
121647.m: In sepsis, the defence reaction damages the body's own organs.

121648.q: Which everyday expression is often used for sepsis?
121648.e: The term blood poisoning is widespread but inaccurate, as there is no poison in the strict sense. Lockjaw is an everyday name for tetanus.
121648.m: In everyday language, sepsis is called blood poisoning.

121649.q: Which signs during an infection can point to the start of sepsis?
121649.e: If a sick person breathes noticeably fast, seems confused or has low blood pressure, sepsis may be present. Then medical help is needed immediately.
121649.m: Fast breathing and confusion during an infection are warning signs.

121650.q: What is typical of septic shock?
a: A drop in blood pressure that needs circulation-supporting drugs despite fluids
High fever with no other symptoms
121650.e: In septic shock, the circulation is so badly disturbed that vasopressors are needed despite drips. The death rate is then especially high.
121650.m: Septic shock is the most severe form of sepsis.

121651.q: According to guidelines, within what time should antibiotics be given if septic shock is suspected?
a: Only after all lab results are in
121651.e: With every hour of delay, the risk of death rises considerably. That is why international guidelines recommend giving antibiotics within the first hour if possible.

121652.q: According to a large study in “The Lancet”, roughly how many deaths worldwide in 2017 were due to sepsis?
121652.e: The study estimated around 49 million cases of sepsis and about 11 million deaths for 2017. That was around one fifth of all deaths worldwide.
121652.m: Sepsis is one of the most common causes of death worldwide.

121653.q: Which people have an especially high risk of developing sepsis?
a: Babies, older people and people with weak immune systems
121653.e: In very young, old or immunocompromised people, the defence system is less able to contain an infection. Sepsis is therefore more common in them.
121653.m: Very young, old and immunocompromised people are especially at risk.

121654.q: Which blood value is measured in sepsis as a sign that the tissues are not getting enough oxygen?
121654.e: When cells lack oxygen, they get energy anaerobically and produce lactate. A raised lactate level shows a dangerous circulatory disorder.
121654.m: A high lactate level warns of a lack of oxygen in the tissues.

121655.q: If sepsis is suspected, what should be taken if possible before the first dose of antibiotics?
a: A saliva sample for a genetic test
121655.e: In blood cultures, the germs can be grown and tested for resistance. After antibiotics have been given, they often no longer grow, so the blood is taken beforehand.
121655.m: Blood cultures help to find the germ causing sepsis.

121656.q: In which year did the WHO declare the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic?
121656.e: On 11 March 2020, the WHO classified the worldwide spread of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 as a pandemic. The first cases had appeared in China at the end of 2019.
121656.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020.

121657.q: On which day did the WHO constitution come into force in 1948, a day now marked as World Health Day?
121657.e: The WHO constitution came into force on 7 April 1948. Since then, World Health Day has been held every year on this day with a focus theme.
121657.m: World Health Day is on 7 April.

121658.q: Which list has the WHO published regularly since 1977 as a guide for healthcare?
a: The Model List of Essential Medicines
The list of World Heritage Sites
The Red List of Threatened Species
The list of banned doping substances
121658.e: The model list names medicines that are important for basic healthcare in every country. It is revised about every two years.
121658.m: The WHO keeps a list of essential medicines.

121659.q: Who is Director-General of the WHO (as of 2026)?
121659.e: The Ethiopian Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has led the WHO since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Margaret Chan was his predecessor, and António Guterres is UN Secretary-General.
121659.m: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus leads the WHO.

121660.q: What is the highest decision-making body of the WHO, in which all member states are represented, called?
121660.e: The World Health Assembly meets every year in Geneva and sets the WHO's policy and budget. The Security Council is a body of the UN.
121660.m: The World Health Assembly is the highest body of the WHO.

121661.q: What status does the WHO have in the United Nations system?
a: It is a specialised agency of the UN
It is an authority of the European Union
121661.e: The WHO is a legally independent specialised agency of the United Nations with its own member states. It coordinates international health work.
121661.m: The WHO belongs to the UN as a specialised agency.

121662.q: Why does the WHO call for antibiotics to be used only in a targeted and sparing way?
a: So that fewer resistant bacteria develop
Because antibiotics only work in winter
Because there are hardly any antibiotics left worldwide
121662.e: Every use of antibiotics favours bacteria that are not affected by them. If resistance becomes more common, the medicines no longer work for dangerous infections.
121662.m: Using antibiotics sparingly slows down resistance.

121663.q: How does the WHO constitution define health?
a: As a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
As simply the absence of illness
As the ability to work fully
As the result of regular visits to the doctor
121663.e: The definition in the constitution stresses that health is more than the absence of disease or infirmity. It includes mental and social well-being.
121663.m: For the WHO, health is more than the absence of illness.

121664.q: Light with a wavelength of 600 nm falls on a double slit with a slit separation of 0.3 mm. How far apart are neighbouring bright fringes on a screen 2 m away?
121664.e: For small angles, fringe spacing equals wavelength times screen distance divided by slit separation. So 600 nm · 2 m / 0.3 mm = 0.004 m = 4 mm.
121664.m: The fringe spacing grows with wavelength and screen distance.

121665.q: What path difference between the two partial waves leads to a bright fringe with a double slit?
a: An odd multiple of half the wavelength
Exactly a quarter of the wavelength
121665.e: With a path difference of k times lambda, crest meets crest and the waves reinforce each other. With an offset of half a wavelength, on the other hand, they cancel out.
121665.m: Bright fringes form when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.

121666.q: Which property of light does the fringe pattern behind a double slit prove?
121666.e: Alternating bright and dark fringes can only come from interference, the overlapping of waves. Pure particles would produce two bright stripes behind the slits.
121666.m: The interference pattern shows that light behaves like a wave.

121667.q: What do you observe if you send electrons through a double slit one at a time?
a: After many electrons, an interference pattern forms
Each electron splits into two halves
121667.e: Each electron lands at a single point, but the hits are distributed according to an interference pattern. This is a key example of wave-particle duality.
121667.m: Even single electrons show wave behaviour.
